title: When expanding volume during mount make sure that node_stage is always set
description:
### What happened?

When a pod is quickly deleted and re-created on a node, it may not be necessary to unstage the volume and in which case only node-publish is called for the volume.

When this happens - stage_path won't be set for `NodeExpandVolume` RPC call because volume was *not* staged even though, volume does have `NODE_STAGE_UNSTAGE` capability. 

We should try and fix this behaviour so that - node_stage_path is always set in `NodeExpandVolume` RPC call. 

### What did you expect to happen?

We should try and fix this behaviour so that - node_stage_path is always set in `NodeExpandVolume` RPC call. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Quickly delete and recreate a pod

title: structured-merge-diff supports only  'set' type for associative list
description:
### What happened?

kube-apiserver has has this kind of entries in log
```
E0126 00:39:45.253562       1 fieldmanager.go:210] "[SHOULD NOT HAPPEN] failed to update managedFields" err="failed to convert new object (default/test-inline-claim; /v1, Kind=Pod) to smd typed: .spec.containers[name=\"with-resource\"].resources.claims: element 0: associative list without keys has an element that's a map type" VersionKind="/, Kind=" namespace="default" name="test-inline-claim"
E0126 00:39:46.700727       1 fieldmanager.go:210] "[SHOULD NOT HAPPEN] failed to update managedFields" err="failed to convert new object (default/test-inline-claim-resource; resource.k8s.io/v1alpha1, Kind=ResourceClaim) to smd typed: .status.reservedFor: element 0: associative list without keys has an element that's a map type" VersionKind="/, Kind=" namespace="default" name="test-inline-claim-resource"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected those lines not to appear in kube-apiserver logs, and structured-merge-diff to support map types, like the comment says at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/vendor/sigs.k8s.io/structured-merge-diff/v4/typed/helpers.go#L233

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I ran into it during Dynamic Resource Allocation usage. It requires a either a CRI-O v1.23, or containerd 1.7+ (has to be built from git at the moment); the cluster has to be initialized "DynamicResourceAllocation" feature-gate and alpha apis enabled, for instance with this config for kubeadm :
<details>

```YAML
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta3
kind: ClusterConfiguration
kubernetesVersion: v1.26.0
imageRepository: registry.local
apiServer:
  extraArgs:
    feature-gates: "DynamicResourceAllocation=true"
    runtime-config: "api/alpha=true"
controllerManager:
  extraArgs:
    feature-gates: "DynamicResourceAllocation=true"
scheduler:
  extraArgs:
    "feature-gates": "DynamicResourceAllocation=true"
---
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
featureGates:
  DynamicResourceAllocation: true
---
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta3
kind: InitConfiguration
nodeRegistration:
  criSocket: "unix:///var/run/crio/crio.sock"
---
apiVersion: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: KubeProxyConfiguration
featureGates:
  DynamicResourceAllocation: true
```

</details>

Deploy pod with inline resource-claim for instance the following (the issue will appear immediately even though the resource-claim is malformed. Proper resource claim would require resource-driver to be deployed, but it's not necessary for issue to be manifested):
<details>

```YAML
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  name: test-inline-claim-template
  namespace: default
spec:
  metadata:
    labels:
      app: inline-resource
  spec:
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-inline-claim
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: with-resource
    image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/busybox:1.29-2
    command: ["sh", "-c", "ls -la /dev/dri/ && sleep 30"]
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: resource
  resourceClaims:
  - name: resource
    source:
      resourceClaimTemplateName: test-inline-claim-template
```

</details>

### Anything else we need to know?

The code where the issue happens appears to be at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/vendor/sigs.k8s.io/structured-merge-diff/v4/typed/helpers.go#L233

title: Deletecollection failing after 34 seconds
description:
### What happened?

In a cluster with large enough numbers of objects, it seems to be impossible to clean them up with `deletecollection`.  Because the deletecollection is failing while listing the objects from etcd.  The failure happens after exactly 34 seconds, due to the 34-second max timeout introduced in PR #96901 (cc @tkashem for insight on that PR).


### What did you expect to happen?

The deletecollection should be able to run for longer, and succeed.

I recognise that there are still risks of the API server using too much RAM, if deleting a very large collection due to issue #90743.  But, until _that_ issue is fixed, it seems like allowing `deletecollection` to run for longer might be a good idea.  As far as I can tell, the 34 second timeout does not apply to normal LIST calls, so on that basis I feel it should not apply to the giant unchunked LIST call that happens inside `deletecollection`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a few hundred thousand objects of some particular type.  (Argo workflowtaskresults happen to be the type I'm looking at while I write this)
2. Call deletecollection. (Optionally passing some kind of fieldSelector, but I don't think that's essential)
3. Observe that a 504 failure code is logged in kube-audit logs, and that a log entry similar to this is logged by the API Server `"List etcd3" key:<some key>,...,limit:0 ... (total time: 34000ms)`  (In practice, the total time may be a little over 34000 ms).
4. As far as I can tell, the delete collection really has failed at this point.  I notice that PR #96901 says that, in general, "The go-routine can keep running, while the timeout logic will return a timeout to the client" but I don't _think_ that's what's happening here.  I think that, because the 34 sec timeout is used in the context of the etcd call, the etcd list call really does fail, and so the code never proceeds to actually deleting anything.


### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

1.22

AKS

comments.text:
@JohnRusk  the `34s` deadline has been in effect before PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/96901 was introduced

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9787f46bbf05349ca53cd8b04cd2f7a76771646a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/delete.go#L181-L184

If we remove this `34s` deadline from here, then the deletecollection request will have at most `60s` to complete (default).  
The list call that is failing in your case, is a direct call to the storage, right? 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9787f46bbf05349ca53cd8b04cd2f7a76771646a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L1142-L1145

on the contrary, we don't enforce the `34s` timeout for LIST 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9787f46bbf05349ca53cd8b04cd2f7a76771646a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/get.go#L166

thinking out loud here:
- I don't know if it makes sense to remove the `34s` from  `DELETECOLLECTION`
- should we allow timeout for DELETECOLLECTION to exceed `60s`?

@deads2k @wojtek-t thoughts?

>The list call that is failing in your case, is a direct call to the storage, right?

It reads from etcd, not from API Server Cache.  Is that what you were asking @tkashem?

Looking at the bigger picture,  I think your question about 60s timeout is a good one. Especially in the context of this: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/90743. In particular, changing the timeouts won't solve all of the problems with DELETECOLLECTION.  My assumption, when logging this issue, is that it might be a quick way to solve just _some_ of them.

> I don't know if it makes sense to remove the 34s from DELETECOLLECTION

I think we should remove this - it's effectively a regression that we introduced with the PR.

> should we allow timeout for DELETECOLLECTION to exceed 60s?

That's a good question, and I'm not entirely sure. Maybe we should, but I would do that separately.

In the meantime, I would much more prefer to switch the DeleteCollection implementation to internally use pagination, as it would allow us to
1) not block on full list (and as a result make some progress)
2) would be some preparation towards potentially exposing a Limit option in the API...

I suggest the following:

1. @tkashem - can you please take care of reverting the 34s timeout for DeleteCollection calls?
2. Once this is done, let's close this issue and continue operating on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/90743
@wojtek-t sounds good, thanks!

title: CR conversion needs to protect against a converter that mutates the input list
description:
### What happened?

If a CR converter is wired in and it modifies the input list, the delegating CR converter does not protect against this.

### What did you expect to happen?

title: kube-apiserver using unregistered and unusual label
description:
### What happened?

The code at
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86f3fa94f1b75da275a8040e4155840a7b473dc1/pkg/controlplane/instance.go#L126 specifies a ~annotation~ label that API servers set on Leases (each API server registers its own lease).

https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/#api-server-identity is likely to document this once v1.26 is released; the alpha for API server identity didn't get documented.

Here's the problems:
- as a project, we use `kubernetes.io` as the domain for labels and annotations - see https://k8s.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/
  - there are a couple of exceptions in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/audit-annotations/, FWIW
- if we document and register this `k8s.io/component` label, people may well confuse it with https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#app-kubernetes-io-component and use the wrong thing

### What did you expect to happen?

I guess ideally we'd have proposed and then been able to review docs for this when it went alpha, and in that alternative history the discrepancy would have been much more obvious, and it could have been fixed earlier.

I think we should fix it so that we follow the convention of nearly every other annotation used in Kubernetes code.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Look at the source code. Any text editor would work.

### Anything else we need to know?

comments.text: ping @andrewsykim @lavalamp

> https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#app-kubernetes-io-component

I think that's already confusing, why would there be an official k8s label about an end-user application component?

Anyway, that ship has sailed, I suggest we use `internal.kubernetes.io/component` instead
My suggestion would be `control-plane.kubernetes.io/component` (explicitly distancing the control plane from node-level components like `kube-proxy`). `internal.kubernetes.io/component` is good too.

> I think that's already confusing, why would there be an official k8s label about an end-user application component?

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/common-labels/#labels is our explanation for this.

If we feel strongly about the name change, I propose we update it now and backport for v1.26.1? I _think_ this should be fine to do because:
1) The label selector is strictly used internally by the gc controller that runs in kube-apiserver, so it would be updated in lockstep to check the new label. In the worse case when a cluster upgrades from v1.26.0 -> v1.26.1, there will be N (1-5) leases that will never be garbage collected because old leases have labels that the new gc controller is not selecting against. 
2) v1.26 is the first version where this is enabled by default, so we shouldn't anticipate many existing consumers of the lease or use of that label. In the worse case we end up with a handful of leases that aren't garbage collected like in 1).
3) No one is _really_ going to use v1.26.0 :)

If we _really_ care about the v1.26.0 -> v1.26.1 corner case, we can update GC controller to garbage collect leases with both labels `k8s.io/component=kube-apiserver` and `internal.kubernetes.io/component`

> If we _really_ care about the v1.26.0 -> v1.26.1 corner case, we can update GC controller to garbage collect leases with both labels `k8s.io/component=kube-apiserver` and `internal.kubernetes.io/component`

When other (usually external) projects or components aren't using labels or annotations the recommended way, I usually recommend handling the old deprecated key for a while (or even indefinitely), but mentioning the fixed key in documentation.

So, that sounds good. I don't feel that a fix is urgent, but I do recommend against leaving it this way all the way to v1.27.0

Summarizing discussion we had on this in SIG API Machinery today:
* We're going to move the identity lease controller and GC controller to generic apiserver (as part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114240), with optional flags to set the lease namespace and component label value. These will always be configured in kube-apiserver in the `kube-system` namespace, but off by default for any aggregated apiservers pulling in generic apiserver.
* The label key / value for `kube-apiserver` will change to something that follows documented best practices, which _should_ be safe as long as GC controller is updated to watch both the old and new labels until v1.28.
* There should be a Role defined to manged identities that any aggregated apiserver can bind to for their own system namespaces

Opened [REDACTED] for just the label rename -- still need to do further testing but I believe it should be safe to do as long as we garbage collect leases for both the old and new label for 1 release.

title: windows cpu maximum incorrect with more than one processor group
description:
### What happened?

When submitting a windows pod using resource limits on a node with more than one processor group, the specified `CpuMaximum` count is incorrect due to the usage of `runtime.NumCPU()` which does not take processor groups into account.

For example:
- node with 96 cores
- cpu limit 94
- `runtime.NumCPU()` returns `48`

This results in a CPU maximum of 10000 since the range is from [1, 10000]:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows.go#L82..L91

```go
	limit := int64(94 * 1000)
	numCPU := 48
	fmt.Println(((10000 * limit) / int64(numCPU) / 1000))


```

Our initial goal for this was to limit a process to not use all available CPU and therefore render the node uncontrollable. 

### What did you expect to happen?

A CPU maximum of `9791` instead of `10000` for that specific case. For the calculation, it should use the CPU count for all available processor groups instead of just the current one. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Launch a node with a lot of CPUs, for example [a Azure Standard_D96a_v4](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/dav4-dasv4-series) and schedule the following pod on it:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: debug-windows
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - args:
    - ping /t 127.0.0.1
    command:
    - cmd
    - /c
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/windows/nanoserver:1809
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    name: main
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "94"
        memory: 300Gi
      requests:
        cpu: "90"
        memory: 200Gi
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/os: windows
```

Then SSH into the node and inspect the running container using `crictl.exe inspect <id>`. The `cpu_maximum` value will be set to 10000. 

### Anything else we need to know?

[tklauser/numcpus](https://github.com/tklauser/numcpus) (which just uses [`windows.GetActiveProcessorCount()`](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sys/windows#GetActiveProcessorCount)) is able to correctly find out the number of CPUs available to a system. Using `golang.org/x/sys/windows` for calculation or incorporating that code might solve this issue.

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25", GitVersion:"v1.25.2", GitCommit:"5835544ca568b757a8ecae5c153f317e5736700e", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-09-21T14:25:45Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.1", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```

title: Ephemeral container fails to be created for Static Pod
description:
### What happened?

I created an ephemeral container for a Static Pod using the `kubectl debug` command. The command succeed.

```console
❯ kubectl debug --image=busybox --share-processes=true --target=kube-apiserver -n kube-system kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane -- sleep infinity
Targeting container "kube-apiserver". If you don't see processes from this container it may be because the container runtime doesn't support this feature.
Defaulting debug container name to debugger-vgkn4.
```



The API server accepted the ephemeral container:
```console
❯ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane --output=jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers}'
[{"command":["sleep","infinity"],"image":"busybox","imagePullPolicy":"Always","name":"debugger-vgkn4","resources":{},"targetContainerName":"kube-apiserver","terminationMessagePath":"/dev/termination-log","terminationMessagePolicy":"File"}]
```

However, the container is not created.

Its status is also not available:

```console
❯ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane --output=jsonpath='{.status.ephemeralContainerStatuses}'

```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these:

(a) the API server rejects the request to create an ephemeral container for a Static Pod
(b) kubelet creates the ephemeral container, and update the Static Pod's status sub-resource

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Using a recent version of [docker engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/), [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/)  v0.17 or newer, and [kubectl](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/#kubectl) v1.25.0 or newer, create a cluster and create an ephemeral container running `sleep infinity`. Since the ephemeral container is not running, the output of `grep` is 0. 

```
kind create cluster
kubectl debug --image=busybox --share-processes=true --target=kube-apiserver -n kube-system kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane -- sleep infinity
docker exec -it kind-control-plane ps -axw | grep --count "sleep infinity"
```


### Anything else we need to know?

The [Ephemeral Containers KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/277-ephemeral-containers/README.md) does not address Static Pods.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

title: Kubectl restmapping cache causes inconsistent behaviour in case of resource name conflict
description:
### What happened?

I deployed a CRD (`teleportroles`) with the shortnames `role` and `roles`, conflicting with `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`.

Initially `kubectl get role` and `kubectl get roles` were both returnning `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

I ran `kubectl get teleportrole`.

Now, `kubectl get role` return my CRs instead of `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

However `kubectl get roles` continues to return `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1` resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect kubectl's behaviour to be consistent. The outcome of `kubectl get X` should not depend on the order the APIs were discovered and cached. I also expect exact names to be preferred over shortnames.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a freshly kubectl context (not one you already used and might have cached RESTMappings):
- create a CRD with a shortname conflicting with another resource, `role` for example
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the kube rbac resources are properly returned
- run `kubectl get yourcrd` once
- run `kubectl get role -n kube-sytem` (because there are roles by default there) and `kubectl get roles -n kube-system`
- observe the `kubectl get role` no longer returns the kubernetes roles, but `kubectl get roles` still does. 

### Anything else we need to know?

During initial resolution, [exact name matches are preferred](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/58861). It seems this property is not true anymore when doing cache lookups. When cache was populated by `kubectl get teleportroles`, it overrode the mapping `role` -> `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`

I believe this is the same issue as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/59812

```console
$ kubectl version
```

comments.text: This looks like a duplicate of these https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102378, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/108573

If I understand correctly those two issues are feature requests to warn users in case of conflict, I would not consider them duplicates of this one.

Here, the issue is not the conflict, but kubectl not consistently choosing the same resource (and also not prioritizing extact name matches over shortnames as it should). The returned  resources depend on the last cached RESTmapping, which depends on the order the commands are run.

The following snippets currently have very different behaviours:
```bash
kubectl get role
kubectl get teleportrole
kubectl delete role my-role  # deletes a teleportrole
```

```bash
kubectl get role
kubectl delete role my-role  # deletes a rbac role
```

This can be harmful in CI environments when each job has a fresh RESTMapping cache.

Note: I'm talking about kubectl but the issue lives in go-client caching mechanism. I guess this not only affects filesystem cache but also memory cache, which means operators or other tools leveraging go-client could also face the same inconsistencies when discovering apis.
I'm going to investigate this issue.

title: Change in semantics for the device plugin registration process
description:
### What happened?

The following refactoring of the kubelet's devicemanager was done as part of the 1.25 release: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/db88676c20629354d8eeb4b7014ae7884481ffca

As part of this, a change in semantics was (unintentionally) introduced which is breaking at least one 3rd party plugin. The logic required to go back to the old semantics is fairly straight forward. However, it's not obvious that we should actually go back to the old semantics because (at least in my opinion) the new semantics are actually more correct.

Previously, the kubelet's devicemanager would do the following upon receiving a plugin registration request:
1. Register the plugin
2. Launch a go-routine to connect to the gRPC service being served by the plugin (with a timeout of 10s)
3. Return

This gave the plugin the opportunity to first register itself with the kubelet and then (within a 10s time window) start its gRPC server.

The new semantics are similar, except that no go-routine is launched to connect to the gRPC service. The connection is attempted synchronously. This means that the plugin must now start serving its gRPC server *before* registering itself with the kubelet. Otherwise the registration call will fail.

As mentioned before, this change was not necessarily intentional, but it's also not clear if it should be reverted. It brings the device plugin's custom registration process more in line with the kubelet's standard registration process and the order is actually a bit more intuitive. Why bother registering if you aren't able to start serving your API?

The first plugin to report this problem was the KubeVirt plugin and a discussion of the issue can be found here:
https://groups.google.com/g/kubevirt-dev/c/HE2lVvsLd3Y

The question now is -- should we revert the kubelet code to the old semantics to avoid breaking plugins that rely on this (somewhat awkward) ordering. Or do we leave the new semantics in place and send out an announcement of this (potentially) breaking change?

One thing to keep in mind -- if we go with the second option (i.e. keep the new semantics and force plugins to update), the updated plugins will continue to work on older versions of kubernetes since the ordering now implied in the new semantics has always been correct.

### What did you expect to happen?

Plugins relying on the old semantics would continue to work on kubernetes 1.25

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a plugin that:
1. Registers itself with the kubelet
2. Only then starts to server the plugin API via a gRPC server

### Anything else we need to know?

I'm interested in the fact that the e2e tests didn't seem to catch this issue. Besides improving our coverage, which rarely hurts, I tend to believe that one of the key factors is that we use sample-device-plugin in the e2e tests, which is understandably updated in lockstep with the core k/k code. I wonder how we can improve in this area, perhaps using _also_ a known set of 3rd party device plugins as part as e2e testing?

The plugin used in the e2e tests uses the standard kubelet plugin registration method (i.e. the one that relies on the plugin dropping a socket file in a well known location to trigger the registration), not the custom / legacy one used by the KubeVirt (and potentially many other) plugins.

TL;DR: if the broken plugins were doing legitimate things (-> were not themselves buggy) we should fix the kube side, even if the new process really seems better.

My initial though is this is the right change done the wrong way. The new registration process should be enabled - for all the good reason @klueska listed - but we should have better docs and a transition process (e.g. deprecating the old process, supporting both for a little while... details to be figured out).

Now: the device manager is stil a [beta feature in 1.25](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.25.0/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L247) (!!!!!!) so we have some slack space, but still this change breaks some device plugins which, AFAIK, were not buggy in the area of the registration process (is my understanding right?). This is not ok for a beta feature AFAIK, and not great in general.

I reserve myself to review in deeper detail and come back, but IMO we should treat this like a bug and revert the change, *then* work towards the better registration process.

> but still this change breaks some device plugins which, AFAIK, were not buggy in the area of the registration process (is my understanding right?)

1. revert it for now
2. add a deprecation message under device manager, that will inform plugins owners to update their device plugins(and probably we also should have updated documentation that will explain the correct way to initialize now the device plugin)
3. revert the revert after one or two releases :)

> As part of this, a change in semantics was (unintentionally) introduced which is breaking at least one 3rd party plugin. The logic required to go back to the old semantics is fairly straight forward. However, it's not obvious that we should actually go back to the old semantics because (at least in my opinion) the new semantics are actually more correct.

I tend to agree that the new semantics (starting gRPC server before registration) are more intuitive and correct.
> The question now is -- should we revert the kubelet code to the old semantics to avoid breaking plugins that rely on this (somewhat awkward) ordering. Or do we leave the new semantics in place and send out an announcement of this (potentially) breaking change?

Based the following points, I am inclining towards the latter (sticking to the new semantics and updating device plugins impacted by this change):

- a plugin once updated would continue to work on older versions of Kubernetes

Reverting the change seems like a step back when we can handle this by sending out communication to highlight the potential issue and capturing explicitly in the documentation that "a device plugin **must** start serving gRPC server before registering itself".
I created a small docs [REDACTED] to update the documentation (which can be used if there is consensus to proceed in this direction).

So @mythi and @swatisehgal pointed out that the correct ordering was already documented. Then the basic assumption in my previous https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/112395#issuecomment-1246475947 is void. I'll have a deeper review myself ASAP, but if this is the case, then retroactively fixing the docs and sending a late announcement seems indeed the best approach, and reverting the changes turns from "overkill" to "actually wrong". I'll update ASAP.

Then yes, my initial reaction is overtuned. title: client-go's InClusterConfig does not implement documented API discovery heuristics
description:
### What happened?

client-go uses `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` to discover the API service address:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/67bde9a1023d1805e33d698b28aa6fad991dfb39/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/config.go#L507-L541 

This at odds with the documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/access-api-from-pod/#directly-accessing-the-rest-api which states:

> While running in a Pod, the Kubernetes apiserver is accessible via a Service named `kubernetes` in the `default` namespace. Therefore, Pods can use the `kubernetes.default.svc` hostname to query the API server. Official client libraries do this automatically.

client-go does **not** do this. Though, it includes a TODO:

```go
		// TODO: switch to using cluster DNS.
		Host:            "https://" + net.JoinHostPort(host, port),
```

Ambiguity around the documented client discovery policy causes problems for client libraries; and cloud providers continue to promulgate the (now undocumented) legacy env configuration, e.g. https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/3183.

Would you accept a PR to remove the environment based in-cluster configuration in favor of always using `kubernetes.default.svc`?

### What did you expect to happen?

client-go should use `kubernetes.default.svc` and it should not honor the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` environment variable.

title: client-go: the retry logic in rest.Request should be thread safe
description:
### What happened?

the newly refactored retry logic introduced in 1.22 by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102217 broke the thread safety of `*Request`. According to Clayton, it's not a release blocker for 1.24. 
So the goal is to fix it in 1.25 and then back port all the way to 1.22.

Please note that there are other members (not related to retry logic) of `Request` that are not thread safe depending on how different methods of a `Request` object is used from multiple go routines.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102217/files#r837633535

Also, the comments on some of these methods and sections for retry logic can be improved:
- For instance, we may want to rename `IsErrorRetryable` to `IsHttpErrRetryable` and `checkWait` to `isServerIndicatedRetry`.

Maintain thread safety of `*Request`

title: Kubelet cannot finish terminating a pod that uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block` if the underlying block device is accidentally disconnected from the node
description:
### What happened? A pod uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block`. The block volume is backed by a block device on the node (which is created by some CSI storage providers). If the underlying block device corresponding to the volume is accidentally disconnected from the node (due to network, hardware problem, etc...), the user cannot delete the pod. The pod would be stuck in terminating forever since Kubelet refuses to unmount the block volume. This prevents the user from cleaning up the pod and spinning up a new replacement pod thus leading to a long service degradation. For example, if the pod is part of a statefulset, the replacement pod cannot come up due to the old pod being stuck terminating. ### What did you expect to happen? Kubelet should be able to finish terminating a pod when the corresponding block device is already removed from the node. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Install a CSI storage provider that supports `volumeMode: Block`. For example, [Longhorn](https://github.com/longhorn/longhorn) 2. Deloy a statefulset that has volumeClaimTemplates with `volumeMode: Block`. For example:
click to open yaml manifest ``` apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: test-bv labels: app: test-bv spec: ports: - port: 80 name: test-bv selector: app: test-bv type: NodePort --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: StatefulSet metadata: name: test-bv namespace: default spec: selector: matchLabels: app: test-bv serviceName: "test-bv" template: metadata: labels: app: test-bv spec: restartPolicy: Always terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10 containers: - name: test-bv image: k8s.gcr.io/nginx-slim:0.8 command: - sleep - infinity ports: - containerPort: 80 name: test-bv volumeDevices: - devicePath: /dev/longhorn/test-blk name: test-bv-volume volumeClaimTemplates: - metadata: name: test-bv-volume spec: accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ] storageClassName: "longhorn" volumeMode: Block resources: requests: storage: 1Gi ```
3. Simulate a network/hardware problem in which the backing block device is removed from the host unexpectedly. In our example, we delete a Longhorn engine instance manager which leads to the underlying block device being removed from the host. 4. Now that the pod cannot access the block volume, try to delete the pod. 5. The pod is stuck in terminating state forever. Logs from kubelet:

title: KeyEncipherment usage should not be required for non-RSA kubelet client/serving CSRs
description:
### What happened?

https://github.com/golang/go/issues/36499 describes why the KeyEncipherment extended key usage does not make sense (and in some cases, is not allowed) for ECDSA keys.

The Kubernetes `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` and `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet` signer names require a `key encipherment` usage.

If the kubelet is not using an RSA key (which it does not [by default](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.23.0/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L640-L642)), it should not need to specify this key usage.

Since relaxing this to make the `key encipherment` usage optional for those two signerNames may involve an API validation change, this may need rollout over 2 releases. The places we'll need to make sure work properly are:

1. API validation of CSR create and update requests
2. Controller tolerating CSR objects with/without that usage
3. Kubelets requesting CSRs properly without that usage if given a non-RSA key

We identified (some of) these mutual-use problems a while ago.  The problem is that changing the API to reject such inputs would be a breaking change.  Now, we can argue "it doesn't work anyway" but I'll bet 100 bucks that somewhere out there is a cluster that has Services in this state.  We could, maybe, go through a process of warning and then disallowing it on NEW Services, but we have to allow it on existing services.  That's a lot of work, but I could see exploring it.  Note that we can't simply wipe those fields on input, or else clients can go into an apply-loop.

We should fix the controllers to ignore ExternalName more completely, so we don't end up with endpoints when we don't want them - that's totally reasonable and I don't think that is a breaking change.

As to whether to do it in Service REST or in controllers... we have some such linkages today.  It makes the code slightly uglier and more convoluted (and tests).  I'd love to explore moving it all to the controllers, but that requires us to clearly define the intersection of the fields.

I have been looking at the throwing warning using api-machinery. I think it is a good idea.

There are two cases here:
1. Service that had selector and thus endpoints that service then changes type to `ExternalName` (we need to delete those endpoints). I don't think controller can handle that logic consistently. Not sure at least.
2. Service that is already an `ExternalName`. If users set endpoints to them then the controller should just ignore them.

> * Service that had selector and thus endpoints that service then changes type to `ExternalName` (we need to delete those endpoints). I don't think controller can handle that logic consistently. Not sure at least.

only in endpointslice controller, endpoints controller doesn't handle updates
it should be something similar to [REDACTED]

> * Service that is already an `ExternalName`. If users set endpoints to them then the controller should just ignore them.

this is the simplest one 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c9baa14d708415225ed030e520970b3e1b6e4349/pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go#L407-L411

More findings

1. ExternalName without selector will not generate endpoints
2. ExternalName with selector will generate empty endpoint
```
NAME                      ENDPOINTS         AGE
echoserver-externalname   <none>            3s
```
3. ExternalName with selector and ports will generate proper endpoint
```
NAME                      ENDPOINTS         AGE
echoserver-externalname   10.24.1.7:80      69s
```

### After switching ExternalName with selector to ClusterIP, it will not respond to traffic

Reproduction:

1. Create deployment

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: echoserver
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: echoserver
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: echoserver
        k8s-app: glbc
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx:1.22
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        name: echoserver
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          hostPort: 80
        startupProbe:
          failureThreshold: 30
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
            scheme: HTTP
          periodSeconds: 20
          successThreshold: 1
          timeoutSeconds: 3
```

2. Create ExternalName Service with selector

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: echoserver-externalname
  namespace: default
spec:
  selector:
    app: echoserver
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: www.google.com
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    protocol: TCP
```

3. Change Service type to ClusterIP

after that, doing curl to ClusterIP (from cluster node) will return
`curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.28.13.144 port 80 after 0 ms: Connection refused`

### iptables probably wrong

I compared node's iptables after creating ClusterIP service from scratch, and after doing ExternalName -> ClusterIP and found the only one different line:

```
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.28.13.144/32 -p tcp -m comment --comment "default/echoserver-externalname has no endpoints" -m tcp --dport 80 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable
```

Which probably is the source of dropped traffic.

Also, I verified, there is endpoints on the service, and you can also get them from kubectl get endpoints
```
$ kubectl describe service echoserver-externalname 
Name:              echoserver-externalname
Namespace:         default
Selector:          app=echoserver
Type:              ClusterIP
IP Family Policy:  SingleStack
IP Families:       IPv4
IP:                10.28.13.144
IPs:               10.28.13.144
External Name:     www.google.com
Port:              <unset>  80/TCP
TargetPort:        80/TCP
Endpoints:         10.24.1.7:80
Session Affinity:  None
```

Testes on GKE 1.25.4-gke.1600

After switching ExternalName -> ClusterIP I see only those logs in kube-proxy

```
I1214 14:45:50.731550       1 service.go:324] "Service updated ports" service="default/echoserver-externalname" portCount=1
I1214 14:45:50.731685       1 service.go:440] "Adding new service port" portName="default/echoserver-externalname" servicePort="10.28.9.45:80/TCP"
I1214 14:45:50.731725       1 proxier.go:850] "Syncing iptables rules"
I1214 14:45:50.776750       1 proxier.go:1487] "Reloading service iptables data" numServices=6 numEndpoints=7 numFilterChains=5 numFilterRules=4 numNATChains=17 numNATRules=39
I1214 14:45:50.781575       1 proxier.go:817] "SyncProxyRules complete" elapsed="49.919239ms
```
So this is probably where we set this reject rule https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1082
That rule is added if kube-proxy doesn't find any endpointSlice associated to the Service 🤔

Found the bug, the endpointslice for a ExternalName Service is created as a HeadlessService

```
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  annotations:
    endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time: "2022-12-14T17:32:29Z"
  creationTimestamp: "2022-12-14T17:32:29Z"
  generateName: externalname-
  generation: 1
  labels:
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: endpointslice-controller.k8s.io
    kubernetes.io/service-name: externalname
    service.kubernetes.io/headless: ""
  name: externalname-qjpmq
```

when the Service is mutated to the ClusterIP type, the endpointslice is not updated and stills have the `service.kubernetes.io/headless: ""`label
```
    uid: 531bf465-8548-4fea-980e-6eeb99e4d6d4
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  annotations:
    endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time: "2022-12-14T17:32:29Z"
  creationTimestamp: "2022-12-14T17:32:29Z"
  generateName: externalname-
  generation: 1
  labels:
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: endpointslice-controller.k8s.io
    kubernetes.io/service-name: externalname
    service.kubernetes.io/headless: ""
``` 

so kube-proxy ignores it, and installs the reject rule thinking that the Service doesn´t have any endpoint associated

The funny thing is that ClusterIP is not really inmutable

ClusterIP service with ip assigned -> mutate to ExternalName, it sets ClusterIP None -> mutate back to ClusterIP service, you have a Headless Service 😄 

Ok, the loophole seems to be only the ExternalName type, if I have a ClusterIP service I can't move it to headless or viceversa, because the ClusterIP field can not be modified

> * spec.clusterIPs[0]: Invalid value: []string{"10.96.0.5"}: may not change once set

title: revisit `PodEligibleToPreemptOthers` func from default preemption
description:
#### What happened:
As the comment here explained, the logic of `PodEligibleToPreemptOthers` func from default preemption is not accurate enough, the deleting pod should be a preemption victim instead of normal deleted pod.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104030#discussion_r680138858

Quote from @Huang-Wei 

> PodEligibleToPreemptOthers currently checks if a nominated node has low-priority terminating pods, then it assumes those terminating pods are preempted by the preemptor. It's actually not that accurate - we should verify the terminating pods are exactly preemption victims; otherwise a possible case is: the victims have been physically deleted, and the terminating pods are due to regular deletion.



#### What you expected to happen:
Refine the logic to make sure the deleting pod is actually a preemption victim.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

#### Anything else we need to know?:

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
- Install tools:
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:

cc @alculquicondor

comments.text: Do we have a way to tell? Add a Pod condition perhaps? Is it worth the extra API call?

It doesn't worth an extra API call.

A possible way is to handle it in [nominator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95ff56c201ae7ccdcd1f01bc36646d1d6496483a/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L828), by introducing a `nominatedPodToVictims` map.
But then it has to be best effort (in case kube-scheduler restarts). What would happen if the information is not present?

> But then it has to be best effort (in case kube-scheduler restarts).

Yes.

> What would happen if the information is not present?

It would fall back to the current logic - once a nominated pod finds terminating and low-priority pods on a node, it doesn't proceed preemption attempt on that node.
Is it really worth the added complexity and extra state to manage? In my opinion, I think not.
As already said, this will introduce extra state and complexity to handle, close for now, maybe the issue will gone alone the way ahead. :)

Given `PodDisruptionConditions` is in place, we have a clear API field to tell whether a terminating Pod is caused by scheduler preemption.

```console
# running in k8s 1.26
# pause2 tries to preempt pause1
⇒  k get po
NAME     READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pause1   1/1     Terminating   0          8m47s
pause2   0/1     Pending       0          2m46s
```

```console
# pause1's condition
⇒  k get po pause1 -o json | jq '.status.conditions[] | select(.type=="DisruptionTarget")'
{
  "lastProbeTime": null,
  "lastTransitionTime": "2022-12-20T22:45:55Z",
  "message": "Kube-scheduler: preempting to accommodate a higher priority pod: default/pause2",
  "reason": "PreemptionByKubeScheduler",
  "status": "True",
  "type": "DisruptionTarget"
}
```

title: Data race when creating isomorphic Events with an "k8s.io/client-go/tools/events".EventRecorder
description:
**What happened**:

I wrote a test creating multiple isomorphic Events with an "k8s.io/client-go/tools/events".[EventRecorder](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/tools/events/interfaces.go#L26) and stumbled upon a data race.

The data race happens in the [recordToSink](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.18.2/tools/events/event_broadcaster.go#L153) function. It seems that the Event Series field can be read and written at the same time by two different goroutines. [Read](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.18.2/tools/events/event_broadcaster.go#L178) [Write](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.18.2/tools/events/event_broadcaster.go#L168-L171).

This seems to happen in only one scenario:
- (1) a singleton Event is created
- (2) an isomorphic Event is created
- (1) lock addition to cache
- (2) wait for the lock to be released
- (1) unlock
- (2) lock + [create](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.18.2/tools/events/event_broadcaster.go#L168-L171) the Series
- (1) [read](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/v0.18.2/tools/events/event_broadcaster.go#L209) the freshly created Series
- (1) singleton Event is now considered as a series

Looks like this error message is a symptom of a more general problem of node-to-pod connectivity issues.

In our case, we confirmed that by using `traceroute` from the node to the pod's internal IP as suggested in https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/who-where-actually-work-liveness-probe-in-kubernetes/4771/6. That IP was perfectly routable from the other pods and even from many other nodes, but not from that particular node it ended up on. The root cause turned out to be that the br-int (bridge) interface that connects the pod networks and the NSX overlay logical switch was failing to come up because of missing static routes. Fixing that magically solved the problem.

In other cases, the root cause may be different, but the first step would be to confirm whether the node can actually access that pod, e.g. ssh and traceroute or curl into the readiness probe (`curl -v http://172.70.3.3:15020/healthz/ready` when Istio sidecar containers fail to get ready), etc.

title: unstable map iteration order causes test to sometimes leave non-GA features disabled
description:
### What happened?

PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115324 was reverted by #116062 because it (erroneously) relied on OpenAPIV3 feature to be enabled, but `TestPodSecurityGAOnly` would non-deterministically leave the feature disabled after running.

I tracked it down to the fact that this test disables all `PreRelease` or `Beta` features in a loop which iterates over a `map`, which are known to have unstable iteration order:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e55f2a9b54e0f6bd9ed12e50752d7d2545ab0cab/test/integration/auth/podsecurity_test.go#L74-L81

When key `AllBeta` is processed before key `OpenAPIV3`, then `AllBeta` would disable `OpenAPIV3` before `OpenAPIV3`s default value is to be saved.

Normally, `AllBeta` ignores features that have been explicitly set, so it only affects those which fall back on the `Default` value. But this issue does not just affect `OpenAPIV3` but any non-GA feature.

I suggest the loop in `TestPodSecurityGAOnly` be made to skip the special feature keys such as `AllBeta`.


### What did you expect to happen?

The value before every feature gate should be restored after running `TestPodSecurityGAOnly`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This test always fails on my machine (just pasted it into `test/integration/auth/podsecurity_test.go`):

```go
func TestRestoreFeatures(t *testing.T) {
	var targetFeature featuregate.Feature

	// Grab a beta feature form the list to test with
	for k, v := range utilfeature.DefaultMutableFeatureGate.GetAll() {
		if v.PreRelease == featuregate.Beta && v.Default {
			targetFeature = k
			break
		}
	}

	if len(targetFeature) == 0 {
		t.Log("no beta features to test against")
		return
	}

        // see if we iterate the feature map with AllBeta first within a few tries
	for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
		attemptFunc := func() bool {
			fg := utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.DeepCopy()
			originalValue := fg.Enabled(targetFeature)

			func() {
				// Disable all alpha and beta features
				for k, v := range fg.DeepCopy().GetAll() {
					if v.PreRelease == featuregate.Alpha || v.PreRelease == featuregate.Beta {
						defer featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, fg, k, false)()
					}
				}
			}()

			return originalValue != fg.Enabled(targetFeature)
		}

		if attemptFunc() {
			t.Fatal("original value for feature not same as new value after restoration")
			break
		}
	}
}
```

Expected the tests to pass

Run the loadbalancer test suite on AWS

While investigating the root cause of these failures, i cam across this function in the cloud-provider-aws:

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-aws/blob/master/pkg/providers/v1/aws.go#L5226-L5236

```go
func checkProtocol(port v1.ServicePort, annotations map[string]string) error {
	// nlb supports tcp, udp
	if isNLB(annotations) && (port.Protocol == v1.ProtocolTCP || port.Protocol == v1.ProtocolUDP) {
		return nil
	}
	// elb only supports tcp
	if !isNLB(annotations) && port.Protocol == v1.ProtocolTCP {
		return nil
	}
	return fmt.Errorf("Protocol %s not supported by LoadBalancer", port.Protocol)
}
```

This function checks to ensure that a specific annotation has been applied to the Service object to determine if it is an NLB. The test in question creates the Service object with no annotations placed upon it, this in turn causes the test to fail.

This [discussion from slack with the AWS maintainers](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0LRMHZ1T/p1676481894305559) confirms the need for the user to add the annotation. It is a continuation of a discussion that started in the SIG Cloud Provider meeting from 15 Feb 2023.

title: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
description:
### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above, with any scheme other than client-go’s.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
```

title: MultiCIDRRangeAllocator requires node reboot to assign ranges
description:
### What happened?

When the `ClusterCIDR` is created *after* a node has booted, addresses are not defined;

```
> kubectl get cc -A

> kubectl create -f kubernetes/clustercidr.yaml

> kubectl get cc -A

default   8                 11.0.0.0/16   1100::/112   5s
> kubectl get node -o json vm-002 | jq .spec
{}
# (reboot node vm-002 ...)
> kubectl get node -o json vm-002 | jq .spec
{
  "podCIDR": "11.0.0.0/24",
  "podCIDRs": [
    "11.0.0.0/24",
    "1100::/120"
  ]
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Addresses shall be allocated for all nodes with empty `spec.podCIDRs` when a `ClusterCIDR` is created (*then* they become immutable).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Probably the easiest way is to check the controller:

* Create the controller with MultiCIDRRangeAllocator enabled and configured
* Create a `ClusterCIDR`
* Check the node.spec on the controller
* Reboot it
* Check again


### Anything else we need to know?

I can't see a clean way to start a cluster without this fixed. It the cni-plugin requires spec.podCIDRs to work the node will not become ready until it's rebooted.

As a work-around in my test env I can create a controller that is _not a node_ in the cluster (I think k3s and AWS does like this).

### What happened?

After the cluster was updated to enable PD CSI Driver, there was a race condition where AD Controller (kube-controller-manager) started to [populate the desired state of world](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L438-L447) BEFORE the PD CSI Driver was up, thus AD Controller gave us the error 

```
Error creating spec for volume "elasticsearch", pod "XXX"/"elasticsearch-0": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "dXX"/"elasticsearch-elasticsearch-0": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/gce-pd is migrated on node gke-stage-XXXXX but driver pd.csi.storage.gke.io is not installed.
```

Then AD Controller triggered the disk detach because the disk/volume was not populated in the desired state of world.

Unfortunately the disk was in use during this detach and got corrupted.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since cluster upgrades can cause the controller manager and CSI drivers to start at different times, the AD controller needs to be more conservative when detaching

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We have not been able to reproduce this, it came up from a customer.

### Anything else we need to know?

### Kubernetes version

<details>
k8s 1.23, CSI migration enabled
</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
GKE
</details>

I think there's potentially two changes we should do:
1) for the initial DSW population, we should skip the check that if the csi driver is not installed.
2) in general, we should not skip volumes during dsw initial population if an error is returned. If we had some temporary api server error then that would cause volumes to not get added to dsw and similar behavior happen. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L446

cc @gnufied @jingxu97

@mattcary for a repro, maybe you can try something like:

cc @sunnylovestiramisu
@songjiaxun was trying to repro this, but on GKE with the managed driver which made it complicated.
Yeah maybe gce kube-up would be easier for a repro

If CSINode says that it has migrated GCP PD volume plugin to CSI, then IMO A/D controller should always attach GCP PD volumes to it using CSI, regardless if the CSI driver is present or not. In-tree volume plugin in the kubelet is disabled and can't mount any in-tree volumes anyway.

To flip the migration feature gate / upgrade / downgrade kubelet, the cluster admin must drain the node first to make sure everything is detached. A/D controller should not see change of CSINode migration annotations with any volume attached to it.

Another option could be to process these volumes anyways but add them to DSOW with migration status as "uncertain", so as they can be re-processed later.  But surely it looks like @jsafrane might be easiest unless it has any downsides.

There wasn't a node update in this case---there was a control plane update which restarted the PD CSI driver, and it looks like the CSIDriver resource was updated or changed in some way which raced with the kube-controller-manager restart.
Is there anyway we can know if the csi driver is up and running(like a health check ping) before populating DSW?

We use the CSINode registration to determine that. The discussion here I think is concluding that we should not use that as a criteria for adding the volume to DSW. We only need to check that CSI migration is enabled on the node.
+1 we need to be very resilient against races, I think we have to assume a driver is in process of being installed at any point in the AD controller reconcilliation.

title: Watchcache doesn't distinguish the RV=0 and RV="" semantic for watches
description:
As Jordan pointed out in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3667/files#r1055906242

watchcache treats RV=0 and RV="" the same way, even though it's not what we document:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch

This should be fixed.

title: kube-apiserver doesn't reload the kubelet client certificate/key on each logs query
description:
### What happened?

We bootstrap our clusters with kubeadm (through clusterapi), but provide our own end certs to shorten the certificate validity period.

Because of the shortened validity period, we rotate the file-based endcerts frequently. Recently we started noticing that after performing a certificate rotation, usage of `kubectl logs` was failing with

```sh
error: You must be logged in to the server (the server has asked for the client to provide credentials)
```

From there, we looked at the kube-apiserver and kubelet logs and found log lines like the following:

```
"Unable to authenticate the request due to an error" err="verifying certificate SN=<REMOVED>, SKID=<REMOVED>, AKID=<REMOVED> failed: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2022-12-17T02:31:09Z is after 2022-12-17T00:16:30Z"
```

So it looks like kube-apiserver didn't reload the new kubelet client certificate. This issue typically goes away if we restart the kube-apiserver container or continue to run `kubectl logs` in a loop.

### What did you expect to happen?

Being able to replace/rotate the kube-apiserver kubelet client certificate/key without causing failure for any logs or node proxy commands/operations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We were able to get a repro outside of our environment with the following steps.

1. Created a cluster-api cluster on azure with CAPZ using the standard quickstart flow plus some minor tweaks:
- Added ` kubelet-certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt` as an apiserver argument.
- Added ` rotate-server-certificates: "true"` as a kubelet argument.
- Used kubernetes version 1.23.6 and 1.23.15
2. Manually approved the kubelet server certificate csrs using `kubectl certificate approve`
3. In one shell continually ran `kubectl logs` and `kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<NODE_NAME>/proxy/logs`
4. ssh'd into the controlplane node in another shell. ran  `mv /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt.bak` and vice-versa.

From these steps I was able to see `kubectl logs` commands be successful when there was no certificate file and failed when the certificate file was present. Eventually, the kube-apiserver picks up the up-to-date certificate/file.

I don't know the internals here, but it seems like kube-apiserver was using some sort of cached-connection which had the stale certificate.

### Anything else we need to know?

We believe this used to work in kubernetes v1.21 and below. Need to confirm this by spinning up downlevel clusters.

Thanks. I don't believe this is a kubectl related issue but I can get another repro with the correct kubectl version.

Did some printf debugging in kube-apiserver. This issue doesn't look like it's a problem with reloading the new kubelet client certificate/key. It actually looks due to existing kube-apiserver => kubelet server connections. 

Verifying with netstat, it looks like during a client certificate reload, kube-apiserver is not closing existing client connections.

I don't have a strong familiarity with the code but I wonder if it would be possible to use [dynamicClientCert](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/transport/cert_rotation.go#L42) with the kubelet_client. It looks like the dynamicClientCert closes connections when it detects a certificate rotation.

Looks like the kubelet_client code ends up using [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/b69cda3e4e09e1b956d42709fbadf12e6c0f24b7/transport/transport.go#L323) certificate loading callback today. (which doesn't close existing connections.)
Also I still haven't been able to trace when this issue first started. Does anyone know if there were some changes in the kube-apiserver => kubelet connections to make them cached/longer-lived?

I have this sample commit that seems to fix the issue. https://github.com/zawachte/kubernetes/commit/b4882c7601c27ed5ce562ecf6c2512fdb1496169

This follows the pattern that client-go uses for client certificate reload. If any of the maintainers think this is the correct approach, I can clean up the commit and add tests.

title: Kubernetes Jobs API rapid-fire scheduling doesnt honor exponential backoff characteristics
description:
### What happened?

# Problem

The job controller appears to "rapidly reschedule" several pods at the same time (without backing off) which ultimately appears almost like a batch or gang scheduling workflow.  

... This is the opposite of what the job docs say, bc they clearly state :
```
 The back-off limit is set by default to 6. Failed Pods associated with the Job are recreated by the Job controller with an exponential back-off delay (10s, 20s, 40s ...) capped at six minutes.
```
So, rather then, 

- 10, 20, 40, 80 wait times between trying things we are seeing
- 0, 3, 3, 3, 3 second wait times before pods are being retried

This is in the 1.25 release, but not sure if it also happens earlier.  You can see this in the latest kind version. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Jobs wouldnt schedule the same pod at rapid fire intervals

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

# Details 

Thanks to Ryan for this reproducer: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1

kind: Job

metadata:

  name: backoff-exp

spec:

  backoffLimit: 100

  template:

    spec:

      containers:

        - name: die

          image: ubuntu

          command: [ "/bin/false" ]

          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

      restartPolicy: Never

```

Now once this is running, you can graph the values like so: 

```
kubectl get pods -o wide | awk '

BEGIN {

    a["d"] = 24*(\

    a["h"] = 60*(\

    a["m"] = 60*(\

    a["s"] = 1)));

  }

  {

    print fx($5); # kubernetes time elapsed in seconds

  }

  function fx(ktym,    f,u,n,t,i) {

    n = split(ktym, f, /[dhms]/, u)

    t = 0

    for (i=1; i<n; i++) {

      t += f[i] * a[u[i]]

    }

    return t

  }

'|sort
```

And youl see a table like this, where the integers below are the AGE OF PODS in SECONDS.  We can see that the pod ages are 3 seconds apart as opposed to (10, 20, 40, 80 ...) or some other exponentiallly increasing number of seconds, apart..... 
```

```

This is broken when the `JobTrackingWithFinalizers` feature gate is enabled. Note that it was disabled and re-enabled before moving to GA:
- enabled by default in v1.23 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/2c1b3fdb5bd109487e47b395f1ca15c63e5663ff#diff-71e3b98f9a6bbf5b8421e26a7ba0c079f397cd8d49abacdad943c66a4f44f03d
- disabled by default from v1.23.9 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109491
- disabled by default in v1.24 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/3b18613be88955e13f8357fb6d73bc1d0e158844
- enabled by default in v1.25 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/a26920b1902dd1d81a203baa4cb9f919db4e015d
- and moved to GA in v1.26 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4948918155012b24e4b1cf987f831639c6dbaf9c

If the feature gate is disabled, the pods are retried by honoring exponential backoff characteristics.

From a quick glance, there are a few reasons why this happens:

1. Given that the code below is triggered everytime `uncounted != nil`, the queue is made to `forget` the `key`, so we always end up with a backoff of zero.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bb6edfb96b362736a66946ca7d88774aca167cb4/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L869-L884

2. Even if we updated the above code to only trigger if a status update is required and get the right backoff period, we will have the backoff being calculated twice for each pod failure i.e. t'll end up being something like 10, 10, 20, 20, 40, 40, ...

Looking at:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bb6edfb96b362736a66946ca7d88774aca167cb4/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L308-L330

We can end up with a scenario where:
- Pod A fails, triggering a resync. Since the pod has failed, backoff is calculated and applied.
- Finalizer is removed from Pod A and job status is updated.
- We receive the job update event, but the pod informer cache is stale. This triggers a sync.
- We noticed that Pod A has the status `Failed` so the backoff is applied again.

I'll send a PR to fix both the issues.

From the documentation description and code implementation, the above verification error is consistent with the design requirements.
docs:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#pod-template
```
Only a [.spec.template.spec.restartPolicy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#restart-policy) equal to Always is allowed, which is the default if not specified.
```

code:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/132f29769dfecfc808adc58f756be43171054094/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L148-L150
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/132f29769dfecfc808adc58f756be43171054094/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L354
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/132f29769dfecfc808adc58f756be43171054094/pkg/apis/apps/validation/validation.go#L738
kubectl explain Deployment/DaemonSet/StatefulSet.spec.template.spec.restartPolicy descriptions can be misleading, perhaps we need to add more descriptions.

Unfortunately, the documentation comes from the PodSpec object, which those workload types embed and then place additional restrictions on.

It wouldn't be appropriate to put documentation specific to those embedded uses on the PodSpec object.

I've read two issues, [24725](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/24725) and [40908](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/40908).

Although both issue have been marked as closed, and I understand current implementation supports only "Always" for these workload types, like Deployment, I'm not convinced that it should support only “Always". Like many of others, I believe this is a valid request to have restartPolicy as OnFailure or Never.

Unless it's clear why OnFailure/Never shall not be valid for these workload types and the Kubernetes [specification](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.25/#podspec-v1-core) and [explanation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#restart-policy) get updated as well, I personally believe the kubectl explain command is correct, and doesn't need any changes. On the other hand, the support of OnFailure and Never should be added.

As said by the [specification](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.25/#podspec-v1-core), restartPolicy is "`Restart policy for all containers within the pod.`"

My interpretation, this is the policy to restart the containers in the pod, but not the pod itself, even though it's in the pod spec. Let's say one of the containers in the pod completed successfully or with failures, this container may or may not restart depending on this policy. Although I don't understand why not each container has its own restart policy, this pod-wide shared common policy is good enough for most cases.

Anyway, I don't see a problem with the Kubernetes spec, and I disagree with this change request. Please reconsider making a change to the explain command. Thanks!

title: cacher watch timeout not handled when it is not ready
description:
### What happened?

In one of our multi tenant cluster, we've observed that all kubelet requests (under `system-nodes` flow schema) eventually started timing out or aborted due to secret watch request occupying all `system` priority level concurrency share. It happened due to our KMS provider was quite latent (& sometimes failing) for brief amount of time. Due to high latency from KMS provider, all the cacher's reflector list & watch calls start failing (repeatedly retried) and cacher was marked as not ready.

Now all the watch request to the cacher was waiting for `ready` conditional variable and never timed out. This led all watch requests stuck in priority and fairness queue for ever & eventually occupying all the concurrency shares, affecting other requests belonging to same priority level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f173d01c011c3574dea73a6fa3e20b0ab94531bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L457-L467

We need to handle watch timeout when cacher not ready to fix the issue.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch requests to get time out eventually when cacher is not ready.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Consider a large cluster (5K nodes) having more than 50K number of secret resources encrypted using KMS provider and mounted by various pods in the cluster. Restart api server & artificially induce high latency on KMS provider (assuming we've configured lower dek cache size of 10 items) and wait for kubelet requests to start failing.

### Anything else we need to know?

May we can implement a way to timeout ready conditional variable (sync.Cond) `wait` function. Let me know if I can raise a pull request to fix this. Roughly along below lines:
```go
type ready struct {
	sync.RWMutex

	ok bool
	c chan struct{}
}

func newReady() *ready {
	return &ready{c: make(chan struct{}, 0)}
}

func (r *ready) wait() {
	r.waitChan(nil)
}

func (r *ready) waitChan(stop <-chan struct{}) {
	r.RLock()
	ok, c := r.ok, r.c
	r.RUnlock()
	if ok {
		return
	}
	select {
	case <-stop:
	case <-c:
	}
}


func (r *ready) check() bool {
	r.RLock()
	defer r.RUnlock()
	return r.ok
}

func (r *ready) set(ok bool) {
	r.Lock()
	r.ok = ok
	close(r.c) // broadcast
	r.c = make(chan struct{})
	r.Unlock()
}
```


We can list the v1 but not v1beta1 version of this CRD:
```

Error from server: conversion webhook for stable.example.com/v1, Kind=CronTab failed: Post "https://crd-conversion-webhook.crd-conversion-webhook.svc:443/crdconvert?timeout=30s": service "crd-conversion-webhook" not found
```
If we issue a watch against this CRD, we can make requests get stuck inflight indefinitely which can max out the given PriorityLevelConfiguration:
```
# Make this request 5 times
kubectl get --raw "/apis/stable.example.com/v1beta1/namespaces/default/crontabs?watch=true"

apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_requests{flow_schema="global-default",priority_level="global-default"} 5
```
Even if we close the watch connection, the request is still counted as an executing request. I confirmed this issue is still present in v1.25.6.
