title: Auto-closing issues is harmful and causes friction
description:
Previously open issue : https://github.com/kubernetes/community/issues/5473
Twitter Discussion : https://twitter.com/BenTheElder/status/1407774856033181696

There's pros and cons to having a bot do this, let me try to enumerate current situation here:
- maintainers don't have to play bad cop
- keep set of open issues at a maintainable level
- bot commands are available to org members to `/reopen` reduces friction
- lifecycle labels help folks specify which issues not to touch
- we currently do not have dedicated team(s) that do issue triage well (except for some SIG like api-machinery that do this really well with twice a week triage session)
- initial issue labeling is still a problem, routing issues to the correct sig
- we have a new triage label which is not widely used yet across sigs

However there are numerous problems with the current situation:
- impression that project does not care about bugs
- folks open new issues for things that may be already present but closed
- too much traffic/noise from the bot activity
- issues where some follow up was requested/needed gets closed 

Options to do better?
- triage party 
- more hands on deck, train incoming folks to do issue triage and manage that as a subproject of some SIG
- stop the bot cold and let the SIGs adjust

What did i miss @BenTheElder ?



PS: It will be ironic if this issue gets auto-closed!

comments.text:
It seems like a good idea to revisit the workflows here. What follows is very much my opinion and not representing any SIG. It also covers more than just autoclose.

Auto close _does_ avoid issues piling up.

- I'm OK with the idea of never closing issues that are triaged as accepted
- I'm also OK with the idea of auto closing issues that have been marked as needs more information or as support, and haven't had a response since they were so labelled.
- I'd be interested in splitting the “backlog” priority level into “stuff we'd clearly like to do as a SIG, and would if there were resources” vs. “it's a valid suggestion but it'll only happen if someone takes it forward”. For an example of the latter see issue 25061 in k/website: *Allow switching website between “light mode” and “dark mode”*.
- That split would help us let things fall off the second backlog, but perhaps let them stay on the first.
- Priorities above backlog should not autoclose, but I do want to see them rot and then be labelled _something_ if we don't get to them. Maybe become “overdue” or “unaddressed”?

For k/website, issues that haven't been triaged in _n_ days could go straight to _unaddressed_, skipping stale and rotten.
Does https://github.com/features/issues provide any new way to track issues and help avoid closing ones that are worth keeping?

I want to point out that while the original somewhat hyperbolic tweet took off far beyond expectation there is an important follow-up: https://twitter.com/bentheelder/status/1407906836175491076

IMHO the biggest issue we have is staffing problems keeping after triage and so on.

> more hands on deck, train incoming folks to do issue triage and manage that as a subproject of some SIG

Perhaps a new role in SIGs recognizing the folks that do issue triage? I think we need some way to recognize and encourage doing this, in addition to some workflow guidance or tooling (such as triage-party instances).

Bot noise impacts me a lot, personally. To keep something like KIND running well @ Kubernetes HEAD + manage SIG testing etc. I am subscribed to a lot of issues and a *huge* amount of comments are just the lifecycle robot and users fending it off.
Frozen issues are cheaper, they see little noise when nobody is working on them and IMHO if these issues are breaking triage workflows then the workflows need to be improved.

But as mentioned above I think the important part is that this harms the reputation of the project immensely because for many people their first interaction is filing a bug or PR that slips through the cracks and then gets harassed by the auto close bot. We have other people exasperated and futilely commenting every time the bot comments to undo it. There is a sub thread about folks who outright said they do not participate anymore after this experience. Once we burn those folks they don't come back.

I think closing issues we never got to hides just how many of those exist except from those in the know about querying the right labels.

> I'd be interested in splitting the “backlog” priority level into “stuff we'd clearly like to do as a SIG, and would if there were resources” vs. “it's a valid suggestion but it'll only happen if someone takes it forward”. For an example of the latter see issue 25061 in k/website: Allow switching website between “light mode” and “dark mode”.

I think this would be useful signaling regardless.

> I'm also OK with the idea of auto closing issues that have been marked as needs more information or as support, and haven't had a response since they were so labelled.

I would add that we should consider poking for information (the bot could do this) at some point in the lifecycle.

+1, there's a big difference between we can't move forward with the issue because the author is not responding and we need information and the issue not getting a response from us. Auto-closing this sort of issue seems unlikely to produce the same response and keeping them open seems unlikely to net much for anyone.

In general +1 to @sftims comment above.

It's worth noting that most of our repos are not kubernetes/kubernetes scale and even a moderately busy repo is probably already more doable to triage without this than our busiest repos, I think we have two different scales of problems but we bluntly apply one workflow org wide.

We are trying disabling it on the KIND repo, which seems to clearly fall into the latter scale.

One thing we're going to start experimenting with in Knative is building an issue-triage report to make this sort of thing more manageable:

The initial focus will be simply on quantifying the bot impact:

How many issues touched in the last 100 days:
* Were marked by the stale-bot?
* And had a human undo the stale-bot?
* First item and never had an org member comment?

If there's interest, it might also be possible to collect org member stats on issue replies (maybe treating first and last specially). This could help highlight people who are doing a great job of triage and issue-closing.

Being mostly on the user side I do feel a lot of frustration with these. I think auto-closing specifically in the case of a ticket/PR being in a "waiting for OP to respond" state is okay but when the issue is accepted as real and there's nothing more to say, then auto-closing them is pretty grumble-inducing. Auto-closing untriaged tickets/PRs feels like a gray area, can see both sides, and probably should be a special case and a sign that our triage process needs improvement.

This reminds me of the different types of strategies used by dictionaries. Some are descriptive -- describing how people use words -- whereas others are prescriptive -- informing people how they should use words. 

https://www.merriam-webster.com/words-at-play/descriptive-vs-prescriptive-defining-lexicography

What strategy should we use for the backlog of issues that no one has engaged with in half a decade?
* prescriptive  -- this issue is still probably broken and someone still ought to fix it
* descriptive -- no one has or will work on this issue, close it so it doesn't distract from the things we are fixing.

Neither is correct per se. Although I would note that most dictionaries these days tend to be descriptive.

Ideally we can figure out how to redirect the energy spent getting angry at automated descriptive processes and towards fixing more issues more consistently.

> impression that project does not care about bugs

The impression that the project does not care about bugs is an accurate conclusion implied by the large number of auto-closed issues. At the very least, the project's ability to generate bugs is higher than the community's current ability to fix them.

Pulling the battery out of a smoke detector is unlikely to put out a fire.

> [auto-closing bugs] harms the reputation of the project immensely because for many people their first interaction is filing a bug or PR that slips through the cracks and then gets harassed by the auto close bot. We have other people exasperated and futilely commenting every time the bot comments to undo it. 

In the same way smoke detectors rarely cause fires, I would not assign the cause of the reputational harm from ignoring bugs to automated processes that flag things as ignored.

Rather I would note the lack of the right processes in place that allow the maintainers on this project respond to incoming issues faster than they are supplied and also identify issues that have fallen through the cracks.

> What strategy should we use for the backlog of issues that no one has engaged with in half a decade?

We close bugs _far_ quicker than half a decade. IMO the amount of time a bug spends open is actually immaterial. If the bug is real and not fixed it deserves to be tracked, it is wasteful to file N bugs for the same problem, and it prevents users from tracking resolution when we spread it out in this way.

We've yet to have any solid arguments as to why open bugs are harmful. At best there is some complaint about issue triage, but that is accomplishable with e.g. just labeling the issue and filtering by label. Closing is orthogonal.

> Ideally we can figure out how to redirect the energy spent getting angry at automated descriptive processes and towards fixing more issues more consistently.

Many people filing bugs are ill equipped to fix them. A user of the project may not be in the right position / experience to resolve a bug. Their frustration is still relevant to the success of the project. There is also a lot of energy wasted in `/remove-lifecycle` comments.

> The impression that the project does not care about bugs is an accurate conclusion implied by the large number of auto-closed issues. At the very least, the project's ability to generate bugs is higher than the community's current ability to fix them.

Not even leaving the bug tracked and dismissively closing it is a bit different than not getting to it.

> In the same way smoke detectors rarely cause fires, I would not assign the cause of the reputational harm from ignoring bugs to automated processes that flag things as ignored.

There is explicitly evidence that there is reputational harm from this. Off hand: https://twitter.com/jordansissel/status/1407857648083472388
"K8s auto closing bot is why I don’t interact with k8s projects anymore. 😭👍🏻"

Further, I'd say this is not comparable to a smoke detector. Tracking the amount of inactive bugs is a smoke detector.
Closing them actually obscures this, I'd have a different impression encountering a project with ~9k bugs open than < 2k. How many people are aware of searching github for the closed issues with special label?

Closing issues is more like having a robot dump the flaming objects in your backyard so the smoke detector stops going off.

> Rather I would note the lack of the right processes in place that allow the maintainers on this project respond to incoming issues faster than they are supplied and also identify issues that have fallen through the cracks.

This is almost certainly the most important thing to address. That doesn't mean that other aspects of the current approach aren't problematic though.

> Tracking the amount of inactive bugs is a smoke detector.

How would you separate active from inactive bugs?

> Their frustration is still relevant to the success of the project. There is also a lot of energy wasted in /remove-lifecycle comments.

Both of these are good signals that a SIG has underinvested in their triage or development process and/or have other problems (bad design/impl causing problems, important unhandled use cases, etc).

> How would you separate active from inactive bugs?

Auto-Labeling + search queries used by triagers or triage tooling still seems potentially relevant, but less heavy handed.

> Both of these are good signals that a SIG has underinvested in their triage or development process and/or have other problems (bad design/impl causing problems, important unhandled use cases, etc).

Yes -- we definitely have signal that triage processes are under-staffed / optimized / not going well, and it is definitely not uniform across SIGs (some are doing quite well).

As for how we might improve that, https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-testing/issues/7 is one issue tracking exploring that.

So people don't have to wade through Twitter, let me summarize my 2c...

Volume:

- We have nearly 7000 issues in k/k closed with the rotten label; realistically that's over 1000/yr: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed+label%3Alifecycle%2Frotten
- On average for the past year, we have 35 new issues opened every day: https://k8s.devstats.cncf.io/d/39/issues-opened-closed-by-sig?orgId=1&var-period=d&var-repo_name=kubernetes%2Fkubernetes&var-repo=kuberneteskubernetes&var-sig_name=All&var-kind_name=All
- From experience with SIG Instrumentation, I estimate that we typically triage about 5 issues per 30m session. I think it's therefore reasonable to estimate that one person could easily fill an entire half of their workday just triaging incoming issues to k/k, 7 days a week.

Contributor and issue filer expectations:

- Allowing a backlog of issues that anyone can file to grow forever fails to set healthy boundaries and realistic expectations around support in a FOSS project. Closed, stale issues illustrates the staffing gap and at least shifts some of the emotional labor on closing stale issues (which no one enjoys doing!! particularly if the reply that comes back is rude!) to a bot.
- I think there's a difference between closing issues that have been confirmed at some point but we're not staffed to handle vs. various user support requests, perhaps where the reporter is unresponsive.
- I frequently struggle with confirmed, legitimate issues that the project doesn't have resources to address, because there are only so many things we can prioritize working on. Even if an outside contributor does the work to fix the problem, reviewer/approver time is very limited.
- Addressing the limited approver time gap is not easy. It is extremely challenging to develop the experience to apply for approver on some of the high volume areas of the codebase (API Machinery, Node, etc.) You need to work on the project full-time, and that requires funding/employment. Many areas of the project have a lottery factor of 1.

At the moment, I think it's clear that SIGs are not resourced to manage the current volume of incoming issues in k/k. I think it's also fair to argue that the stale bot has discouraged issue filing, so I suspect that if we staffed the project for current issue load, we could easily see it increase in a short time and would find ourselves understaffed again.

Could the project hire someone to do full-time issue triage and management? And, if we did this, would we have sufficient staffing in SIGs to manage the workload of legitimate bugs and feature requests after moving the bottleneck?

FWIW:
- the way the comments are done right now is via a commenter tool that comments on anything matching a certain github query
- it's super boilerplate-heavy and not able to be concisely configured in a way that would allow certain repos to opt-opt, or configure different thresholds, or different lifecycles, etc.
- if someone wanted to invest the effort in writing a purpose-built lifecycle management tool, this would probably be way easier to accomplish

I feel like with the possible exception of kubernetes/kubernetes, it would be super cool to use a default that is selectively overridable by specific subprojects or SIGs.

As to effectiveness, I don't know anyone who's bothered to gather data on:
- whether perma-unstaling issues has been effective in getting them addressed (aka is this an alternate way of people spamming +1 or :thumbsup: on the issue to vote? does anyone pay attention?)
- whether auto-closed issues resurface later as larger-impact / higher-priority issues (aka we could have saved ourselves pain if we had addressed it earlier)

What would be a friendlier way to express that there isn't sufficient contributor capacity to even look at a given issue / PR? 

How would folks propose increasing contributor capacity to ensure that all issues / PRs can be looked at?

> it's super boilerplate-heavy and not able to be concisely configured in a way that would allow certain repos to opt-opt, or configure different thresholds, or different lifecycles, etc.

Overall I would agree that this is true but opt-out entirely is not really problematic, we're piloting this on the KIND repo.

You can see the three line diff necessary here: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/22675/files

> if someone wanted to invest the effort in writing a purpose-built lifecycle management tool, this would probably way easier to accomplish

I don't think anyone needs to alter the tool to support this or alternate per-repo comments, the tool is flexible and uses github search parameters for choosing where to comment. GitHub search is well documented and plenty powerful enough to exclude and include specific projects.

> What would be a friendlier way to express that there isn't sufficient contributor capacity to even look at a given issue / PR?

At the very least the phrasing can be a bit less blunt / more helpful, see also https://github.com/knative/community/issues/665#issuecomment-873873770, https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/22911

Marking issues as needing triage and a perhaps a comment explaining the limited bandwidth etc. seems more useful than people `/remove-lifecycle`ing for years.

> How would folks propose increasing contributor capacity to ensure that all issues / PRs can be looked at?

I don't think you have to address that issue to resolve that the current approach to closing them out is noisy and frustrating.

Resolving capacity is not something people can solve with their own time and efforts, we need more staffed contributors, which at most we can raise to our employers.

I think we can reduce the issue count differently however:

We should also probably consider entirely removing / auto-closing the feature type in favor of asking people to file KEPs. And also the support type. Realistically most of the time we are manually re-pointing these issues to the the enhancements rep and the forums respectively, which could be automated, leaving only bugs, flaking/failing tests to deal with.

It is perhaps worth noting that this is factoring into the decision to donate kube-rs into the project https://github.com/kube-rs/kube-rs/issues/584, there should probably be a discussion somewhere (else?) about formally allowing subprojects to opt out of this.

> We close bugs far quicker than half a decade

I know that in k/website / SIG Docs we struggle to make improvements even when they've been _marked_ as important for some time. https://github.com/kubernetes/website/issues/4322 springs to mind. Folks are chipping away at the pile of frozen issues that have ended up at the end of the far end of the list.

Automatic closure has “helped” by making those frozen issues stand out. However, there's definitely a risk that some good idea never made it past triage and disappeared into the pile of closed suggestions.

I wanted to add a good example which IMHO shouldn't be auto-closed:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/7890 is the [the top 5 of all upvoted issues](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc) but it is/was scheduled by the bot to be autoclosed.

At the time I think the project was trying to tamp down the entropy of every repo having different rules of engagement.  Onboard a contributor to the project, and they should be capable of contributing to any of our 200+ repos.  The bot was a way of maintaining some kind of expectation that issues that haven't been touched in 150 days are implicitly deemed as not urgent enough to work on.

The way I see it, issues should never be closed, and it doesn't really matter if you have 100 open issues or 10,000.

- resolved

And other than issues that lack info and don't receive more info after some time, all issues are considered accepted without the triage labeling.

I think it works well, and we should consider this for smaller repos. I understand concerns with Kubernetes/Kubernetes issue volume, though I also don't think the current approach is desirable.

If folks are reluctant to disable the bot entirely (Ben's suggestion), I have an alternate proposal:

1. Triaged issues are never marked stale or closed.
2. _(optional)_ After 1 year (or some long timeline) of no activity, require triaged issues to be re-triaged (this is sort of like marking them as stale)
3. Regular stale/rotten/closed rules are applied to untriaged issues
AIUI, the bot was originally brought in for PRs and issues were adding later. For that reason I have +1'd https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103151#issuecomment-1279262642.

> not enough info and unable to get a follow-up from the author with sufficient detail (which we eventually close ourselves when reviewing issues)

This is a major use-case for me.  If we only auto-close issues which are "needs-triage" AND "needs-information", I'd be happy.  

>  After 1 year (or some long timeline) of no activity, require triaged issues to be re-triaged 

I like this too!  "needs triage" is a good signal, so far.

To throw out another suggestion specific to k/k, I run the weekly SIG Auth Issue triage meeting with @ritazh @aramase @nilekhc @ibihim @natalisucks and others.  We are slowly getting through our issues, slowly improving the automation around the triage process, etc.

I find this bot to be harmful, abrasive and an incredible waste of the community's time.

My proposal is very simple: if a k/k issue or PR has the `sig/auth` label and the total number of SIG labels is 3 or less, the bot should ignore it completely.  I and the other SIG members will take complete ownership of our issues and their triage.  I have no problem closing issues and PRs directly.  The passage of time does not solve bugs.

Who (which group) own's the bot? Who are the deciders on a change to it's behavior? It sounds like there's pretty broad agreement that it needs a change, do we just need someone to open a PR and make it so?

The code is implemented by SIG Testing but workflow changes need to go through contributor experience (https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/28021), as reminded when recently shipping https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/28021 to stop auto-closing "help-wanted" and "good-first-issue" labeled issues.

title: Mutation of a cached object in kubelet through in place resizing of pods
description:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/76d351065e504e23b7962158ef0e9067b6bd96ed/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2682

mutates the pod object in place (vs creating a copy first).  That's illegal and can cause data races or potentially panics (the panic is unlikely here but I can't rule it out).

This line should be:

```
pod = updatedPod
...
kl.podManager.UpdatePod(pod)
```

This should be fixed because we might serialize the object in the middle of this from somewhere else and if the object changes midway the protobuf object we create may not be valid, leading to panics in kubelets with this gate turned on.

No mutation of pod objects from within `Sync*Pod` methods (in fact no mutation of `pod` should occur in most loops).

title: API-initiated eviction does not work on first try in certain scenarios, but does work on second try
description:
### What happened?

Scenarios that require setting resourceVersion either

- explicitly to the eviction request
- or when the eviction API needs to make sure that the pod has not become ready when deleting unready pods https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L232

fails to evict a pod. This is caused by a conflict with PodDisruptionConditions feature, which adds a condition to a pod, and the delete itself fails. The second eviction works correctly and results in a pod deletion.

### What did you expect to happen?

eviction should succeed on a first try 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a simple pod

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  containers:
    - name:  nginx
      image: registry.k8s.io/nginx-slim:0.8
```

```
$ kubectl apply -f nginx.yaml
```

2. obtain its resource version

```
$ kubectl get pod nginx -oyaml | grep resourceVersion
> resourceVersion: "313"
```

3. try to evict it

```
$ kubectl create -f - <<EOF --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/nginx/eviction
{"apiVersion": "policy/v1", "kind": "Eviction", "metadata": {"name": "nginx"}, "deleteOptions": {"preconditions": {"resourceVersion": "313"}}}
EOF
$ Error from server (Conflict): Operation cannot be fulfilled on Pod "nginx": the ResourceVersion in the precondition (313) does not match the ResourceVersion in record (425). The object might have been modified
```

the eviction request fails, but we can see that the DisruptionTarget condition has been added to the pod

```
$ oc get pod nginx -oyaml | grep DisruptionTarget -B 5
>   - lastProbeTime: null
>    lastTransitionTime: "2023-03-13T21:29:04Z"
>    message: 'Eviction API: evicting'
>    reason: EvictionByEvictionAPI
>    status: "False"
>    type: DisruptionTarget
```

4. second eviction with updated resouce version succeeds


```
$ kubectl create -f - <<EOF --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/nginx/eviction
{"apiVersion": "policy/v1", "kind": "Eviction", "metadata": {"name": "nginx"}, "deleteOptions": {"preconditions": {"resourceVersion": "520"}}}
EOF
> {"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Success","code":201}
```

title: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
description:
### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What did you expect to happen?

Every deleted running pod is transitioned to a terminal phase if there is a finalizer.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a pod like this:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: running-pod
  finalizers: ["example.com/my-finalizer"]
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: centos:7
    command: ["bash"]
    args: ["-c", 'echo "Hello world" && sleep 1800']
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```
2. Delete the pod by `kubectl delete`
After 30s check the pod status with `kubectl get pods -oyaml`. You can see:

```yaml
    containerStatuses:
    - ...
      state:
        terminated:
          exitCode: 137
          reason: Error
    phase: Running
```
**Issue**: the pod remains the in the **Running** phase forever.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Service publishNotReadyAddresses and EndpointSlices Conditions
description:
The EndpointSlice API says

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fafa45d13c21dcf99801631413fc58e9cf91226c/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go#L111-L116

and it works as expected in normal circumstances

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: terminating
  labels:
    app: MyApp
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 300
  containers:
  - name: agnhost
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.39
    args:
      - netexec
      - --http-port=80
      - --delay-shutdown=300
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: terminating-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: MyApp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
```

I delete the pod and the endpoints conditions are the expected
```
    ready: false
    serving: true
    terminating: true
```

However, if during this time I set `service.spec.publishNotReadyAddresses: true` 

```
    ready: true
    serving: true
    terminating: true
```

we run into an incoherence with the API doc, but it seems that we already documented this edge case in the code

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fafa45d13c21dcf99801631413fc58e9cf91226c/pkg/controller/endpointslice/utils.go#L44-L60

I think that at this point is just to amend this information to the API, no? 

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go b/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go
index efc2d331ec9..1a19ad5ecaa 100644
--- a/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go
+++ b/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go
@@ -112,7 +112,8 @@ type EndpointConditions struct {
        // according to whatever system is managing the endpoint. A nil value
        // indicates an unknown state. In most cases consumers should interpret this
        // unknown state as ready. For compatibility reasons, ready should never be
-       // "true" for terminating endpoints.
+       // "true" for terminating endpoints, except when the Service associated has
+       // enabled the field PublishNotReadyAddresses.
        Ready *bool
 
```

title: VPA panics in standalone kubelets
description:
1. Start a standalone kubelet (not registered to an API server)

2. Manager construction short-circuits `Start()` here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/253ab3eda71f250ad6692bb16f035cebaf0651c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L186-L192

3. VPA state is never initialized here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/253ab3eda71f250ad6692bb16f035cebaf0651c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L195-L200

4. All pod syncs then panic on this line:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a1b12e49eac237a37939642d0c3395008b9ab380/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2412

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x18 pc=0x3b5f21f]
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet.(*Kubelet).HandlePodAdditions(0xc00073c400, {0xc001816c00?, 0x27, 0x40})
  pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:2412 +0x4df
```

_Originally posted by @liggitt in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102884#issuecomment-1454089210_

cc @thockin @vinaykul

comments.text:
also, if VPA state cannot be constructed here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/253ab3eda71f250ad6692bb16f035cebaf0651c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L195-L200

logging an error, setting state to nil, and continuing means every use of `checkpointState := kl.statusManager.State()` in the pod sync loop is a potential NPE

title: kubectl apply requires CRDs to apply non-CRD resources if we use `kind: List`
description:
### What happened?

kubectl apply performs validation before the apply. 

Non-CRD resources (e.g. pods / deployments) don't need CRD schema for validation, but if we use `kind: List` resource, kubectl calls `LIST apis/apiextensions.k8s.io/v1/customresourcedefinitions`.

```yaml
      app: nginx
```

title: Cacher may not send events if it reinitializes at the time of watch initialization
description:
Found when reviewing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116024

I'm still not 100% convinced it's true, but I believe this is a faulty scenario:
1. new watch is being established `Watch()` method
2. `c.ready` is still initialized so we successfully pass the c.ready.wait() check
3. `ListAndWatch` in `startCaching` fails (for whatever reason)
4. `c.ready.set(false)` is called (from defer in `startCaching`)
5. `startCaching` is called again and we call `terminateAllWatchers()`
6. the Watch call (started in point 1 above) only now continues to be processed and is established (and added to watchers) - init events are being send in the meantime
7. `ListAndWatch` is being called from `startCaching` which reinitializes watchCache to a new (higher RV)
8. if some events missed in the meantime, they will not be delivered to this newly established watch

title: PVs with annotations are not being dynamically provisioned on k8s 1.26.1
description:
### What happened?

We observed that when deplying manifests to a cluster running 1.26.1-gke.200, the StorageClass and PVC get created successfully. However, the PVC is stuck in a Pending state and no PV is provisioned.

The workaround is to add storageClassName to one of the pending PVCs on cluster, and it did go from Pending to properly provisioned a PV and reaching Bound state. 

We looked at the logs and found that according to the doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/#class,

```
In the past, the annotation volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-class 
was used instead of the storageClassName attribute. This annotation
 is still working; however, it will become fully deprecated in a future 
Kubernetes release.
```

Is this annotation is fully deprecated in the new 1.26.1 release? If yes can we add this detail to documentation or release note?






### What did you expect to happen?

the PVC should not stuck in a Pending state and PV is provisioned in 1.26.1

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a 1.26.1-gke.200 cluster in GKE
2. Create via yaml

```
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: sunnytest-sc
parameters:
  type: pd-ssd
provisioner: kubernetes.io/gce-pd
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: storage-class-issue-test
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: storage-class-issue-test
  serviceName: storage-class-issue-test
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: storage-class-issue-test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: writer
        image: busybox
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 100Mi
          requests:
            cpu: 10m
            memory: 80Mi
        command:
          - "/bin/sh"
          - "-c"
          - touch /data/${MY_POD_NAME} && while true; do echo $(date) >> /data/${MY_POD_NAME}; sleep 1; done
        env:
          - name: MY_POD_NAME
            valueFrom:
              fieldRef:
                fieldPath: metadata.name
        volumeMounts:
        - name: local-disk
          mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    metadata:
      annotations:
        volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-class: sunnytest-sc
      creationTimestamp: null
      name: cassandra-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
      volumeMode: Filesystem
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The error comes form the code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/915924e64d08b7b2d3e6da81840e46d96304cdc9/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller_base.go#L275 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/915924e64d08b7b2d3e6da81840e46d96304cdc9/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L2259

There are some hypotheses here:

The annotation volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-class does not work on 1.26.1 any more, so a default storage class is being populated to the PVC.
For some reason, the [DefaultStorageClass admission controller](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/#defaultstorageclass) did not work, so the PVC was deployed with an empty StorageClass nil.
Then the kube controller manager tried to update the PVC with the default StorageClass, which triggered the error:

```console
$ kubectl version
```

title: Cannot create ingress with ingressClass annotation and IngressClassName both set
description:
### What happened?

An ingress resource with both `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation and `spec.ingressClassName` set cannot be **created**. Ingress resources can be updated to include both the annotation and the `ingressClassName` without issue.

Kubernetes response:

> The Ingress "example-ingress" is invalid: annotations.kubernetes.io/ingress.class: Invalid value: "nginx": can not be set when the class field is also set


### What did you expect to happen?

The ingress should be deployed with both annotation and `spec.ingressClassName` set, as it is supported by updating an existing ingress.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this resource:

```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: example-ingress
  annotations:
    ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
```

description:
It can be observed in any kubelet log, just pick one from a random job in CI, per example

The `lastFinishedPulling` time is always `0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000`, that is the golang zero time IIRC.

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go b/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go

                        m.logIt(ref, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.PulledImage, logPrefix, msg, klog.Info)
                        return imageRef, "", nil
                }
@@ -164,6 +166,7 @@ func (m *imageManager) EnsureImageExists(ctx context.Context, pod *v1.Pod, conta
 
                return "", imagePullResult.err.Error(), ErrImagePull
        }
+       m.podPullingTimeRecorder.RecordImageFinishedPulling(pod.UID)
```

but this means that we are lacking testing on these, feature, I'd expected to see at least 2 new tests in

`pkg/kubelet/util/pod_startup_latency_tracker_test.go`
`pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager_test.go`

### What happened?

A status of Pod mounted NFS PV remain as terminating when a node shutdown and restart.

### What did you expect to happen?

A Pod is completely terminated.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

### Summary

- Deploy a Pod mounted NFS PV
- Shutdown the node where the Pod is running
- Wait for 5 min and the Pod status become `Terminating`
- Restart the node
- The Pod status is still `Terminating` and the Pod is never terminated completely

<details>

### Reproduce

Prepare a NFS Server.(I used `nfs-kernel-server`)  

Deploy a Pod mounted NFS PV like this.  
`nfs-pv-test-pod.yaml`
```yaml
apiVersion: v1

metadata:
  labels:
    run: nfs-pv-test-pod
  name: nfs-pv-test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - image: ubuntu
    name: nfs-pv-test-pod
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while :; do sleep 10; done"]
    volumeMounts:
      - name: nfs-test-volume
        mountPath: "/srv"
  volumes:
    - name: nfs-test-volume
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: nfs-test-pvc
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: node02

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: nfs-test-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Mi

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: nfs-test-pv
spec:
  capacity:

  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany

    server: <NFS Server IP Address>
    path: <NFS Server Dir Path>
```

title: kube-scheduler: Bring back the ability to stop at the first failed filter
description:
#108829 changed the default behavior of scheduler framework's `RunFilterPlugins` - from stopping at the first failed filter to always running all filters. This change breaks Cluster Autoscaler at scale. Cluster Autoscaler imports the scheduler framework to simulate filters on artificial nodes. In a (pretty common) one-pod-per-node scenario, the number of `RunFilterPlugins` calls is ~quadratic wrt. the number of nodes needed for unschedulable pods - it can be a lot of calls. Before #108829, in such scenario the vast majority of `RunFilterPlugins` calls would stop at failing Fit or NodeAffinity filters, and not run the rest of them (e.g. PV-related filters). After the change, every call to `RunFilterPlugins` runs all filters, which completely breaks Cluster Autoscaler at scale (an example scenario of 300 1-pod-per-node pods and 200 node groups takes >10min in 1.24, and ~50s in <1.22).

Can we get the old behavior back? Or re-introduce the config option so that Cluster Autoscaler can set it accordingly? Ideally, we'd also like to get this backported as far as possible (the change was introduced in 1.24).

comments.text: This seems to be a regression. I would be interested in adding a toggle flag that allows one to toggle on that behavior if this was done on purpose.

> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108829 changed the default behavior of scheduler framework's RunFilterPlugins - from stopping at the first failed filter to always running all filters.

That PR wasn't supposed to change the behavior actually. Scheduler is always defaulted to stop upon the first Filter failure, and it's just we offered an option to continue go through other Filter plugins upon failures, and that option was removed recently.

Let me check the code to see if there is a regression.
Thanks Kuba, this is indeed a regression on the scheduler end.

title: Discovery memCacheClient has inconsistent error behavior with other DiscoveryInterfaces
description:
### What happened?

I think this got stale and closed because it was posted on `kubernetes/client-go` but is still very relevant:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/745

The [memCacheClient](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/f81a9405fae9d2a97f479bab1ab540fad1d2f178/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L47) created by memory.NewMemCacheClient(...) returns an error when calling ServerResourcesForGroupVersion if the APIResources list returned is empty, as seen here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/6d14209323d355841b67c4d9ca8c22fb1ca930a6/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L214-L216

Our particular case came up due to the `external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1` API group being registered with the API server, but having no resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

If using [NewMemcachedDiscoveryClient](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/cmd/root.go#L425) like [here](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/pkg/kubecfg/validate.go#L48) to discover `apiservices` with zero current resources there should not be an error returned.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Do a discovery with a [memCacheClient](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/f81a9405fae9d2a97f479bab1ab540fad1d2f178/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L47) against a Kubernetes cluster that has at least one `apiservice` with zero resources. The condition on the server that triggers the described issue can be expressed as e.g.:
```
$ kubectl get --raw /apis/external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1
{"kind": "APIResourceList","apiVersion":"v1","groupVersion":"external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1","resources":[]}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I would be good to get to know the reasoning behind the emptiness check in the `memCacheClient`, maybe there is good reason for it.

<details>
Client Version: v1.20.15
Server Version: v1.22.8-gke.202

Reviving this issue based on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/issues/146.

This behavior has become quite annoying for the custom/external metrics aggregated APIs since after https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/b8fe2c7b8061e6ab0b093a49351bac256606da4a, client-go is now producing a very spammy error log when an aggregated API is found without resource.

This is a very common scenario with the metric APIs since metrics are dynamically registered as Resources to the aggregated APIs so on startup the aggregated apiserver may not expose any resource and that's completely normal. It is even more common for implementations of these APIs that register metric Resources from CRDs as CRs tend to be created later than APIServices and the aggregated apiserver.

I can see a few path forward to improve the situation for us:
1. Remove the error if we consider that having no resources exposed by an aggregated API is acceptable
2. Increase the verbosity of the log to just show it in debugging scenarios
3. We somehow update https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/ to defer registration until we have at least one Metric resource.

@deads2k could you perhaps share your insight on that one please?

Hello folks!
Any update on this topic? The message is really spammy
Removing triage accepted manually since there was no update on this for more than 6 months.

For context, I traced it back and `len(r.APIResources) == 0` check has been considered an error since the first iteration of the in-memory discovery client in #48502:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8e7db3a0d34399e8235daed4b20abcd222cf1b34/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/memcachediscovery/client.go#L143-L150

It is unexpected for a built-in or CRD groupversion to have no resources, but for aggregated-apiservice I can see it being possible that the `APIService` object is created and set up for discovery before the aggregated-apiservice is ready.

I think this is [the commit in kube-client](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773) which introduces [the error we are facing in KEDA](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/issues/146) (but maybe I'm wrong).  
There is also [an issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/1223) in that repo about the same issue after upgrading the kube-client pkg. [Could the option I suggested](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/issues/146#issuecomment-1402467093) in custom-metrics repo be correct from Kubernetes pov?
IMO we need to find a solution soon or the amount of noise will increase once people bump their deps and tooling ([helm is affected](https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/11772), kubectl is affected, and any tool which uses kube-client is affected)

title: Improve readiness times for clusters that use envelope encryption and create large numbers of secrets.
description:
**What would you like to be added**:
Remove the need to call remote KMS for every new Secret.

**Why is this needed**:
Due to the serial processing of List requests, the initialization of informers may take significant time due to the large number of consecutive trips to KMS. For example, assuming a 40 milliseconds round-trip to a KMS and two thousand secrets, the initialization of an informer may take 80 seconds.

Relevant PRs:
Reduce the number of trips to KMS by caching DEKs. #87438
Transform from storage concurrently during List operation. #88633

comments.text:
Breaking the problem up a bit, we can reduce the number of calls across two boundaries:

1. kube-apiserver -> kms plugin
2. kms plugin -> non-local kms

Most ideas are around DEK reuse. Writing down notes from the brainstorm:

### Boundary 1

We've discussed a lot of options. I like the idea of keeping the DEKs one to one with objects, but reusing DEKs to encrypt the same object. If we use a counter to generate nonces (vs generating nonces randomly), we don't have to worry about the birthday problem and can switch to AES-GCM for data encryption without concern.

### Boundary 2

Plugins can reduce calls to remote KMS services by implementing a multi level KEK hierarchy. I.e. a plugin keeps local KEKs that it reuses across DEKs for some number of operations.

With ad hoc symbolic notation for operations:

```
| = concatenate
kid(key) -> key identifier
enc(key, data) -> cipher text
dec(key, cipher text) -> data
```

For an example key hierarchy:

![Key Hierarchy](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1787169/81361125-66a5fa80-9092-11ea-8df8-24e2f00ca9d9.png)

object_0_0_1 is stored as:

```
kid(kek_0) | enc(kek_0, kek_0_0) \
| kid(kek_0_0) | enc(kek_0_0, dek_0_0_1) \
| kid(dek_0_0_1) | enc(dek_0_0_1, object_0_0_1)
```
@enj @kubernetes/sig-auth-bugs

I am adding some background on GCM to help us navigate the decision on approach - caching DEK vs.  hierarchical key structure (as suggested by @mikedanese). 
 
From [NIST 800-38D](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf) (emphasis and omissions are mine):
### Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC.
- The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed
**2^32** ... with the given key. 

**My interpretation of the above (in the context of envelope encryption feature):**
Given the upper limit of 2^32 invocations, it is safe cache DEKs when:

1. TTL is in the range of minutes (very conservative)
2. IV is produced via /dev/urandom (or via a counter as suggested by @mikedanese). 

Note that setting the cache TTL in the range of several minutes will dramatically reduce the number of trips to KMS since requests for Secrets creation are typically batched (ex. cluster creation or service deployment). The drawback of caching DEKs is that uses would need to wait for the duration of the cache TTL before performing storage migration.

I am adding PCI DSS requirements relevant to the protection of secrets at rest:

**3.5.3 Store secret and private keys used to encrypt/decrypt cardholder data in one (or more) of the following forms at all times**:

- Encrypted with a key-encrypting key that is at least as strong as the data encrypting key, and that is stored separately from the data-encrypting key

- Within a secure cryptographic device (such as a hardware (host) security module (HSM) or PTS approved point-of-interaction device)

- As at least two full-length key components or key shares, in accordance with an industry accepted method  

**3.6.4 Cryptographic key changes for keys that have reached the end of their crypto period** (for example, after a defined period of time has passed and/or after a certain amount of cipher-text has been produced by a given key), **as defined by the associated application vendor or key owner**, and based on industry best practices and guidelines (for example, NIST Special Publication 800-57). 

**3.6.5 Retirement or replacement (for example, archiving, destruction, and/or revocation) of keys as deemed necessary when the integrity of the key has been weakened** (for example, departure of an employee with knowledge of a clear-text key component), or keys are suspected of being compromised.

So I tried reading the hierarchical key structure but I will admit I am unable to parse what the image is trying to say ...

---

@immutableT would it be valuable to perform this experiment:

1. Create a cluster with KMS configured (to some cloud KMS) and create a large number of encrypted at rest secrets (100k?)
1. Set KMS `cachesize` cache size to > 100k
1. Restart cluster
1. Measure start up time
1. Calculate mean and standard deviation of gRPC calls.  This will give us the overhead of `kube-apiserver -> kms plugin` + `kms plugin -> non-local kms` calls.

Perform the same experiment but change the KMS to https://github.com/enj/citadel with a static KEK (i.e. `echo $secret_key`).  This will give us a good idea of what the overhead of the `kube-apiserver -> kms plugin` calls.

We can then determine `kube-apiserver -> kms plugin` vs. `kms plugin -> non-local kms` overhead.  In particular, it would tell us if a KMS plugin proxy that caches a KEK temporarily is viable or if we need to make changes directly to the API server.

Yes it would be. Furthermore, I think it would be a useful metric to have (see [REDACTED]

While I am working on this experiment, I can provide some rough numbers based on my environment.

title: client-go/kubectl rejects discovery API responses with charset encoding info
description:
We are using `client-go` (and `kubectl`) to interact with Kubernetes clusters behind a couple of proxy layers. One of these proxies completes the `Content-Type` headers to include character encoding details.

This was working fine until recently, when client-go/kubectl have started to fail when interacting with the discovery API. It seems that a recent change has made kubectl more restrictive of the content-type that it expects. I suspect that it is related to this commit: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773

For example, this is an error from a kubectl command:
```
...
E0422 16:28:02.626222   86629 memcache.go:265] couldn't get current server API group list: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626258   86629 cached_discovery.go:120] skipped caching discovery info due to Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626346   86629 shortcut.go:100] Error loading discovery information: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
```

We can of course try to fix it on our end, removing that charset information. However, it is a valid content-type and the way kubectl is handling the content-type there seems like it is relying on implementation details of kube-apiserver (that it does not add metadata to the content-type). I propose to fix this issue in `kubectl`, by properly parsing and handling the content-type.

title: Strategic Merge does not handle directives for empty slices.
description:
### What happened?

When performing a strategic merge for a slice of maps with `patchStrategy=merge`, directives in the patch slice are ignored if the original list is empty. Instead, the merged slice still contains the directives. This causes the patched object to fail subsequent validation since it has directives in a slice.

This behavior can be seen if one attempts to patch `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration.admissionregistration.k8s.io` specifically changes to the optional field [Webhooks](https://github.com/kubernetes/api/blob/master/admissionregistration/v1beta1/types.go#L93-L97).

If the original object has the following value
``` json
{
    "apiVersion": "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "ValidatingWebhookConfiguration",
    "metadata": {
        "creationTimestamp": "2023-04-19T13:41:39Z",
        "generation": 2,
        "name": "base-validation",
        "resourceVersion": "200160",
        "uid": "70d47b26-ddba-430a-82d2-3fe7f8b4b840"
    }
}
```
And we attempt to do a strategic patch with the following information 
``` json
{
    "$setElementOrder/webhooks": [
        {
            "name": "new.foo.com"
        }
    ],
    "webhooks": [
        {
            "admissionReviewVersions": [
                "v1"
            ],
            "clientConfig": {
                "url": "https://foo.com"
            },
            "name": "new.foo.com",
            "sideEffects": "None"
        },
        {
            "$patch": "delete",
            "name": "foo.bar.com"
        }
    ]
}
```
The resulting object will look like the following JSON and fail validation.
``` json
{
    "apiVersion": "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "ValidatingWebhookConfiguration",
    "metadata": {
        "creationTimestamp": "2023-04-19T13:41:39Z",
        "generation": 2,
        "name": "base-validation",
        "resourceVersion": "200160",
        "uid": "70d47b26-ddba-430a-82d2-3fe7f8b4b840"
    },
    "webhooks": [
        {
            "admissionReviewVersions": [
                "v1"
            ],
            "clientConfig": {
                "url": "https://foo.com"
            },
            "name": "new.foo.com",
            "sideEffects": "None"
        },
        {
            "$patch": "delete",
            "name": "foo.bar.com"
        }
    ]
}
```
Errors:
```
The ValidatingWebhookConfiguration "base-validation" is invalid: 
* webhooks[1].sideEffects: Required value: must specify one of None, NoneOnDryRun
* webhooks[1].clientConfig: Required value: exactly one of url or service is required
* webhooks[1].admissionReviewVersions: Required value: must specify one of v1, v1beta1
```


### What did you expect to happen?

Strategic merge always handles any directives in the patch.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

## Repo steps with kubectl
1. Apply the following webhook configuration `kubectl apply`
    ``` yaml
    apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
    kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
    metadata:
      name: base-validation
    webhooks:
      - name: foo.bar.com
        admissionReviewVersions:
          - "v1"
        clientConfig:
          url: https://foo.com
        sideEffects: None
    ```
2. Edit the newly created webhook and remove the Webhooks list. `kubectl edit validatingwebhookconfiguration base-validation`

3. Attempt to apply the following webhook configuration with `kubectl apply`
      ``` yaml
      apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
      kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
      metadata:
        name: base-validation
      webhooks:
        - name: new.foo.com
          admissionReviewVersions:
            - "v1"
          clientConfig:
            url: https://foo.com
          sideEffects: None
    ```

Notice that the request fails with the following errors
```
The ValidatingWebhookConfiguration "base-validation" is invalid: 
* webhooks[1].sideEffects: Required value: must specify one of None, NoneOnDryRun
* webhooks[1].clientConfig: Required value: exactly one of url or service is required
* webhooks[1].admissionReviewVersions: Required value: must specify one of v1, v1beta1
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The logic causing this behavior for the example can be seen here in [apimachinery](https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/util/strategicpatch/patch.go#L1179-L1194)
In this code, we see that if the original value was not found, we blindly assign the `patchFieldValue`

Filed a PR which should fix the issue. The AWS controller isn't erroring when syncing nodes which are missing the providerID, as reported in the original issue. Would it have done that: the Node sync would have been retried until the providerID was set. 

Given this: I've added the providerID as a predicate when syncing Nodes. This will enforce that it is always set when the cloud-provider code gets invoked and we always trigger a new sync once the providerID gets set.

Thanks for the PR with the fix and if we want the cloud provider to error out in such scenarios, then I think it would make sense to update the comments for the method in the interface such that we are setting the right expectations for the providers who are going to implement the interface

description:
### What happened?

On a new 1.27 kubernetes cluster, Using server-side dry-run to apply a custom resource with an older version results in the following error:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a94d7b76a3550c240b8fa0c18894ab43852778c8/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/conversion/converter.go#L266-L270
@liggitt thank you so much for the quick turnaround. When 1.27.1 gets released we'll let Flux users know they can safely upgrade.

This appears to have started with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112450/files#diff-4dc8e8f75c3aae18ff37f80d409ed39256f134bdc54f4a42deb81f1694c19fb4R115, since each call of `rest.TransportFor` in `k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apiserver.(*proxyHandler).updateAPIService` accesses the cache with a unique `DialHolder` pointer.

### What did you expect to happen?

Even with a zero cache hit rate, the cache should not grow indefinitely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Trigger many APIServiceRegistrationController resyncs by repeatedly patching an APIService (e.g. update an annotation with random bytes). Watch kube-apiserver's heap inuse_space grow.

title: `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` always fails when called for wrapped volume
description:
### What happened?

Every time `volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed)` from `empty_dir.go` is called for a projected volume, it fails with "no such file or directory" error.

The problem comes from the fact that `SetVolumeOwnership()` always calculates the root dir for ownership changes as `mounter.GetPath()` while projected.go explicitly passes another dir as the first arg of `SetUpAt()` call:
```
	if err := wrapped.SetUpAt(dir, mounterArgs); err != nil {
		return err
	}
```
(see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/96306f144a3c917a97fe27c9ad5dd89e4213f741/pkg/volume/projected/projected.go#L203)

### What did you expect to happen?

`volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` must succeed when a projected volume is created.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Print return value of `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` when called from `empty_dir.go`:
```
diff --git a/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go b/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
index 9ad981c54bd..ce3f7d330fe 100644
--- a/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
+++ b/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
@@ -280,7 +280,10 @@ func (ed *emptyDir) SetUpAt(dir string, mounterArgs volume.MounterArgs) error {
                err = fmt.Errorf("unknown storage medium %q", ed.medium)
        }
 
-       volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed, mounterArgs.FsGroup, nil /*fsGroupChangePolicy*/, volumeutil.FSGroupCompleteHook(ed.plugin, nil))
+       e := volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed, mounterArgs.FsGroup, nil /*fsGroupChangePolicy*/, volumeutil.FSGroupCompleteHook(ed.plugin, nil))
+       if e != nil {
+               klog.Infof("ZZZ: SetVolumeOwnership() returned error: %v (dir: %v; ed.GetPath(): %v)", e, dir, ed.GetPath())
+       }
 
        // If setting up the quota fails, just log a message but don't actually error out.
        // We'll use the old du mechanism in this case, at least until we support
```

Start an arbitrary pod, then look at kubelet logs:
```
$ kubectl apply -f fedora.yaml

$ grep ZZZ /tmp/kubelet.log
I0330 12:59:06.614097    2985 empty_dir.go:285] ZZZ: SetVolumeOwnership() returned error: lstat /var/lib/kubelet/pods/a2f6e58f-7edf-4c48-a97c-ef1b8fd3caf6/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/wrapped_kube-api-access-knvkv: no such file or directory (dir: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/a2f6e58f-7edf-4c48-a97c-ef1b8fd3caf6/volumes/kubernetes.io~projected/kube-api-access-knvkv; ed.GetPath(): /var/lib/kubelet/pods/a2f6e58f-7edf-4c48-a97c-ef1b8fd3caf6/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/wrapped_kube-api-access-knvkv)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

title: daemonset stuck in `Completed` state after a reboot (with graceful kubelet shutdown)

### What happened?

I can reproduce this reliably with Calico v3.25.0 CNI, installed straight from the upstream [manifest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.25.0/manifests/calico.yaml).

It seems to be a **regression** in Kubernetes 1.27.0-rc.0 compared to 1.27.0-beta.0, at least I can't reproduce it with beta.0.

Cluster is deployed, and everything is ready & healthy. After a series of node reboots some `calico-node` pods are stuck in `Completed` state and never recover:

The pods are restarted.

comments.text: I wonder if that is related to the change #115331
cc @smarterclayton @bobbypage @mimowo this might a regression in 1.27.0-rc.0 with this PR #115331

@mimowo I also have complete output of `kubectl get` under the details in the issue itself.

> I think there might be something with the fact that Calico terminates with exit code '0', so it feels like a "successful" run.

The daemonset controller should still recreate the pod in that scenario.

The reproducer is to follow the [Talos QEMU guide](https://www.talos.dev/v1.4/talos-guides/install/local-platforms/qemu/), but it should be same under any Talos platforms except Docker (which doesn't have a graceful node shutdown, and any kind of shutdown).

I verified it with the assets from the latest [1.4.0-alpha.4 release](https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/releases/tag/v1.4.0-alpha.4).

The smallest I can reproduce it with is 1+1 cluster, but it looks same way e.g. in 3+2 cluster:

```
sudo -E talosctl cluster create --provisioner=qemu --controlplanes 1 --workers 1 --custom-cni-url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.25.0/manifests/calico.yaml
```

Once the cluster is up, all the pods are running & healthy (`kubectl get pods -A -o wide`). If I issue a reboot of the worker node with `talosctl -n 10.5.0.3 reboot`, with `watch -n 2 kubectl get pods -A -o wide` shows that `calico-node` pod on the worker node quickly enters `Completed` state, and never recovers.

At the same time I don't quite understand what is exactly wrong, as if I just do a daemonset with `sleep 10` command, the pod also enters `Completed` state, but it gets quickly restarted by the `kubelet` via `CrashLoopBackOff` transition.
I can also send kubelet logs, and anything else which might be helpful to debug the issue, I'm also open to do a debug session with screen sharing.

> At the same time I don't quite understand what is exactly wrong, as if I just do a daemonset with `sleep 10` command, the pod also enters `Completed` state, but it gets quickly restarted by the `kubelet` via `CrashLoopBackOff` transition.

This is because of `restartPolicy: Always`. The pod doesn't reach the `Succeeded` phase in this case. The kubelet just recreates the containers. However, when a pod is actually marked as "Succeeded" then kubelet would stop looking at it.

However, it should be the responsibility of the daemonset controller to recreate a pod.

Following the sig-apps advise opened the PR [REDACTED] with an integration test for DaemonSet. 

It passes for Failed pods, but fails for Succeeded. In other words, the succeeded pods are not restarted. I'm yet to investigate (probably tomorrow) why this is so, but it seems like a bug. In the meanwhile some expertise about DaemonSets would be helpful.

Thanks for reporting this. I suppose this might be related to the fact that `restartAlways` pods (created by daemonset) can now be marked as [terminal phase](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d89d5ab2680bc74fe4487ad71e514f4e0812d9ce/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L1463-L1486) in v1.27.

When graceful node shutdown happens, we terminate the pod with `killPodNow`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d89d5ab2680bc74fe4487ad71e514f4e0812d9ce/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L377

which will trigger kubelet to terminate the pod in pod worker (`syncTerminatingPod/syncTerminatedPod`) and eventually I assume set a terminal phase on the pod. We should verify if that is what is happening here.

In either case, +1 on comment that I would expect that daemonset controller should recreate a pod if it is marked completed.

I will note that the intent for graceful shutdown was always that pods could be marked Succeeded (vs just Failed), since the pod is indeed terminal.  It's likely that this was previously racy (no guarantee succeeded made it to the apiserver) and #115331 fixed that.

However, outside of graceful shutdown this should never occur - do we have any evidence a RestartAlways pod went succeeded in that case (wasn't clear from the thread)?  That would be a serious bug.

> However, outside of graceful shutdown this should never occur - do we have any evidence a RestartAlways pod went succeeded in that case (wasn't clear from the thread)? That would be a serious bug.

I think Succeeded would also be possible in other scenarios, like deletion (deletionTimestamp!=nil). This I've tested for Job pods, but I think DS pods would behave the same. 

Except for deletion I think the behavior is limited to graceful node shutdown, which invokes the kill function, but respects the Succeeded phase: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L377-L381. Other uses of the kill function unconditionally set Failed, such as the eviction manager: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L586.

EDIT: oh, actually for Jobs we don't use restartPolicy=Always, but still deleted pods with  restartPolicy=Always may still terminate with Succeeded phase as shown in this test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d89d5ab2680bc74fe4487ad71e514f4e0812d9ce/test/e2e_node/deleted_pods_test.go#L142
Deletion with RestartAlways is ok, because the pod goes away reasonably fast (but we are adding latency in 1.27 to that path) as you note.

title: `creationTimestamp: null` still causes unnecessary etcd-write with SSA
description:
### What happened?

Sending a patch built from a typed client to SSA will force a write to etcd (and bump resourceVersion) since creationTimestamp is serialized to null. This is a follow-up of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106388 which doesn't solve the issue properly.

### What did you expect to happen?

Sending a no-op SSA request with creationTimestamp to null shouldn't do anything

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Kubectl apply an object with creationTimestamp null twice and see that it updates the object.
Probably something like this would cause it:
```
for i in "$(seq 1 10); do kubectl apply --server-side=true -f - -o yaml <<EOF
kind: ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
    name: some-configmap
    creationTimestamp: null # This is unfortunately done automatically when using typed client
data:
EOF
done
```

title: Memory leak in kubelet volume_manager populator processedPods
description:
### What happened?

If a pod is created and then deleted an entry in processedPods map remains forever (sometimes, it's racy).

The problem comes from the fact that `podWorker` calls volume_manager `WaitForUnmount()` asynchronously. If the last call happens after populator cleaned up resources, an entry is added to processedPods and will never be seen.

### What did you expect to happen?

An entry in processedPods map must be deleted if pod doesn't exist and pod runtime should removed according to `dswp.podStateProvider`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To verify that the issue really exists I applaied a simple [patch](https://github.com/jsafrane/kubernetes/commit/40ffc8e62836244ea6cffde8b9dff2c402d058c5) printing resources in `processedPods` map. Here is a reproducer:

1. Start brand-new fresh k8s cluster with `hack/local-up-cluster.sh`
2. Check entries in `processedPods`:
```
I0321 15:03:42.131049    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:03:43.131815    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 1
```
3. Create a pod, check its uid:
```
$ k get po fdroot -o yaml |grep uid
  uid: a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a
```
4. Verify that this uid is accurately reported:
```
I0321 15:05:06.193326    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 2
I0321 15:05:06.193412    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:05:06.193434    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: true
```
5. Delete the pod, wait for a few mins, check for `processedPods` again:
```
I0321 15:48:29.113233    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:262] JSAF: processed pods size: 3
I0321 15:48:29.113252    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod ac109c78-ce77-4426-9421-53fbcfe2175b: true
I0321 15:48:29.113259    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: false
I0321 15:48:29.113262    2149 desired_state_of_world_populator.go:264] JSAF: processed pod 213bcdcb-c9e7-4d96-af41-353d651cbd86: true
```

The entry `a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a: false` will be kept forever because kubelet doesn't know anything about this pod anymore:
```
$ k get pods --all-namespaces -o yaml |grep "a0158a6e-3b23-4a68-a50b-5d44e0fc009a"
$
```
so no more events will ever come to populater for this uid, and the loop in `findAndRemoveDeletedPods()` won't find it because it was already deleted from `dswp.desiredStateOfWorld`.

### Anything else we need to know?

n/a

title: Last apiserver to shutdown doesn't remove its IP from k8s svc endpoints
description:
### What happened?

As part of the apiserver's pre-shutdown sequence, we stop the lease-controller from renewing the apiserver's etcd lease anymore and delete the lease:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/controller.go#L211-L215

As part of the `RemoveEndpoints` call we expect that after the lease is deleted, the apiserver's IP is also removed from the k8s service endpoints object:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L315-L321

However, `doReconcile` isn't removing the IP if it's the last remaining one:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L210-L215

The comment there is assuming that `doReconcile` is always called after renewing the lease, which is incorrect since it can also be called as part of the shutdown workflow.

### What did you expect to happen?

The IP of the apiserver (even though it's the last one remaining) should be removed from k8s svc endpoints on shutdown.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Shutdown the last apiserver of the cluster and you'll see logs like this:

```
I1031 17:34:49.517758      12 controller.go:181] Shutting down kubernetes service endpoint reconciler
E1031 17:34:49.534880      12 controller.go:184] no master IPs were listed in storage, refusing to erase all endpoints for the kubernetes service
```

And the audit logs also confirm that the IP isn't removed from k8s endpoints object.

### Anything else we need to know?

Why is the above an issue?

If the IP isn't removed from the k8s endpoints object, clients (using in-cluster API mode) will try to continue talking/connecting to that instance even after the apiserver is dead. There are at least two issues with this:
- Causes confusing `i/o timeout` and `connection refused` errors for clients, instead of a cleaner `no route to host` error
- If the apiserver pod is restarted by kubelet (let's say due to healthcheck failure), clients may start talking to it prematurely even without healthz/readyz passing. This is not a recommended behavior ([xref](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/health-checks/)) as a bunch post-startup hooks like informer sync, internal controllers, etc may not have initialized yet
