comments.text: The most prefered solution is to cache serialized metav1.Event objects and reuse its result in all watchers.
+1 for addressing this, but I won't have time to look into it any time soon.
Hi, is it okay for me to try implement the cache solution if I'm totally new to the codebase?
Hey,  can I take a stab on it? if no one is working on it?

@mborsz @wojtek-t @shyamjvs poke ... anything we can do here for 1.26?

@akankshakumari393 looks like no one is working on this yet. so go for it.

Yes, I'm not aware of anyone working on this.

I'm afraid there is no trivial fix. The options I see:
* caching encoded metav1.WatchEvent inside of *cachingObject to allow reusing it for all watchers
   * the problem is that it requires some very specific handling of *cachingObjects in *WatchService.ServeHTTP which increases complexity of the code.
* making the serialization of metav1.WatchEvent cheaper, e.g. by somehow avoiding json.compact, e.g. by:
   * changing to other json serialization library (potentially quite large change)
   * changing golang's json serializer to drop the expensive json.compact validation of the MarshalJSON() result (this requires much more context on why it is needed), potentially conditionally.
     * @mknyszek, are you able to help us with understanding why this is needed/contacting us with someone from golang who can be able to help here?
* Some ugly hacks

Any other options?

I think that `json.compact` goes beyond a validity check. If I understand the code correctly, it's main purpose is to append JSON produced by a `MarshalJSON` method to a buffer, while simultaneously checking its validity (so you get an error if the `MarshalJSON` method produced something invalid) and compacting it (producing compact JSON is I believe the common case?). I think it may also escape characters but I didn't look too closely. Specifically, it's for situations like this: https://go.dev/play/p/U2j27dhAogr.

I'm not totally sure this can be avoided in general. It could do less, like just append the JSON it gets, but you lose some positives like better error checking and more consistent output (by compacting it).

Perhaps I'm misunderstanding the code though; I'm not too familiar on this codebase. Maybe @dsnet knows more?

Without looking into it further, this seems may be a similar problem as kubernetes/kube-openapi#315, but in the marshal direction, rather than unmarshal.

If you have benchmark to run, I can look into deeper later.
[REDACTED] adds benchmark for this issue.
If we don't find a volunteer to tackle this in the next 2 weeks, I'll be happy to give it a try.

While thinking about the alternatives that @mborsz linked - @mknyszek, are you able elaborate a bit more about the problem you linked in the Go Playground snippet, specifically about the errors that additional validations in `compact` can uncover?

In our case the output is already compacted, hence attempting to compact it second time doesn't make sense. If we had, purely theoretically, an additional interface w/ a method named e.g. `MarshalAlreadyCompactedJSON` then we'd get rid of the problem altogether here, hence the question about other reasons for running the validations in `json.compact`.

Sure thing. AFAICT, the JSON encoding package needs to handle potentially arbitrary inputs from a `MarshalJSON` method call which may not be valid or compacted. I think any alternative interface would have to be "unsafe" in some sense as it might break internal `encoding/json` invariants (or if those invariants could be avoided, that probably needs a bigger restructuring of the package, which I know @dsnet was looking into at some point).

> Changing Go to solve the CRD watchers-related problem here would be pretty time-consuming, however. I'll probably try writing some POC with the solution @mborsz proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110146#issuecomment-1289296713 related to caching metav1.WatchEvent inside the cachingObject.

I think that having some quick POC for this option would help making a decision. I think it shouldn't be that complicated on top of what we already have, but I may be missing something. Seeing how invasive the changes are would help here - I don't think we will make reasonable decision without knowing that.

I took a quick look at it (can't comment on the branch, but here are my few comments)
- adding `GetCachedEvent` seems acceptable to me - I think there is a question about the exact interface it should have, but at the high-enough level it seems reasonable to me
- I need to double check, but I think outer encoder determines the embedded one - so maybe we could actually simplify stuff a bit; otoh, thanks to your current approach we're reusing most of existing logic/code which seems to be highly beneficial

So overall, the above approach makes a lot of sense to me.

I think the next steps are:
- clearing this branch a bit, so that it compiles and can be run (without yet adjusting/adding appropriate unit tests)
- running tests to assess the impact of this change
- getting a feedback from someone else from sig-apimachinery

Thanks Wojtek for early feedback.

@tosi3k will help with cleaning the code and making it reviewable.

json.compact hogging memory is a symptom of json encoding hogging memory.

I have no idea if the go team will accept it, but I'm working on a change which should fix it in the std library: https://go-review.git.corp.google.com/c/go/+/455776

After the refactoring that I did before, I have a PR that seems to generally address the problem describe here in a pretty clean way:

title: creationTimestamp: null is invalid since it isn't a string
description:
### What happened?

There seems to be a discrepancy between the Kubernetes openapi spec and the Go package with the `creationTimestamp`

### What did you expect to happen?

CRDs generated by `controller-gen` which uses `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` to be valid according to the Kubernetes openapi spec.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```console
# wget https://github.com/fluxcd/source-controller/releases/download/v0.22.5/source-controller.crds.yaml
# kubeconform -schema-location default -schema-location "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yannh/kubernetes-json-schema/master/master/customresourcedefinition.json" source-controller.crds.yaml
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition gitrepositories.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition buckets.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition helmrepositories.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition helmcharts.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
```

### Anything else we need to know?

At first I raised an issue at https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/2623 since they seemed to be the culprit.
But received a response that they use `controller-gen` to generate the CRDs. So I looked into [controller-gen](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-tools) and they also do not set the `creationTimestamp` they import `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` for the generation of the metadata (where the creationTimestamp is part of)([source](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-tools/blob/8cb5ce83c3cca425a4de0af3d2578e31a3cd6a48/pkg/crd/spec.go#L26)).

So now the issue, in the package documentation ([link](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1#ObjectMeta)) of `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` it says the following about the `creationTimestamp`
```golang

Creation[Time](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1#Time)stamp Time `json:"creationTimestamp,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,8,opt,name=creationTimestamp"`
```

So there is something in the docblock about Null for lists(?) but in the openapi spec of Kubernetes is this `Time` resource marked as string:
```json
"io.k8s.apimachinery.pkg.apis.meta.v1.Time": {
      "description": "Time is a wrapper around time.Time which supports correct marshaling to YAML and JSON.  Wrappers are provided for many of the factory methods that the time package offers.",
      "format": "date-time",
      "type": "string"
},
```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/master/api/openapi-spec/swagger.json

So now, what is wrong here? Is it indeed allowed to be a string or null and should the openapi spec be an enum? Or is there something in`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` wrong? Or should `controller-gen` explictly set the creationTimestamp to an string? 
The last one seems kinda wrong to me since it seems to me that the `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` should return data valid to the api spec.

I am sorry for all the text and if I did not understand something correctly :)
I don't develop in golang (or at all really) and the relation between the package and the openapi spec is quite vague for me.

I opened the issue here since it seems an issue affecting multiple things within the kubernetes namespace (golang package, openapi spec in this repo).

### Kubernetes version

kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.5", GitCommit:"c285e781331a3785a7f436042c65c5641ce8a9e9", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-03-16T15:51:05Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.8", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/arm64"}

comments.text: Hi I am new to K8s. Would like to try this issue out.  Any hints ?

@prakharporwal I think there needs to be a decision or discussion from one of the maintainers how this is supposed to work before there could be looked at a fix.

Appreciate the enthusiasm though ❤️

@jpbetz @sttts Sorry for the ping but could one of you chime in, which one of the proposed solutions is the way forward?

The current state of an official package generating invalid YAML according the the spec seems something that needs to be solved :)

And again a little nudge @jpbetz @sttts 

The current discrepancy breaks linters like [yannh/kubeconform](https://github.com/yannh/kubeconform) since they generate their ruleset based on the API spec.
The current state makes a generated CRD from an official package invalid according to rules based on the API spec.
Would be great if this can be fixed, so that we don't have to remove lines with `creationTimestamp: null` manually for our CI linting.

~`creationTimestamp` is an optional field in openAPIv3 and may be absent from the JSON but should never be set to `null`.~

~The go struct contains `json:",omitempty"` to direction serializers to omit the field from JSON if the go struct is null.~

~Would someone provide more more details on how the resources were serialized such that they contain `creationTimestamp: null`?~

edit: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e26e104bdf9d0dc3c4046d6350b93557c67f3f4/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time.go#L144 will set the field value to null, so for backward compatibility the correct fix here it probably to add `nullable: true` to the openAPIv3 schema for Time.

see https://gist.github.com/jpbetz/5a27c20b4f29d8ee1144af8f43e57a0b for the exact behavior.
cc @jiahuif @apelisse

From @liggitt, there is a bunch of backstory here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67610, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53464, https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/issues/68, https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/issues/119, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104857

@apelisse pointed out to me a couple issues here that make this less practical to fix on the k8s side:

- Even if we add `nullable: true` in OpenAPIv3, it will only help in toolchains that are correctly consuming openapiv3, which is often not the case, and I'm not clear if it is the case in this specific issue.
- While `creationTimestamp` is one of the most obvious examples of a field that is allowed to be set to `null` but is not marked as nullable, the Kubernetes marshalling code allows for `null` in many cases, none of which are explicitly marked as `nullable: true`. For example, IIRC, in CRDs, all non-required fields may be set to null, and we don't require CRD authors to explicitly add `nullable: true` to the schemas.

Would it be possible for kubeconform to be modified to uniformly allow `null` for all non-required fields?

Also, code that uses the [applyconfigurations](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/doc.go) instead of the go structs will not produce null fields like this. It might be sufficient to use applyconfigurations for this case to avoid the immediate problem.

> While creationTimestamp is one of the most obvious examples of a field that is allowed to be set to null but is not marked as nullable, the Kubernetes marshalling code allows for null in many cases, none of which are explicitly marked as nullable: true. For example, IIRC, in CRDs, all non-required fields may be set to null, and we don't require CRD authors to explicitly add nullable: true to the schemas.

I'm not sure I agree the list of all types needing annotation is innumerable. My interpretation is that `nullable` controls whether `null` is ignored/omitted for during both serialization and deserialization, respectively. 

Go's JSON deserializer implicitly treats all null values as unset (in line with `nullable: false`). This applies to both native types and CRDs: 

> The JSON null value unmarshals into an interface, map, pointer, or slice by setting that Go value to nil. Because null is often used in JSON to mean “not present,” unmarshaling a JSON null into any other Go type has no effect on the value and produces no error. [source][(https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#Unmarshal))

There is only one exception to this: native types with custom `UnmarshalJSON` that directly handle `null` to override the default behavior. 

> To unmarshal JSON into a value implementing the Unmarshaler interface, Unmarshal calls that value's UnmarshalJSON method, including when the input is a JSON null. 

The (likely) exhaustive list of native types that I've found that implement custom JSON marshaling to handle null are:

(found using regex `\) (Unm|M)arshalJSON((?!func).|\n)*null`)

1. [runtime.RawExtension](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03b434c9d447d3e78f91f130420c5a83e11c81b4/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/extension.go#L1-L51)
    used as a value
1. [runtime.Unknown](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9f9e7177a328ae47bac6b823d57a99dfbfd310b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/embedded.go#L73-L95) (doesnt roundtrip for null/"" case. likely bug?)
    used only as pointer
1. [meta.v1.Time](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9f9e7177a328ae47bac6b823d57a99dfbfd310b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time.go#L98-L152)
    used as both a pointer and a value
1. [meta.v1.MicroTime](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9f9e7177a328ae47bac6b823d57a99dfbfd310b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/micro_time.go#L110-L161)
    used as both a pointer and a value
1. [meta.v1.FieldsV1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c5a8015bbae1e1095813d8e0719f017477dc7112/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/helpers.go#L279-L295)
    only used as a pointer
1. [apiextensions.v1.JSON](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/694698ca3801fe5aa258d58c1e27ac7f88c29d35/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/marshal.go#L123-L136)
    used both as pointer and value. 
1. [apiextensions.v1.JSONSchemaPropsOrStringArray](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/694698ca3801fe5aa258d58c1e27ac7f88c29d35/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/marshal.go#L62-L92)
    only used as a pointer
1. [resource.Quantity](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c5a8015bbae1e1095813d8e0719f017477dc7112/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L650-L702)
    used both as pointer and value. Unmarshals `null` but does not marshal `null`

We need to apply the `nullable` annotation in the schema only to all places where `null` does not mean `unset` - where `null` is an interpreted value. This is especially important if our types possibly marshal into `null`.

To avoid cases where pointer usages are marked nullable, I think we also need to ensure the code generator only  insert `nullable: true` into the non-pointer usages of types with a `+k8s-openapi:nullable` marker, and not the pointer-based ones.

> Go's JSON deserializer implicitly treats all null values as unset. This applies to both native types and CRDs:

That's true for native types, but it's not correct for custom resources. Go's JSON deserializer will unmarshal `{"foo":null}` to `map[string]interface{}{"foo":null}`. https://go.dev/play/p/u4nxaMn-iqo

We do a specific post-process step to drop explicitly null fields which were not marked as nullable in the schema (see `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults`). Setting `nullable` in the schema will *break* this pruning step and will preserve explicit `null` values.

> This applies to both native types and CRDs:
> That's true for native types, but it's not correct for custom resources. 

My mistake. The property that non-nullable null => unset for CRDs is not given by the the JSON deserializer. But the overall argument still holds. `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` is what gives the property to CRDs that `nullable: false` implies `null = unset` in k8s schemas. JSON deserializer for native types.

> Setting nullable in the schema will break this pruning step and will preserve explicit null values.

I'm not sure I would see this as broken for the cases I've proposed. I am proposing to add  `nullable` only to value-typed usages of the listed types which  marshal their empty value into explicit null values. 

`PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` would not prune fields like `creationTimestamp` as we've specified in OpenAPI since they also have a default set (kube-openapi code generator forces all structs to have `{}` default).

```json
          "creationTimestamp": {
            "allOf": [
              {
                "$ref": "#/components/schemas/io.k8s.apimachinery.pkg.apis.meta.v1.Time"
              }
            ],
            "default": {},
            "description": "..."
          },
```

I see two alternatives for fixing schema to be able to validate JSON that these types marshal into:

1. Permit the null by adding nullable annotation
2. Ignore the null by removing implicit `{}` default applied to struct types that marshal their empty values into `null`. Clients should know to also apply `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` as we do to both native types and CRDs.

Both options are consistent and work for my purposes (kubectl-validate & Declarative Validation). The second carries the risk of not representing the reality in apiserver if `null` possibly could unmarshal into anything other than empty, but I dont think that applies to any of our current concrete cases.

> `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` would not prune fields like `creationTimestamp` as we've specified in OpenAPI since they also have a default set (kube-openapi code generator forces all structs to have `{}` default).

wow... that default is completely invalid for metav1.Time, which serializes as a string... first we need to stop setting defaults of an invalid type in the openapi

> I see two alternatives for fixing schema to be able to validate JSON that these types marshal into:
> 
> 1. Permit the null by adding nullable annotation

I don't think we should add `nullable` for fields which the server doesn't return null for, like creationTimestamp.

> 2. Ignore the null by removing implicit `{}` default applied to struct types that marshal their empty values into `null`. Clients should know to also apply `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` as we do to both native types and CRDs.

Knowing that both built-in types and custom resource types will drop null for property fields (or unmarshal to empty), this seems like the best option among several not-great ones.

> The second carries the risk of not representing the reality in apiserver if null possibly could unmarshal into anything other than empty, but I dont think that applies to any of our current concrete cases.

A custom unmarshaler turning null into a not-empty case would be bizarre... there's already problems with nulls in some patch types (like json merge patch) explicitly meaning "drop this value", so we already try to steer people away from nullable fields, and a `null` meaning something other than `empty` would be problematic already.

title: CRI getFsInfo logs errors for valid filesystems mounted after kubelet start
description:
**What happened**:

New overlay filesystems created for Pods after kubelet start trigger repeated error messages. For example:

```
cri_stats_provider.go:375] Failed to get the info of the filesystem with mountpoint "/var/lib/containers/storage/overlay/2243263dc8ba6c55d8867d3e47bcaaa145d15f0ace19420824d639d86defe2e3/merged": failed to get device for dir "/var/lib/containers/storage/overlay/2243263dc8ba6c55d8867d3e47bcaaa145d15f0ace19420824d639d86defe2e3/merged": could not find device with major: 0, minor: 83 in cached partitions map.
```

Error messages are logged every 10 seconds for every filesystem created after kubelet start. For large kubelet nodes, this issue creates an excessive amount of error logs.

**What you expected to happen**:

New overlay filesystems created for Pods after kubelet start should not log error messages.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Use cri_stats_provider with cri-o and configure overlay storage. UsingLegacyCadvisorStats() needs to return false per https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/pull/3054 for cri_stats_provider to be used. Start with an empty /var/lib/containers/storage and schedule Pods on the node.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

As part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/59475, cadvisor.GetFsInfoByFsUUID() was changed to cadvisor.GetDirFsInfo() in getFsInfo(); however, the test for cadvisorfs.ErrNoSuchDevice was not modified, changing how getFsInfo() handles a cache miss from cadvisor. 

cadvisor caches UUIDs/partitions/mounts on kubelet start and the cache is never refreshed. Given that it's expected that getFsInfo() will fail to retrieve data from cadvisor (see comments in ImageFsStats() and https://github.com/kubernetes/heapster/issues/1793), this condition should not be logged as an error. Alternatively, cadvisor fs could be modified to refresh on cache miss enabling getFsInfo() to return data on these filesystems.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.18.6
- CRI: CRI-O

title: Running conformance test on 1.29.0-alpha.3 cluster with sonobuoy fails
description:
### What happened?

@rtheis reported that conformance testing with the latest version of sonobuoy against a version 1.29.0-alpha.3 cluster fails on the support the 1.17 Sample API Server using the current Aggregator test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283#issuecomment-1812399851, related to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283.

I found the reason why the test is working fine in Kubernetes CI jobs but fails with sonobuoy is because **the service account used by sonobuoy "sonobuoy-serviceaccount" doesn't have read permission of the non-resource url "/"**, which is used by the test to confirm the removal of group path:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec5096fa869b801d6eb1bf019819287ca61edc4d/test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go#L744-L746

```
I1121 14:31:40.149085       1 rbac.go:119] RBAC: no rules authorize user "system:serviceaccount:sonobuoy:sonobuoy-serviceaccount" with groups ["system:serviceaccounts" "system:serviceaccounts:son
thenticated"] to "get" nonResourceURL "/" cluster-wide
I1121 14:31:40.149099       1 authorization.go:87] "Forbidden" URI="/" reason=""
I1121 14:31:40.149218       1 httplog.go:132] "HTTP" verb="GET" URI="/" latency="327.429µs" userAgent="e2e.test/v1.29.0 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/1f69e12 -- [sig-api-machinery] Aggregator Should b
 the 1.17 Sample API Server using the current Aggregator [Conformance]" audit-ID="46c27282-7af6-48d1-bf3e-ca439c57bc92" srcIP="172.18.0.4:36878" apf_pl="workload-low" apf_fs="service-accounts" ap
eats=0 apf_additionalLatency="0s" apf_execution_time="105.94µs" resp=403
```

The permission of "sonobuoy-serviceaccount" is as below:
https://github.com/vmware-tanzu/sonobuoy/blob/6f9e27f1795f10475c9f6f5decdff692e1e228da/pkg/client/gen.go#L502-L505
```
cr.Rules = []v1.PolicyRule{
	{
		APIGroups: []string{"*"},
		Resources: []string{"*"},
		Verbs:     []string{"*"},
	},
	{
		NonResourceURLs: []string{"/metrics", "/logs", "/logs/*"},
		Verbs:           []string{"get"},
	},
}
```

There may be two ways to fix it:
1. Update the RBAC rule of sonobuoy to include "get" of "/". However, could other test runners encounter this issue? Is there a doc listing the required permissions for running e2e tests?
2. Update the e2e to skip checking the removal of the group path if the service account doesn't have permission to access the root path.

Which way do we usually prefer? 

### What did you expect to happen?

Running e2e with sonobuoy should succeed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a v1.29.0-alpha.3 cluster.
2. Run `sonobuoy run --e2e-focus "Sample API Server using the current Aggregator"`

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

$ kubectl version
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"29+", GitVersion:"v1.29.0-alpha.3", GitCommit:"1f69e121482db6664e4a1c1d21ec4dcf2b36b080", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2023-11-02T18:24:31Z", Go

```

@tnqn thank you for opening this issue and working on a solution. I'm probably not the right person to decide on which solution is preferred. From my perspective, either solution is fine.

Note: Sonobuoy is not owned by any Kubernetes SIG. 
At most it is between SIG Architecture and the CNCF to choose whether to recommend it for running tests.
SIG Testing owns the e2e image that sonobuoy can be used to schedule but not sonobuoy.

IMHO this is a bug in running the tests via a pod, which is not how we develop the tests (they're run outside the cluster, by a cluster admin account typically).

I would say 1) is the correct answer. xref: [REDACTED]



cc @johnbelamaric @Riaankl

> IMHO this is a bug in running the tests via a pod, which is not how we develop the tests (they're run outside the cluster, by a cluster admin account typically).
> 
> I would say 1) is the correct answer. xref: [REDACTED] [REDACTED]

@BenTheElder thanks for your comment. I guess 1) means non of the existing sonobuoy versions can pass K8s conformance test against a cluster > 1.29.0-alpha3, as the RBAC rule is hardcoded. I will file an issue to sonobuoy first.

question here is what are the set of client permissions required to run the conformance suite?
perhaps a `cluster-admin`  level of access or a more granular recommendation should be documented.

@sttts what is your take on the root path requirement as approver for:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283/files#diff-d9472590663e3c095a5e1f62d1483eb7cda4f61fc725daebb0934db5f5bccdd8R744-R746

EDIT: added slack thread:
https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C78F00H99/p1700676182564719

> perhaps a cluster-admin level of access or a more granular recommendation should be documented.

I agree, we already require e.g. privileged pods for a long time in conformance tests and we should make it clear that we expect a highly privileged client.
@neolit123 +1 for what @BenTheElder is saying, that we should expect that the user running the tests has required permissions. These tests are not built for being run unprivileged.

i wanted to PR the admin note in our conformance docs under sig-arch, but then i saw this:
https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/conformance-tests.md

> it is non-privileged (e.g., does not require root on nodes, access to raw network interfaces, or cluster admin permissions)

so https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283 broke this guarantee.
sounds like SIG Arch needs to comment.

> so https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283 broke this guarantee.

This statement surprises me. Root discovery is one of the least-privileged permissions you can have on a cluster. For years this was even open for unauthorized users on the internet (if your api endpoint has been exposed).

In other words, just add the `/` permission. While thinking about it, it is surprising that the user in question does not have this access already. Don't we allow that for every authorized user?

In contrast, I hope that lots of privileged operations are tested by conformance today. If we don't test things like admission webhooks for example, we have much bigger problems. And admission webhooks are basically equivalent to cluster-admin.

> i wanted to PR the admin note in our conformance docs under sig-arch, but then i saw this: https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/conformance-tests.md
> 
> > it is non-privileged (e.g., does not require root on nodes, access to raw network interfaces, or cluster admin permissions)

that is outdated, we use hostNetwork pods one some of the tests IIRC

looks like we don't.

```bash
$ kubectl get clusterrole cluster-admin -o yaml

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:

    rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate: "true"
  creationTimestamp: "2023-11-24T18:34:38Z"
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac-defaults
  name: cluster-admin

  - /api # <------------- modified from the default of '*'
  verbs:
  - '*'

$ kubectl get --raw /
Error from server (Forbidden): forbidden: User "kubernetes-admin" cannot get path "/"

$ kubectl get --raw /api
{"kind":"APIVersions","versions":["v1"],"serverAddressByClientCIDRs":[{"clientCIDR":"0.0.0.0/0","serverAddress":"10.0.2.15:6443"}]}
```

> In contrast, I hope that lots of privileged operations are tested by conformance today. If we don't test things like admission webhooks for example, we have much bigger problems. And admission webhooks are basically equivalent to cluster-admin.

before this ticket, i was under the impression that the conformance suite already requires admin and that all testers (like Sonobuoy) use admin level credentials.

>> it is non-privileged (e.g., does not require root on nodes, access to raw network interfaces, or cluster admin permissions)

> that is outdated, we use hostNetwork pods one some of the tests IIRC

looks like we may have to change that sentence completely.
adding to milestone and making release blocking ... we should not release 1.29 in a state that the most commonly used conformance tool will fail

IMO we should clarify the state and go fix the tool, but we should keep the test and we should NOT add skip.

Conformance docs are not a release artifact, and sonobuoy release lifecycle is not a conformance artifact.

If we can't get sonobuoy working in a reasonable time, we already know the tests can be run by scheduling the image (which is ours) directly with kubectl instead and we can document that in the upstream conformance docs.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/conformance/image/conformance-e2e.sh
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/conformance/image/conformance-e2e.yaml

We need to fix the for this image: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-testing-kind#conformance-image,%20master%20(dev)
And it should probably be added to release-blocking in the future.

it looks like the e2e change made in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283 was not consciously made part of conformance, it was just trying to functionally test the bugfix being made.

For 1.29, I think we should revert the change to test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go and make an integration test that validates the fix instead. We can revisit whether content of `/` is part of conformance or not for 1.30

title: [KCCM]: service update while node sync is processing might impact ingress
description:
### What happened?

The Kubernetes cloud controller manager uses resource watchers to sync load balancers, a Node/Service watcher. The Node watcher is slower by nature since any Node event will sync all service load balancers on the cluster. The service watcher is quicker since it only syncs the service load balancer which the event relates to. 

How slow a Node sync is will vary on the cluster, i.e: amount of Services of `type: LoadBalancer` and Nodes, but on big clusters with a lot of churn: the time to process one Node sync can be sufficiently slow to have the cache of Nodes go stale w.r.t the actual cluster state. The cache of Nodes is here the resource informer cache. When syncing Nodes the Node control loop will list all Nodes in its cache and then iterate over all Services and sync their load balancers in parallel, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L799-L818

If any Service experiences an update needing a load balancer sync, the Service controller will also list the Nodes in the informer cache, but retrieve a more up-to-date copy, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L438-L451. 

During upgrades or similar operations where a lot of Nodes get added/deleted: it's rather easy for the following to occur;

1. Node sync is processing, N load balancers are synced
2. NodeY is added
2. Service update triggers sync for load balancer X. It lists and adds NodeY to the load balancer set
3. Node sync processes load balancer Y and removes NodeY from the load balancer set 

This add + remove from the load balancer set might impact ingress SLOs for any application running on NodeY after its creation. 


### What did you expect to happen?

Any node added to the load balancer set which doesn't have a reason (i.e: [predicate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L996-L1016)) to be removed should not be removed from the load balancer's set of backend nodes.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Update a Service while an upgrade is on-going. Nodes risk being added/removed/added from the load balancer's set of backend nodes at sporadic moments. Alternatively, I have written a unit tests that exhibits the issue and while file a fix PR where this can be seen.  

### Anything else we need to know?

title: [kubelet-image-gc] minimum-image-ttl-duration not work,when kubelet restart.
description:
### What happened?

when kubelet restart,all images which notused cleaned.
but there is a flag in kubelet,`minimum-image-ttl-duration`,explain：Minimum age for an unused image before it is garbage collected.  Examples: '300ms', '10s' or '2h45m'.
i set `minimum-image-ttl-duration` to `20m0s`,it's means if a image not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet（if has disk pressure）.if kubelet not restart, it work,but if restart ther is a bug, `minimum-image-ttl-duration` not work,image will be clean，even if it's no enough  time.

### What did you expect to happen?

`minimum-image-ttl-duration` work, image even if not used,it will live 20m and then clean by kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1）make node trigger disk pressure.
2）pull some image which not used by pod
3）restart kubelet
4）image cleaned by kubelet after around 10s

### Anything else we need to know?

i see the source code, and maybe there is a bug.

in [detectImages](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L261-L262) func,well detect image and update firstdetect time for every image.
```go
	// New image, set it as detected now.
		if _, ok := im.imageRecords[image.ID]; !ok {
			klog.V(5).InfoS("Image ID is new", "imageID", image.ID)
			im.imageRecords[image.ID] = &imageRecord{
				firstDetected: detectTime,
			}
		}
```
and in  [freeSpace](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L394C1-L397) func,well check images livetime by firstDetected.
```go
		if freeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge {
			klog.V(5).InfoS("Image ID's age is less than the policy's minAge, not eligible for garbage collection", "imageID", image.id, "age", freeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected), "minAge", im.policy.MinAge)
			continue
		}
```
if kubelet running normal,it work,because there is a [Start](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/97c7dbcd227ec253bb277a91575706fe30f519dc/pkg/kubelet/images/image_gc_manager.go#L190-L204) func.
```go
func (im *realImageGCManager) Start() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	go wait.Until(func() {
		// Initial detection make detected time "unknown" in the past.
		var ts time.Time
		if im.initialized {
			ts = time.Now()
		}
                // in first time,ts is zero. 
               // in first time,ts is zero.
		_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)
		if err != nil {
			klog.InfoS("Failed to monitor images", "err", err)
		} else {
			im.initialized = true
		}
	}, 5*time.Minute, wait.NeverStop)


```
in this line,`_, err := im.detectImages(ctx, ts)`,in first time,ts is zero. so image's firstDetected time is zero,and in freeSpace
`reeTime.Sub(image.firstDetected) < im.policy.MinAge` this check is always false,so image will be cleaned.


maybe we can change to `im.detectImages(time.now())`,can fix this bug.

title: k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollUntilContextCancel immediately executes condition twice
description:
### What happened?

While trying to update https://github.com/flatcar/flatcar-linux-update-operator/blob/7a1b0ff2769af91e8ff2bae82fc93f2f5baf0b0c/pkg/agent/agent.go#L328 to use latest version of `wait` package and to migrate away from deprecated `PollImmediateUntil`, function, our tests fail as it seems new `PollUntilContextCancel` function immediately executes given condition twice, which is not mentioned anywhere.

Result of executed test specified below:
```console
$ go test . -v
=== RUN   Test_test
=== PAUSE Test_test
=== CONT  Test_test
=== RUN   Test_test/PollUntilContextCancel
    prog_test.go:25: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:25: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:25: Unexpected early timestamp
=== RUN   Test_test/PollImmediateUntil
    prog_test.go:31: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:00 +0000 UTC m=+0.000000001
    prog_test.go:31: Executed at 2009-11-10 23:00:02 +0000 UTC m=+2.000000001
--- FAIL: Test_test (3.00s)
    --- FAIL: Test_test/PollUntilContextCancel (0.00s)
    --- PASS: Test_test/PollImmediateUntil (3.00s)
FAIL
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Since `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollImmediateUntil` has been deprecated and it recommends using `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.PollUntilContextCancel`, I expected it to have the equivalent semantics to allow easy migration from deprecated functions, as no changelog or documentation mentions new semantics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Playground: https://go.dev/play/p/qQBnWM4nufF

Local:
1. `go mod init foo && go get k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait`
2. Create `main_test.go` file with the following content:
```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait"
)

const (
	testTimeout           = 3 * time.Second
	callsExpectedInterval = 2 * time.Second
)

func Test_test(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), testTimeout)
	t.Cleanup(cancel)

	t.Run("PollUntilContextCancel", func(t *testing.T) {
		f := testIntervals(t)

		wait.PollUntilContextCancel(ctx, callsExpectedInterval, true, func(context.Context) (bool, error) { f(); return false, nil })
	})

	t.Run("PollImmediateUntil", func(t *testing.T) {
		f := testIntervals(t)

		wait.PollImmediateUntil(callsExpectedInterval, func() (bool, error) { f(); return false, nil }, ctx.Done())
	})
}

func testIntervals(t *testing.T) func() {
	t.Helper()

	timestamps := make(chan time.Time, 1)

	timestamps <- time.Now().Add(-1 * 2 * callsExpectedInterval)

	return func() {
		t.Helper()

		t.Logf("Executed at %s", time.Now())

		if timestamp := <-timestamps; timestamp.After(time.Now().Add(-1 * callsExpectedInterval / 2)) {
			t.Fatalf("Unexpected early timestamp")
		}

		timestamps <- time.Now()
	}
}
```
3. Run as `go test . -v`.

title: Follow up #121985: Conformance test regarding the access of "/"
description:
### What happened?

The issue is to follow up discussions in #121985: running conformance test with the commonly used tool, sonobuoy, failed because the tool's test runner is lack of permission towards `/`. The original issue was resolved by changing the e2e (conformance) test of `/` to an integration test. Several problems remained:

1. The privilege requirement in [conformance-tests.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/conformance-tests.md) is outdated. 
    > it is non-privileged (e.g., does not require root on nodes, access to raw network interfaces, or cluster admin permissions)
2. Root discovery is one of the least-privileged permissions, and is expected to be granted to every authenticated user but is not actually.
3. Should the result returned by `/` should be part of conformance?

1st and 2nd are straightforward to fix, not sure about 3rd, should we add a separate test or add a verification step in existing one like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121283? With the fix of 2nd, e2e for `/` should no longer fail with any test runner.


cc @liggitt @sttts @BenTheElder @neolit123 @aojea 

### What did you expect to happen?

1. conformance-tests.md should be reflect the accurate permission requirement
2. Root discovery permission should be granted to all authenticated users.

title: Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled
description:
### What happened?

Scheduler's default plugin returns an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100], resulting in no Pods being scheduled:
```
E1127 19:48:13.221979   66549 schedule_one.go:130] "Error selecting node for pod" err="applying score defaultWeights on Score plugins: plugin \"PodTopologySpread\" returns an invalid score 300, it should in the range of [0, 100] after normalizing" pod="default/test-multi-point-xxxxxxxx"
```

After investigation, I found that there was a bug in the code that built the framework when the scheduler started. When using the plugins declared in the regular extension point to override the plugins declared in the MultiPoint, the traversed variable `enabledSet` will be modified in the following loop:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L523-L534

This may cause **a same scoring plugin** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`) **to be loaded multiple times**:
```
f.scorePlugins: []framework.ScorePlugin{(*noderesources.Fit)(0xc000922e10), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*podtopologyspread.PodTopologySpread)(0xc0000ab100), (*tainttoleration.TaintToleration)(0xc0003f3690), (*nodeaffinity.NodeAffinity)(0xc0003997a0), (*volumebinding.VolumeBinding)(0xc0003db7a0), (*interpodaffinity.InterPodAffinity)(0xc00038f3b0), (*noderesources.BalancedAllocation)(0xc000063680), (*imagelocality.ImageLocality)(0xc000b45320)}
```

Further, this results in **a node being processed multiple times by a plugin's** (e.g. `PodTopologySpread`'s) **`NormalizeScore` method**, resulting in an invalid score that is not in the range of [0, 100]:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad9b60e2c9ddb21e8b00cabbe27e639638a0ea88/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L1095-L1108

### What did you expect to happen?

If the scheduler's MultiPoint feature is used (either through the default plugins or through manual configuration), and the configuration (e.g. the scoring weight) of a certain plugin is overridden in a regular extension point, the plugin will only be loaded once in this extension point, and no illegal scores will be returned.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

An example KubeSchedulerConfiguration:

```yaml
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1beta3
...
profiles:
- schedulerName: default-scheduler
  plugins:
    score:
      enabled:
      - name: PodTopologySpread
        weight: 3
...
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

K8s v1.24.15 or higher

title: No proper scheduling retries could be made when Extender filters out some Nodes
description:
### What happened?

When Extender filters out some Nodes, we don't set any unschedulable plugins at all. It means Extender is completely ignored during the requeueing process.

So, what's happening is:
- If Extender filters out all Nodes during scheduling, this Pod is soon retried because this Pod doesn't have any plugin name in unschedulable plugins.
- If Extender filters out some Nodes during scheduling and plugins filter out all other Nodes, this Pod is retried based on plugins' QueueingHint. Even if any cluster events happen and it could change Extender's decision (but not any plugins' decision), this Pod won't be requeued to activeQ/backoffQ.

The latter case is serious because it could make Pods being stuck in unschedulable pod pool in 5min.

### What did you expect to happen?

We should have a short-term solution for the latter case. 
We can requeue Pods, which were rejected by Extender, by any kind of cluster events because we cannot know which events make Pods schedulable.

Eventually, this issue makes us wonder how Pods rejected by Extender should be requeued. We cannot implement QHint equivalent in Extenders because it'd be too slow to call Extender every time any cluster events happen. Probably, somehow implementing EventsToRegister equivalent in Extender? 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use Extender which does something in Filter.

title: Does noderestriction also need to be extended for node references in tokens?
description:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120780 recently merged, adding nodes as something we can put in bound object refs (yay!)

Today while reading noderestriction code for a different reason, I realized we never extended noderestriction to block Kubelets from binding tokens to nodes other than themselves. Today, noderestriction _does_ block Kubelets from binding tokens to Pods on other nodes, so perhaps it should do the same for bound node references. 


### What did you expect to happen?

noderestriction to block it, probably.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Read the code here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/263ab254ef6a847fdd3dc69250a2ac0b12c42eb3/plugin/pkg/admission/noderestriction/admission.go#L531-L570

And note that we didn't modify noderestriction.go in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120780/files

To summarize Slack discussion: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EN96KUY/p1699051321839849

- TokenRequest can only bind to one object at a time.
- kubelet (node identity) is already required to bind to Pod by noderestriction. 
- kube-apiserver automatically inserts the node information based on the Pod binding. kubelet does not set it.

So this is technically still node bound.

We should still add a comment in noderestriction.go to avoid future confusion.

There may be other reasons to add a check, like future proofing...

title: endpoints not configured with MinimizeIPTablesRestore
description:
### What happened?

To test out the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature enabled in 1.27 by default we enabled the setting in 1.26 and discovered that it appears to not configure endpoints properly everytime.
While the version in 1.26 is still alpha I have not found any significant changes, bug reports or backports in the changelog regarding this.

It seems sometimes kube-proxy does not see that the endpoints of a service need to be updated despite the api endpointslice having changed. This typically is not that visible with externalTrafficPolicy Cluster services as some other endpoint still is configured, but in the case of low replica services or externalTrafficPolicy Local services this can lead to service disruption due to the only endpoint on the local node not getting configured while other components see the update correctly and direct traffic there.


For example this two pod deployment both pods ready since hours:

```
$ kubectl -n ns get pods pod1 pod2-o yaml | grep -B 2 Ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:21:19Z"
      status: "True"

--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:20:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: Ready
--
      lastTransitionTime: "2023-10-19T10:20:19Z"
      status: "True"
      type: ContainersReady

```

and the chain on one node only contains one of the ready endpoints:

```
KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.78.44.163/32 -p tcp -m comment --comment "svc:serviceport loadbalancer IP" -m tcp --dport 4000 -j KUBE-EXT-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43
KUBE-EXT-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 -m comment --comment "masquerade traffic for svc:serviceport external destinations" -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
KUBE-EXT-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 -j KUBE-SVC-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43
KUBE-SVC-APW7J2FZSAAP4Z43 ! -s 100.64.0.0/13 -d 100.72.16.186/32 -p tcp -m comment --comment "svc:serviceport cluster IP" -m tcp --dport 4000 -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ

```

The kube-proxy logs show nothing unusual, just lots of partial syncs (which in our cluster take about 1-2 seconds for a partial sync while the full sync takes 20-40seconds).

### What did you expect to happen?

On endpoint change the iptables are always configured.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We see this in clusters with 1500 services, 14000 pods and 300 nodes on most nodes for a small handful of the services.

> no jump to the local chain, no local chain and notably no "no local endpoints" DROP.

right; the EXT chain is stale. At some point in time there are actually no endpoints, and it writes out a DROP rule and an EXT chain with no jump to the SVL chain. Then an endpoint appears, and it removes the DROP rule but for some reason _doesn't_ rewrite the EXT chain.

exactly, the reason for that is that the DROP rule is part of the code that is always rewritten, but the EXT chain is skipped if it thinks nothing changed https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1200

> This imo indicates a problem with the `endpointsChanged` function:

(`endpointsChanged` is a set; the function there is just `endpointsChanged.Has()`. So the problem would be "a problem with the contents of the `endpointsChanged` set".)

OK, so here are my thoughts so far...

1. If there's a bug in `EndpointsChangeTracker.PendingChanges()`, such that `endpointsChanged` ends up not including some changed endpoints despite the tracker having noticed that they changed and triggering a resync, then we'd fail to rewrite the rules for those endpoints. Alternatively, the same could be true for `ServiceChangeTracker.PendingChanges()`/`servicesChanged`.
    - This seems unlikely: the logic for deciding what's in `endpointsChanged`/`servicesChanged` is pretty closely tied to the logic for triggering syncs. It seems like if the tracker noticed the change at all, it ought to show up in `endpointsChanged`/`servicesChanged`. Or at least, if there _was_ a bug here, it ought to be pretty obvious, not something rare/subtle.
2. If there's a bug in `EndpointsChangeTracker` more generally such that it fails to trigger syncs on some EndpointSlice changes, then the endpoint also wouldn't show up in `endpointsChanged` and so we wouldn't rewrite its chains. (Or again, the problem could be with `ServiceChangeTracker` rather than `EndpointsChangeTracker`.)
    - In this case there would have been a bug even in the pre-MinimizeIPTablesRestore behavior, but it's possible we just never noticed it, since _any_ later change would pick up the previously-ignored Service/EndpointSlice change as well, so the effect would only be that the update was slightly delayed, not missed entirely.
    - If there was a missing mutex lock somewhere then there could be a data race that causes an update to be missed?
3. If set of "usable" endpoints for a Service (i.e., one of the return values of `CategorizeEndpoints`) changes without the Service itself or any of its EndpointSlices having changed (in a relevant way), then we might need to rewrite the service/endpoint chains but not do so.
    - e.g., if either (a) `hasEndpoints` changed from `false` to `true`, or (b) `localEndpoints` changed from empty to non-empty, _without_ `servicesChanged` or `endpointsChanged` including the service, then we would end up with the set of rules you quoted above.
    - At first I was thinking that must be it, but after looking at the code some more, I don't think that can actually happen...
      - The return values of `CategorizeEndpoints` will change for a Cluster policy service if the result of `canUseTopology()` changes, but that can only change if either (a) the service changes (in which case it should be in `servicesChanged`), (b) at least one endpoint changes (in which case it should be in `endpointsChanged`), or (c) the node labels change (in which case `OnNodeUpdate` would force a full resync).
      - The return values of `CategorizeEndpoints` can change when a service flips between using Ready endpoints and using Serving-Terminating endpoints. e.g., if endpoint A is Local,Ready, and endpoint B is Local,Serving,Terminating, then the returned `localEndpoints` would be `[A]`. If endpoint A then terminates, then `localEndpoints` would change to `[A, B]` _even though B didn't change_. But that shouldn't actually cause any problems, because `endpointsChanged` tracks whether _any_ endpoint for the service changed, and in this case A changed, so we should be ok.

I'm leaning toward (2), though (3) still worries me...

but how can we get more nat rules with the same number of Services and less Endpoints?

`numServices` and `numEndpoints` are the *total* number of Services and Endpoints. `numNATRules` is the number of *updated* nat rules, which is not directly proportional to `numServices` and `numEndpoints`. It's more proportional to the *change* in `numServices` and `numEndpoints` since the last sync.

IOW, `numNATRules` is larger in the second sync because it had to rewrite all of the `KUBE-SVC-*` chains that used to jump to the 28 endpoints that just got deleted.

```

defer proxier.mu.Unlock()
```

to the start of `OnServiceAdd`, `OnServiceUpdate`, `OnServiceDelete`, `OnEndpointSliceAdd`, `OnEndpointSliceUpdate`, and `OnEndpointSliceDelete` and see if that makes the race go away.

title: Request timeout not respected while listing from storage
description:
### What happened?

It is possible to issue a list request which exceeds the duration set by the request-timeout apiserver flag. The request-timeout flag does not appear to be enforced when the apiserver is decoding the response from etcd. 

Specifically, listing a large number of CRDs from etcd can result in high request latency from using json encoding compared to protobuf encoding. While overall etcd latency is low, the overall listing from storage latency may be over the 1 minute timeout, particularly if the apiserver needs to fetch multiple pages from etcd.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the list requests to be subject to the duration specified by the request-timeout flag when this latency is coming from the listing from storage phase of the request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create 4000 CRs and list all the objects from etcd in 2 pages of 2000 objects. If the time to list 1 page + decode takes around 50s, listing 2 pages will result in the listing from storage phase of the request taking  around 1 minute and 40s before the request fails and the client is returned a 500 response code.

Logs for apiserver Trace message:

Interesting.. - do you know where exactly we stuck?

In the call to storage:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go#L708

we pass the context that has timeout set, so that shouldn't hang.

OTOH, for the processing part:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go#L732-L751

(a) I don't know if transformer honors the context - it probably depends on the implementation

So (b) might definitely be a problem, even independently from from the transformer


So I guess what I'm saying is that if listing from etcd finishes fast but the decoding is what takes most of time, then what you described can certainly be a problem.

title: Mount point may become local without calling `NodePublishVolume` after node rebooting
description:
### What happened?

This issue is very similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117513, they have the same symptom: remote volumes of the pods are becoming local mount point after rebooting the Node. And this issue is triggered by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117513.

The difference is that in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117513, kubelet didn't call `NodeStageVolume`, so the global mount point is local, but it will still call `NodePublishVolume` for the pod to bind mount the pod volume to the global mount point. Whereas in this issue, kubelet neither call `NodeStageVolume` globally nor call `NodePublishVolume` for the pod. 

This is more harmful: After writing some data to the pod volume, pod can't be deleted because kubelet encounter `directory not empty` error while unmounting the pod volume:
 
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/44308864/b1cc4e04-15ac-4730-a862-54eddf2a4960)


Reproduce steps:
1. Create a cluster with one Node
2. Create a deployment with **two replicas**(say `pod-1` and `pod-2`) using Non-attachable volume (for example Azurefile)
3. Shutdown the Node
4. Delete `pod-1` with option `--force` (Use force deletion to simulate the situation that mount point was left over before rebooting the Node.)
5. Bring back the Node
6. `pod-2` is always in Running state, however, after rebooting, it won't call `NodePublishVolume` and the volume it uses is local volume.

### What did you expect to happen?

`pod-2` should call `NodePublishVolume`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

As mentioned above.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Kubelet cannot finish terminating a pod that uses a PVC with volumeMode: Block when poweroff the node and then restarting the node
description:
### What happened?

A pod uses a PVC with volumeMode: Block. The block volume is backed by a block device on the node (which is created by some CSI storage providers).  If the node operating system is powered off , if the user delete the pod or the pod be eviceted by kcm, And then restarting the node, The pod would be stuck in terminating forever since Kubelet refuses to UnmapBlockVolume. kubelet  cannot delete the pod successfully.  

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should be able to finish terminating a pod  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.Install a CSI storage provider that supports volumeMode: Block.

2.Deloy a pod that has volumeClaimTemplates with volumeMode: Block. 

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-pod
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-pod
      name: test-pod
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx:1.17.9
        name: test
        volumeDevices:
        - devicePath: /dev/blk-vol-1
          name: blk-vol-1
        volumeMounts:
      volumes:
      - name: blk-vol-1
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: test-bv
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: test-bv
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes: [ "ReadWriteMany" ]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
  storageClassName: FILLIN
  volumeMode: Block
```
3.After pod is running ,to  power off the node
4.delete the po: kubectl delete po test-pod
5.restart the node

title: kubernetes-1.24.0 reproducible builds: kubelet binary varies
description:
### What happened?

While working on [reproducible builds](https://reproducible-builds.org/) for [openSUSE](https://en.opensuse.org/openSUSE:Reproducible_Builds), I found that our kubernetes1.24 package stopped to produce bit-identical results on 2 fresh builds.

```

The first chunk is likely just the hash of the remainder, so can be ignored.
The other chunks indicate that a random build temporary path is used for `_cgo_gotypes.go`

### What did you expect to happen?

Sources should be able to reproduce bit-identical binaries e.g. for SLSA level4

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On Debian or openSUSE do
```bash
osc co openSUSE:Factory/kubernetes1.24 && cd $_
for i in 1 2 ; do
  osc build --clean --noservice --keep-pkg=RPMS.$i \
  --define='%source_date_epoch_from_changelog Y' \
  --define="%_buildhost reproducible" \
  --define='%clamp_mtime_to_source_date_epoch Y' \
  --define='%use_source_date_epoch_as_buildtime Y'
done
sha256sum RPMS.*/kubernetes1.24-kubelet-1*.rpm

> somewhat related to #120507

The scenarios that trigger panic are similar(the apiserver fails to call webhook), but the log shows that the location of panic is different.

For context of [`k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/filters`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/filters/OWNERS)
Thank you.

again, full stack logs:
[kube-apiserver-panic.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/14062163/kube-apiserver-panic.txt)
I'll try to test the mr: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189

Let me try to explain the panic - both goroutines are trying to write to the `Header` of the `ResponseWriter`

first goroutine: This request has timed out, and consequently the `timeout` filter is trying to send a `StatusGatewayTimeout` response to the caller. This is the client facing goroutine from the timeout filter.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/filters/timeout.go#L248-L261

Note that the call to `WriteHeader` is protected by a mutex, that means that if the other goroutine is using the delegated `Responsewriter` object via the `baseTimeoutWriter` adapter, then this panic should not happen.

second goroutine: let's check the other goroutine, it is also trying to write to the `Header` of the `ResponseWriter` object:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/authentication/token/cache/cached_token_authenticator.go#L138-L140

Now `warning.AddWarning` uses an unprotected version of the ResponseWriter object:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/warning.go#L31-L37

The `WithWarningRecorder` filter precedes the `timeout` filter in the execution order, so the `recorder` in  `recorder := &recorder{writer: w}` is not using the thread safe `baseTimeoutWriter` implementation.

This is the order today:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a8a1abc25cad87333840cd7d54be2efaf31a3177/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/config.go#L944-L955

one quick resolution is to move the `WithWarningRecorder` after the timeout filter: [REDACTED] but there could be code that precedes that needs to write warning?
Also note that the panic mentioned in 115282 `Header called after Handler finished` is not as severe, it does not cause the apiserver to crash. 

For a more proper solution, i think we would want https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189

any thoughts? /cc @liggitt @wojtek-t

I tend to remove the timeout filter, the sooner the better, and I think the Apiserver panic is the P0-level bug, directly affecting the availability of the cluster

I have cherry-picked [pr114189](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114189) and tested it in my cluster, and I still need to continue to observe for 1-2 days

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy using CRDs as paramKind always fails after restarting kube-apiserver
description:
### What happened?

I'm using ValidatingAdmissionPolicy(VAP) with setting my own CRD to paramKind in my on-premise cluster. It works fine, but once I restarted one of the kube-apiserver instances it changed to reject both valid and invalid requests with the error message like:

```
error: failed to create rolebinding: rolebindings.rbac.authorization.k8s.io "view" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'test-vap' denied request: failed to configure policy: failed to find resource referenced by paramKind: 'example.com/v1alpha1, Kind=Foo'
```

### What did you expect to happen?

VAP using CRDs as paramKind should continue to work fine even when one of kube-apiserver instances is restarted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

You can reproduce it locally using kind cluster by following procedure.

<details>

```

kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: ClusterConfiguration
    apiServer:
      extraArgs:
        feature-gates: "ValidatingAdmissionPolicy=true"
        runtime-config: "admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1beta1=true"

title: E2E test is not setting the EndpointSlices conditions to ready
description:
The test create custome EndpointSlices to validate some behaviors sending traffic, so it is clear that it expects the EndpointSlices to be ready, 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b529e6ff1c7edb3bb1eaca185b9662d8e42ac2d0/test/e2e/network/endpointslice.go#L698-L712

The API doc is vague about this situation and leaves room to interpret the "unknown behavior", quoting @danwinship

> I was going to say that the API docs say that Ready: nil means it is ready, but actually it says "A nil value indicates an unknown state. In most cases consumers should interpret this unknown state as ready". FTR, kube-proxy interprets nil as true for Ready and Serving, and false for Terminating. It's possible we should update the API docs to make that official. Or if not, probably we should change the e2e tests to not rely on undefined values

Since the test expects the EndpointSlices to be Ready we should set them, if we decide to change the API behavior, then we should add an additional e2e test to validate this behavior, but not use the same test to validate two different things

title: `--proxy-mode=nftables` fails if non-canonical (but standardized) IPv6 addresses are used
description:
### What happened?

When a non-canonical IPv6 address, e.g. `fd00::10.0.0.34`, is used as a loadBalancerIP, communication fails.


### What did you expect to happen?

Addresses like `fd00::10.0.0.34` should work, as they do for proxy-mode ipvs and iptables

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a dual-stack service with type loadBalancer
2. Assign a non-canonical ipv6 loadBalancerIP
3. Try to access the service with the non-canonical ipv6 address

I will add a manifest for test, and more instructions later.

### Anything else we need to know?

What "canonical" really is can be debated. The [rfc5952](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5952) seems to accept "embedded ipv4", as long as the prefix follows the rules. So, as I understand it, `fd00::10.0.0.34` *is* a canonical IPv6 address.

Use the manifest below, and the [assign-lb-ip](https://github.com/Nordix/assign-lb-ip) tool:

assign-lb-ip -n alpine-nc -svc alpine-nc -ip 203.0.113.1,2001:db8::203.0.113.1
echo | nc 203.0.113.1 7007
echo | nc 2001:db8::203.0.113.1 7007
```
The loadBalancerIPs are taken from the documentation ranges, specified in [rfc5737](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5737) and [rfc3849](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3849).

<details><summary>alpine-nc.yaml</summary>

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: alpine-nc
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: alpine-nc
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: alpine-nc
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: alpine
        image: alpine:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        command: ["nc", "-lk", "-p", "7007", "-e", "hostname"]
        ports:
        - name: nc
          containerPort: 7007
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine-nc
spec:
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  selector:
    app: alpine-nc
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
  - port: 7007
    name: nc
```

</details>

If you are using KinD, you can set static routes to your control-plane for testing (--name default assumed below):
```
ipv4=$(docker inspect default-control-plane | jq -r .[0].NetworkSettings.Networks.kind.IPAddress)
sudo ip ro replace 203.0.113.0/24 via $ipv4
ipv6=$(docker inspect default-control-plane | jq -r .[0].NetworkSettings.Networks.kind.GlobalIPv6Address)
sudo ip -6 ro replace 2001:db8::203.0.113.0/120 via $ipv6
```
Since the addresses are reserved for documentation, it shouldn't disturb your network setup (in theory :smile: )

> What "canonical" really is can be debated. The [rfc5952](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5952) seems to accept "embedded ipv4", as long as the prefix follows the rules. So, as I understand it, `fd00::10.0.0.34` _is_ a canonical IPv6 address.

No, `fd00::10.0.0.34` is a _valid_ IPv6 address, but it's not "canonical" because it can't be "distinguished as having IPv4 addresses embedded in the lower 32 bits solely from the address field through the use of a well-known prefix" (RFC 5932 §5). (IOW, `fd00::/96` isn't one of the prefixes that is normally used with embedded IPv4 addresses, so the _canonical_ representation of an address that starts with `fd00::/96` doesn't have an embedded IPv4 address. It should be `fd00::a00:22`.)

But anyway, that said, it seems like this could only be failing if the nftables CLI doesn't handle those IPs (which would be a bug in nftables), _and_ kube-proxy is directly passing the value from the Service object to nftables, which it shouldn't be doing anyway because of the whole "IPv4 with leading 0s" fiasco. (I _just_ wrote [a warning about this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122549/commits/938721a88393b65cf9126538f06642b852d7a856#diff-f4b3c1b088debfb8229ad7432d5f86310c531d3c9c4a2e8f3cdba9bf665f01c0R104-R110) in another PR!). We should be parsing-and-restringifying the IP from the Service and passing the restringified version to external APIs. (The service tracker code enforces this for ClusterIP but it looks like we're not doing that for other Service/Endpoint IPs...)

> @danwinship If you don't mind I would like to take a shot at this myself to get acquainted with the code

Go ahead, but as above, I think the fixes will be in `pkg/proxy`, not `pkg/proxy/nftables` specifically.

> you should see in the logs if it fails in nftables , because we should open a bug there if that is the problem

Yes.
```
E0106 05:36:20.530237     365 proxier.go:1564] "nftables sync failed" err=<
        /dev/stdin:73:50-55: Error: syntax error, unexpected string, expecting comma or '}'
        add element ip6 kube-proxy service-ips { fd00::10.0.0.3 . tcp . 7007 : goto external-45IHSLOA-default/alpine/tcp/nc }
                                                         ^^^^^^
 >
I0106 05:36:20.530298     365 proxier.go:958] "Sync failed" retryingTime="30s"
```

Also manually tested with the latest `nft` 1.0.9:
```
nft -v
nftables v1.0.9 (Old Doc Yak #3)
nft add table ip6 test6
nft 'add chain ip6 test6 test6 { type filter hook prerouting priority 0; }'
nft insert rule ip6 test6 test6 ip6 saddr fd00::10.0.0.1 log
Error: syntax error, unexpected log
insert rule ip6 test6 test6 ip6 saddr fd00::10.0.0.1 log

nft insert rule ip6 test6 test6 ip6 saddr fd00::a00:1 log
nft list table ip6 test6
table ip6 test6 {
        chain test6 {
                type filter hook prerouting priority filter; policy accept;
                ip6 saddr fd00::a00:1 log
        }
}
nft delete table ip6 test6
```

If a user specifies `externalIPs` with "fd00::10.0.0.1", _then every sync for ipv6 will fail_ until the address is removed. So, services added after that will not work for ipv6, and on a reboot, ipv6 services may not work at all.

title: kube-scheduler extender.IsIgnorable() is not work for bind path
description:
### What happened?

I use extenders to add webhook for default-scheduler:
```
extenders:
- enableHTTPS: false
  filterVerb: filter
  bindVerb: bind
  weight: 1
  httpTimeout: 0s
  nodeCacheCapable: true
  ignorable: true
  urlPrefix: http://10.108.198.121:9040/v1
```
And set `ignorable: true` to ignore scheuler error when scheduler extender is not working.
But I got an error: `Post "http://10.108.198.121:9040/v1/bind": dial tcp 10.108.198.121:9040: connect: connection timed out`.

I suppose  `ignorable` work fine in predicate path, but not work fine in bind path.

The Ignorable logic in kube-scheduler:
_pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go: 637:_
```go
...
		feasibleList, failedMap, failedAndUnresolvableMap, err := extender.Filter(pod, feasibleNodes)
		if err != nil {
			if extender.IsIgnorable() {
				logger.Info("Skipping extender as it returned error and has ignorable flag set", "extender", extender, "err", err)
				continue
			}
			return nil, err
		}
...
```
and,
_pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go: 905:_
```go
...
func (sched *Scheduler) extendersBinding(pod *v1.Pod, node string) (bool, error) {
	for _, extender := range sched.Extenders {
		if !extender.IsBinder() || !extender.IsInterested(pod) {
			continue
		}
		return true, extender.Bind(&v1.Binding{
			ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Namespace: pod.Namespace, Name: pod.Name, UID: pod.UID},
			Target:     v1.ObjectReference{Kind: "Node", Name: node},
		})
	}
	return false, nil
}
...
```
the `ignorable` is not judge in `extendersBinding`.


### What did you expect to happen?

Schedule should not error when set `ignorable=true`.

1.add extenders to kube-scheduler config(which has filterVerb and bindVerb and ignorable flag), example:

title: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
description:
### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the first pod was eventually assigned to the node.

On the scheduler side, what we need to do is make the 30s longer for large clusters, and ideally adaptable to cluster state.


### What did you expect to happen?

No race conditions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a large scale cluster.

### Anything else we need to know?
