@pacoxu This issue is getting observed frequently on `ppc arch`.

Link to failure : https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/ppc64le-kubernetes/logs/periodic-kubernetes-unit-test-ppc64le/1755260242423189504

So I dig into it, and I'm sure this is a bug...

In #122435, we introduced this logic in `findNodesThatPassFilters`, and this doesn't consider about extenders
```
	if !sched.hasScoring(fwk) {
		numNodesToFind = 1
	}
```

Say that we have two nodes(node1, node2), some filter plugins but no score plugins.
With this line, we'll return only one node in `findNodesThatPassFilters`, probably `node1` but also probably `node2`(due to we check nodes parallel).

And if we have one extender which rejects node2, we'll fail in `findNodesThatPassExtenders` 
if `findNodesThatPassFilters` returns `node2`, but before  #122435, we'll return both nodes in `findNodesThatPassFilters`, and node2 will pass `findNodesThatPassExtenders` .

I'm not sure if this is included in `1.29.1`, if so, then this is a regression, I think we should just revert it now.

And as we can't stop checking nodes in `findNodesThatPassFilters`.
I think the only performance we can improve is here in `prioritizeNodes`:
Change `if len(extenders) == 0 && !fwk.HasScorePlugins() ` to something like: ` if len(ScoreExtenders) == 0 && !fwk.HasScorePlugins() `
I doubt this will have a considerable improvement, and I'm not sure if we should implement #122435 again.
The default `numNodesToFind` is 100. If it happens to be the case that the extenders reject these 100 nodes, but there is another node that could have fit, we still reach this situation, wouldn't we?

title: Scheduler evaluates many nodes even if there are no scoring plugins defined
description:
### What happened?

Even when no scoring plugins are defined, scheduler always attempts to find multiple nodes where the pod can run. This is unnecessary (and therefore inefficient) when we know ahead of time that there will be no difference between how those nodes are scored. 

### What did you expect to happen?

If we're going to pick a random node, we can just as well cut short the search after finding the first match.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure scheduler without any scoring plugins and see that mulitple nodes are evaluated anyway.

Do you have any idea which variable is nil here?
oops, sorry, it's the deletionTimestamp

Is it actually a panic though? It seems that the logger is parsing a nil value as `<panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference>` and proceeding.

I think we could use `ptr.Deref` and provide a default value.
Possibly this is just logger indeed. Still it is important imo because it makes looking for real panics in logs hard. This was my use case to understand another issue.

The logger sees an `any` (= `interface{}`) value which implements `fmt.Stringer` and calls it's `String` method - in this case, https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.21.3:src/time/format.go;l=527. That then panics.

We've gone back and forth whether the logging call should try to call the `String` method and recover from a panic or try to do some advance checks whether the `any` value is perhaps nil. There could be `String` implementations for pointers which produce some nice output for `nil`, so not calling it would be a loss. Also, detecting nil values is surprisingly hard, if I remember correctly (the `fmt.Stringer` interface is non-nil, only the value hidden inside it is)), therefore currently the code simply calls it.
I can work of this 😊

@kaisoz: how do you want to solve this?

Besides some potential klog improvement, fixing https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1#Time to not crash for a nil pointer would be good. https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.28.3/pkg/apis/meta/v1/generated.pb.go#L4762 already does this.

Hi @pohly !

Sorry I didn't answer yesterday. I like the idea of doing the check at type level and we already have a precedent. 
Should we provide a default value as @alculquicondor suggests? Tbh I'm not sure what would be a a proper default value here
When logging an object's `DeletionTimestamp`, "is nil" is the right information to log when the pointer is nil. There is no default that can or should be used instead.

Thanks!

However, in this case the next release this could go into is 1.30, right? This would be unfortunate because we wouldn't be able to fix 1.29 with the klog changes. If this is the case, I think we may need to do the quick if in `controller_utils`?

So we can keep 1.29 as is, or do the quick fix in `controller_utils`. 

I would suggest to do something about it, because it makes our log artifacts not so useful to detect real panics - a simple grep does not work anymore. @alculquicondor do you think it makes sense to patch 1.29?

title: APF API: change storage version to v1 in 1.30
description:
### What happened?

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121089 adds new version `v1` for `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io` in 1.29. 
- For 1.29, we retain the storage version in use (`v1beta3`), because vN-1 understands this version.  
- In 1.30, we should change the storage version from `v1beta3` to `v1`.

title: Kubelet didn't respect --resolv-conf when resolv.conf is empty or full of comments
description:
### What happened?

When I passing `--resolv-conf` to kubelet, it did not respect the option, and still copy the `/etc/resolv.conf` to the pod.

What makes it special is that the `resolv.conf` provided by myself is empty.

> https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/

After skimming the code, I found the logic here is problematic:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.2/pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go#L225-L274

Because `resolv.conf` is empty, an empty array and no error is returned. Then, if the dnsPolicy is `default` (that is the default config for CoreDNS deployment), the `podDNSType` turns to be `podDNSHost`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.2/pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go#L316-L317

Then, containerd will get an empty `dns_config`, so it will copy `/etc/resolv.conf` from the host to the container:

https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/v1.7.6/pkg/cri/server/sandbox_run_linux.go#L282-L287

Finally, CoreDNS reports forwarding loop error.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should refuse to use the wrong empty `resolv.conf` to create a pod, and complains with errors.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Pass `--resolv-conf` to kubelet, and make sure the specified `resolv.conf` file is empty.
2. Check the output of CoreDNS, and its `/etc/resolv.conf`.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

k8s v1.28.2
containerd v1.7.6

</details>

Is it valid to pass an empty file to `--resolv-conf` ?  If yes, should it mean the same as not passing that flag or should it mean "no config".

I think it IS valid and it SHOULD mean "no config".  What really happens is that kubelet gets empty slices (but no error, so not ambiguous).  When it creates the DNSConfig message,  it appears empty, because it is comprised entirely of `repeated` fields with no instances.  That is ambiguous - it could mean "no data" or "not specified".  It's unclear to me if we can tell the difference between those?  @samuelkarp @SergeyKanzhelev @ndixita - do you know?  `PodSandboxConfig.GetDnsConfig()` *can* return nil.

Containerd further conflates those two by parsing into a string, and assuming `""` means "not specified".  Even if it WAS specified!

Then, containerd "helpfully" decides that, if you don't specify any contents, it should copy the host's resolv.conf.
 
I am not 100% confident in CRI semantics - is it valid for CRI to NOT populate the `PodSandboxConfig.DNSConfig` message?  Or is that effectively required?  If a CRI caller does not specify `PodSandboxConfig.DNSConfig`, is the CORRECT behavior to go look at the host?  That seems like over-stepping, to me.  If I wanted a DNS config, I would have sent it.  Agree or disagree?

1) containerd should not fall back on host's resolv.conf AT ALL
2) containerd should differentiate "not provided" from "provided and empty" (`PodSandboxConfig.GetDnsConfig()` returned nil)
3) we should add a "this struct intentionally left blank" marker to `DNSConfig`, so containerd can do the above

So I think this very much *is* a SIG Node issue.

@thockin This is because CoreDNS reports a forwarding loop issue due to systemd-resolved is used in the node, and I pass `--resolv-conf /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` to kubelet. But it has a race condition here when the node restarted, the file may be full of comments if there is no available name server at the time.

And after a while, systemd-resolved got an available dns server by any way, then the UPLINK config should be recreated, however the kubelet have taken the stale and full-of-comments `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf`.

Of course passing an empty `--resolv-conf` is incorrect, but it is not deliberately.

title: Flag to Disable the 6-minute Force Detach Window
description:
### What happened?

Certain online upgrade workflows might need to restart kubernetes as a part of their upgrade procedure. This can lead to the following sequence:
* As a part of draining a kubernetes node, a pod might get deleted.
* The unmount of a pod could take more than 6 minutes.
* If the node is deemed unhealthy when the 6 minute timer fires for the pod being deleted (for example, because kubelet is still restarting), then the underlying PV will be force detached (via a `ControllerUnpublishVolume` RPC)

These workflows would likely benefit from disabling this feature in lieu of the Non-Graceful Node Shutdown feature that hit GA in kubernetes 1.28 (see [here](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/08/16/kubernetes-1-28-non-graceful-node-shutdown-ga/) for more details).

When these issues are encountered in our testbeds, we are left with Zombie iSCSI LUNs. If pods end up migrating to a node with such a Zombie LUN present, those pods might end up attaching themselves to the Zombie LUN leading to data corruption.

This data corruption has caused a number of our cluster-management applications to lose all access to their data, requiring them to be deployed from scratch (occasionally causing downtime for the entire cluster).

### What did you expect to happen?

The ControllerUnpublishVolume request to wait indefinitely until NodeUnstageVolume has succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See the “What happened?” section for more details.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Kubelet panic when allocates device for pods.
description:
### What happened?

It is suspected to be a concurrent bug of kubelet.

When we delete the last pod that requires GPU on the node and create two or more pods that require GPU at the same time, kubelet may panic on `allocateContainerResources` as following.

I think it's a concurrency issue.

1. Create a pod with GPU request, then kubelet will allocate resource for it. Kubelet try call device plugin to choose preferred device for it. **It will unlock the mutex!.** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L984-L1006
2. Then we delete the last pod that requires GPU.
3. Create the second pod with GPU request, kubelet will allocate resource for it also. Kubelet will call `UpdateAllocatedDevices` to recalculate device (delete allocated device if pod deleted). Moreover, such a race seems being triggered when Device Plugin periodically calls podresources API.

We will work on a fix.

title: Aggregated Discovery doesn't show aggregated apiservices as Stale before initial health check
description:
### What happened?

[Quote from KEP 3352](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/3352-aggregated-discovery#aggregation):

> A post start hook will be added and the kube-apiserver health check should only pass if the discovery document is ready. Since aggregated api servers may take longer to respond and we do not want to delay cluster startup, the health check will only block on the local api servers (built-ins and CRDs) to have their discovery ready. For api servers that have not been aggregated, their group-versions will be published with an empty resource list and a Stale for Freshness to indicate that they have not synced yet.

Yes

That's the cache for the downloaded discovery for each apiservice. The list probably doesn't grow very large. Fix is in [REDACTED] Considering the pain of non-aggregated discovery on some users, and the time they have had to wait to get the feature, I'd say the trade-off is that this isn't nearly as bad.

This is a very rare case and especially at release a minuscule number of people on the bleeding edge might run into it. And even then it is not likely to be changing the `Spec.Service` so often once it is working enough to store a cache entry.

title: Kubelet does not respect container-log-max-size on time, during heavy log writes from container
description:
### What happened?

We are running a Statefulset that logs pretty aggressively on disk. The rate is around 6M/second. The kubelet configs around container log management are set to:
- container-log-max-files: 5
- container-log-max-size: 50Mi

We are running with containerd as the CRI on Kubernetes version 1.20. 


For this specific workload, we notice that the logs DO NOT get rotated upon hitting the 50Mi limit. Instead, the rotation happens at a much later size, depending on the number of containers/Pods on the node. In some extreme cases, if there are several Pods that are aggressively logging to disk, on the same node, then the kubelet lets the log size grow up to several tens of GBs before noticing that the log size has grown out of control. Then, it steps in to rotate the logs (compress and replace). 

This problem is letting nodes consume Terabytes of disk space, as opposed to a few hundred MBs of data for logging. 

### What did you expect to happen?

container logs should be rotated out as specified in the container-log-max-size kubelet configuration.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

My coworker (Venkata Gunapati) has a simple repro for the issue using the following Statefulset spec.

Upon applying this spec, we observe that the Pod/container's log file grow beyond 50Mi to uptown 256Mi, before rotating the logs. It is obvious how the problem gets extreme when dozens of such Pods run on the same node.


```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: logging-test
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: logging-test
  serviceName: "logging-test"
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: logging-test
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10
      containers:
      - name: logging-test
        command: ["sh", "-c", "i=1; while [ $i -le 100  ]; do j=1; while [ $j -le 2000 ]; do echo 2022-06-16T20:02:18,308+0000  ; j=$(( j+1 )); done; sleep 0.001; i=$(( i+1 )); done"]
        image: busybox
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The code to `rotateLogs` handles one container at a time, for all containers on the node. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/64e83a7e43afd038b3d5a0179e85099a0958de4c/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go#L222-L223

This is a serial processing of all the container logs that need rotation, which is a bottleneck in this use case.

I am able to reproduce it with v1.29, but only with dirty hacks. Something bad must happen during node reboot.

1. Run a Pod that uses a CSI volume + **file** on the volume as a subpath.
2. Stop kubelet service on the node where the pod runs.
3. Force-delete the Pod.
4. Manually remove vol_data.json from the pod local volume directory, i.e. `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod_UID>/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/<pv_name>/vol_data.json`. I don't know how to reproduce the issue without this step. How else can it happen that the file gets missing or its reconstruction fails?!
5. Hard reboot the machine.

After reboot, newly started kubelet will not see the Pod in the API server, and it will try to reconstruct its CSI volume mount from vol_data.json. That file is missing, and therefore it will declare the volume as unmounted and cleaned, without cleaning its subpaths.

The orphan cleanup routine will then try to remove subpaths of the volume, but it can handle only directories as subpath, not files -> `rmdir` will fail.

title: NewVolumeManagerReconstruction: Volumes are reported as unmounted after reboot
description:
### What happened?

Kubernetes 1.27 with `NewVolumeManagerReconstruction` feature gate **enabled** and `SELinuxMountReadWriteOncePod` **disabled**, a rebooted node is not able to re-start pods that were running there before the reboot.

The node reports in Pod events:

```
Warning  FailedMount             2m4s (x5 over 11m)  kubelet                  Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[myvol], unattached volumes=[], failed to process volumes=[]: timed out waiting for the condition
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The Pod should start just fine.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On Kubernetes 1.27:
1. Enable NewVolumeManagerReconstruction feature gate.
2. Run a StatefulSet that uses a volume.
3. Force-reboot the node which runs the StatefulSet Pod.

### Anything else we need to know?

The reason is that kubelet's VolumeManager reconstructs the volume as _uncertain_ during startup and it uses a provisional _outer volume name_ for it, because it has not seen the API server and Pods in it yet. This provisional volume ID is then used in ActualStateOfWorld forever.

While kubelet _does_ mount the volume after reboot, it's not able to match it with the Pod that needs it. Kubelet reports `unmounted volumes=[myvol]`, while the volume is mounted with ID `pvc-6357c1ec-bac1-45fd-822f-2d6a014a9721` in my case (= the provisional name, we use PV.name for it) and not `myvol` (=`pod.spec.volumes[*].name`).

It is not reproducible with `SELinuxMountReadWriteOncePod` enabled.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

title: Issues with runtime handler supported feature lookup
description:
There were a couple changes to merged in v1.30 to guard user namespaces & recursive read only mounts based on runtime self-reported support. When looking through the code, I noticed the following issues:

title: SetFeatureGateDuringTest doesn't work if test is run in pararell.
description:
### What happened?

`defer featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate, features.ConsistentListFromCache, true)()` should change the feature flag to true, however feature flag is a global state, so if somewhere in the test we call `t.Parallel()` there is a risk that some other test changes the flag state in the mean time.

Found this when we launched broken ConsistentListFromCache to Alpha and only noticed issues in Beta as the test didn't really test anything. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123674/files#r1511492942.



### What did you expect to happen?

We should protect against usage of `featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest` and `t.Parallel` in a single test. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
func TestFeatureGateOn(t *testing.T) {
	defer featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate, features.ConsistentListFromCache, true)()
	runFeatureGateTest(t, true)
}

func TestFeatureGateOff(t *testing.T) {
	defer featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate, features.ConsistentListFromCache, false)()
	runFeatureGateTest(t, false)
}

func runFeatureGateTest(t *testing.T, expectEnabled bool) {
	t.Parallel()
	time.Sleep(time.Second)
	gotEnabled := utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.ConsistentListFromCache)
	if gotEnabled != expectEnabled {
		t.Errorf("unexpected feature gate state, got: %v, want: %v", gotEnabled, expectEnabled)
	}
}
```

title: [kubeadam][structured authz] can't use structured authz due to default `--authorization-mode` flag
description:
### What happened? **TL;DR** https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7c11cc9cfcdc54a7ca4efdc10609bf421bfa54d4/cmd/kubeadm/app/phases/controlplane/manifests.go#L232 prevents us from using structured authz (setting `--authorization-config` flag) as those flags are mutually exclusive FYI @stealthybox @robscott To use structured authz you need to define the authorization configuration using the `--authorization-config` flag. However this flag is mutually exclusive with `--authorization-modes` and `--authorization-webhook-*` flags. (refer to [1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7c11cc9cfcdc54a7ca4efdc10609bf421bfa54d4/pkg/kubeapiserver/options/authorization.go#L113) & [2](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authorization/#configuring-the-api-server-using-an-authorization-config-file)) Kubeadam adds `--authorization-mode` by default ([1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7c11cc9cfcdc54a7ca4efdc10609bf421bfa54d4/cmd/kubeadm/app/phases/controlplane/manifests.go#L232) & [2](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7c11cc9cfcdc54a7ca4efdc10609bf421bfa54d4/cmd/kubeadm/app/phases/controlplane/manifests.go#L241)) which prevents us from using `--authorization-config` ### What did you expect to happen? I should be able to define the `authorization-config` flag and have structured authz working. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Spin up a kind cluster using this kind config (make sure the images are > 1.29 for structured authz to be avaliable) ```yaml kind: Cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 featureGates: StructuredAuthorizationConfiguration: true kubeadmConfigPatches: - | kind: ClusterConfiguration metadata: name: config apiServer: extraArgs: authorization-config: "/files/authorization_config.yaml" extraVolumes: - name: api-server-basic-auth-files hostPath: "/files" mountPath: "/files" readOnly: true nodes: - role: control-plane # add a mount from /path/to/my/files on the host to /files on the node extraMounts: - hostPath: /refgrant-poc/files containerPath: /files ``` (For this bug, the content of `/files/authorization_config.yaml` doesn't matter.) However, the cluster become unhealthy. docker exec to the kind cluster container, where we can see the inner container of the apiserver has exited. Running `crictl logs ` we can see this error ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console The kind cluster version image: `kindest/node:v1.29.2` ```

title: PodSpec.hostAliases has a potentially misleading comment about hostNetwork
description:
### What happened?

there is a note above hostAliases that this feature does not work with hostNework=true, yet it seems it does:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/api/core/v1/types.go#L3672-L3679

> This is only valid for non-hostNetwork pods.

when testing with a hostNetwork pod + hostAliases, there are no errors in kubelet logs at --v=10 related to this, in fact i don't see any hostAlias entries at all in there.

i could not find anything blocking this in the kubelet, in fact there is normal handling of hostNetwork:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L330

i could not find any validation performed on the hostAliases field of PodSpec if hostNetwork is true on the API level.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/38f4f9d8c4c0519917464b40997e8bcb478c8f8c/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L3888

i could not find any unit tests or e2e tests related to this.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We identified an edge case here with Kubernetes v1.29.

If a cloud provider did not yet initialise the node's `.status.addresses`, the code for creating the `/etc/hosts` file including the hostAliases does not get run.

To be concrete, in:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3f7a50f38688eb332e2a1b013678c6435d539ae6/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L160

`podIPs` is empty in this case which leads to `mountEtcHostsFile` to be `false`.

I was able to trace it back to this change which leads to this behaviour for static pods:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121028

For confirmation: I reverted the above commit, rebuilt kubelet and it got back to the old behaviour.

> For confirmation: I reverted the above commit, rebuilt kubelet and it got back to the old behaviour.

> This behavior has undesired consequences if the cloud-provider addresses are different than the original ones, specially for hostNetwork pods, that inherit these addresses from the Node.

> Since some cloud-providers depend on this behavior, in order to keep backward compatibility, assume that the specifying addresses via the node-ip flags means that the intent is to keep the existing behavior to temporary initialize the addresses.

there is no perfect solution, but reverting is wrong because opens another bug, we need to study this more carefully but in the meantime installers that know the nodes addresses beforehand should set the --node-ip flag or not use cloud-provider external

yeah, as i mentioned downstream, revering https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121028 is out of the question. it fixes some long standing problems.

title: plugins that register nodeAdd in EventsToRegister must register nodeUpdate
description:
Part of: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122284#issuecomment-1853346333.

---

Plugins may miss Node-related events that make Pod schedulable because of preCheck.
It's similar to: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119177#issuecomment-1820091877

1. Node is added. But, it's filtered out by preCheck (due to node's unready or whatever) and the scheduling queue doesn't receive NodeAdded. (noderesourcefit cannot receive NodeAdded.)
2. Node is updated and ready now. But, this event is NodeUpdated.

So, no matter whether plugins have QueueingHint or not, plugins must register NodeUpdate event when they're interested in NodeAdd. Also, in case they have QHint, they should take this scenario into consideration.

title: --hostname-override flag on kubelet is no longer used for Addresses.Hostname value in Kubernetes 1.29
description:
### What happened?

It looks like there was a change that first appeared in Kubernetes 1.29, where in 1.29 the `--hostname-override` flag on kubelet is no longer being used to populate the Node's Addresses.Hostname value.  Here is the relevant output from a `kubectl describe node` for a 1.28 cluster with `hostname-override=10.X.X.X`:

```
Addresses:
  InternalIP:  10.X.X.X
  ExternalIP:  52.X.X.X
  Hostname:    10.X.X.X
```

And here's the output from a 1.29 cluster with the same configuration:

```
Addresses:
  InternalIP:  10.X.X.X
  ExternalIP:  52.X.X.X
```

Here is the full `kubelet` list of parameters in case that is helpful:

`/usr/local/bin/kubelet --config=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet-config.yaml --root-dir=/var/data/kubelet --node-labels=privateVLAN=XXXXXXX,publicVLAN=XXXXXXX --cloud-provider=external --v=2 --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet-kubeconfig --hostname-override=10.X.X.X --enable-controller-attach-detach=false --version=v1.28.9+IKS --runtime-cgroups=/podruntime/runtime`

This is from an IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service 1.28 and 1.29 cluster.  We do not think there was any cloud-configuration-manager or any other related change that would cause this difference.  Is it possible it is a side effect of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121028 ?

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the behavior to be consistent between Kubernetes releases, since I didn't find any reference to this change in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.29.md

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create an IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service cluster at 1.28 and 1.29 and see the difference

title: SCTP Server on agnhost image crashes when a client connects from the same pod
description:
How to repro:
1. Run an agnhost pod listening on sctp
```
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - /agnhost
    - netexec
    - --sctp-port
    - "8080"
    image: registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.39
```

2. Exec into the pod and use the connect command to probe against the same pod
```

bash-5.0# FATA[0014] execing command in container: command terminated with exit code 137
```

The stack trace 


```
I0406 18:21:17.102027       1 log.go:195] Started HTTP server on port 8080
I0406 18:21:17.102399       1 log.go:195] Started UDP server on port  8081
I0406 18:21:17.102465       1 log.go:195] Started SCTP server
I0406 18:22:07.943777       1 log.go:195] SCTP server exited
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x15097bb]

goroutine 77 [running]:
k8s.io/kubernetes/test/images/agnhost/netexec.startSCTPServer(0x0?)
        /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/images/agnhost/netexec/netexec.go:696 +0x3fb
created by k8s.io/kubernetes/test/images/agnhost/netexec.main
        /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/images/agnhost/netexec/netexec.go:217 +0x22f
root@kind-worker:/#

```

that points to 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f8930f980d2986f9e486b04c14c3e93e57bdbe12/test/images/agnhost/netexec/netexec.go#L696

and this is from the vendored library vendor/github.com/ishidawataru/sctp/sctp.go ,

comments.text:
here we are immediately closing the connection after successful connect leading to EOF at server end (it is expecting data) causing the failure.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22140b6a070e09589b5b2bcdf5c396114f25274f/test/images/agnhost/connect/connect.go#L116-L122


We can tweak this to connect send some data just like UDP and then exit?
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22140b6a070e09589b5b2bcdf5c396114f25274f/test/images/agnhost/connect/connect.go#L55

Works locally writing "hostname" to the connection.

[EDIT]

For me it sometimes failed with EOF, sometime with nil pointer exception at `conn.RemoteAddr().String()`.
https://github.com/ishidawataru/sctp/blob/master/sctp.go#L602 This reads sock opts via syscall and we immediately close the connection .. kind of a race between the client closing connection and server reading fds?

the panic seems a bug in that project, no?
Also SCTP, has a establishment handshake, so the data should not be relevant in this case

[Accept(4)](https://linux.die.net/man/2/accept4) returns fd and socket address, for [TCP the returned socket address](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/internal/poll/sock_cloexec_accept.go#L22) is used to implement `RemoteAddr` (always read from struct field).

The SCTP implementation discards the returned socket address by `Accept` call.
https://github.com/ishidawataru/sctp/blob/7ff4192f6ff2b4b181ec7dce269bdf4076ff90a0/sctp_linux.go#L235, and `RemoteAddr` is always a new syscall ([SCTP_GET_PEER_ADDRS](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sctp.7.html#:~:text=passed%20to%20users.-,SCTP_GET_PEER_ADDRS,-This%20option%20is)). 

In our case the client immediately closes the connection, there can be chances where SCTP_GET_PEER_ADDRS will fail and `RemoteAddr` will return nil in these cases.  I think this is reasonable for their project. 

We call `conn.RemoteAddr().String()` and panic is raised by calling `String()` on nil object. We can easily avoid this by not null check. Also, I strongly believe that the client handling should be done in a separate go-routine instead of the main loop to avoid errors like this crashing the pod.

[EDIT]

The client in our case needs to send some data after connection, or else the server will throw EOF and we currently have assertions that use `log.Fatal` for errors.

>  I think this is reasonable for their project.

panicing does not seem very reasonable

It looks to me that the problem is that the SCTPConn struct needs to check if the connection is still valid before trying to access the file descriptor , see the std library implementation https://github.com/golang/go/blob/5c20d5faeb3d048a31896f3edfb54dbd960d07cc/src/net/net.go#L173

and then, all methods implement this check 

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/5c20d5faeb3d048a31896f3edfb54dbd960d07cc/src/net/net.go#L226-L230

to me it is a bug on the implementation

> panicing does not seem very reasonable

The implementation is not causing any panic, it simply returns nil. 
```go
conn.RemoteAddr() -> nil
```
Panic is caused when we try to call `.String()` on nil object.
```go
conn.RemoteAddr().String() 
```

oh, sorry, my bad I should read your comment with more detail, is well explained there

I recognize I have zero idea of how sctp works internally, maybe we can just be more resilient on our tests and code and detect if is nil and avoid getting into the complexity of this protocol ... sending some random data also sounds good, we do this for udp IIRC
@aroradaman are you able to send a PR to add those improvements to the test image?

Even after putting this in `c:\config.toml` then I am not able to get the error called out by @HuShaoRu it ends up being resovled to `C:\var\log\pods`

I don't use --config but directly use command line arguments.
I can get the error even when no arguments are provided:
```cmd

```
cc @pacoxu @Vyom-Yadav

Based on the following, Windows kubelet has never been able to start without passing a `config`. or overriding some values. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f4e246bc93ffb68b33ed67c7896c379efa4207e7/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation_windows.go#L30

Is this how you typically start a Windows kubelet?  What parameters do you usually use?  If you pass the config it will be resolved in this code path: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f4e246bc93ffb68b33ed67c7896c379efa4207e7/pkg/kubelet/kubeletconfig/configfiles/configfiles.go#L99-L107. 

There does seem to be a bug here, in that the pod log path, now goes through the `resolveRelativePaths` code path and `filepath.IsAbs(*path)` which it is treating it like a relative path which could end up putting the path somewhere not expected.

> validateKubeletOSConfiguration


this is related to my open PR here:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123137

the kubelet on Windows should not throw errors with the defaults (which are Linux defaults).

title: Docs: When the `--bind-address` parameter of kube-proxy is configured as ipv6, the ip address of metrics listens to 127.0.0.1 by default, instead of::1
description:
### What happened?

The `--bind-address` parameter of kube-proxy is configured as ipv6
```
--bind-address=aaaa:bbbb::2e8

```
The metrics port of kube-proxy listens to the ipv4 address
​```
netstat -nlap|grep 10249
tcp        0      0 127.0.0.1:10249         0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      5412/kube-proxy     
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When the `--bind-address` parameter of kube-proxy is configured as ipv6, the ip address of metrics listens to ::1 by default

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The `--bind-address` parameter of kube-proxy is configured as ipv6

_No response_

Thank you for this. 

Please use `--metrics-bind-address` flag to change metric listening address, docs are here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-proxy/

as for the `--bind-address`, the docs are a bit confusing wrt to this field.

--metrics-bind-address          ipport     Default: 127.0.0.1:10249
  | The IP address and port for the metrics server to serve on, defaulting to "127.0.0.1:10249" (if --bind-address is unset or IPv4), or "[::1]:10249" (if --bind-address is IPv6).

Set metrics-bind-address to ::1, the effect is as follows：
tcp6       0      0 ::1:10249               :::*                    LISTEN      30567/kube-proxy 

So the document can also be updated. --bind-address may  not be useful.

title: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
description:
### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue, or it could be a kube-proxy bug. Is it related to the following code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a07b1aaa5b39b351ec8586de800baa5715304a3f/pkg/proxy/metaproxier/meta_proxier.go#L55-L58
Additionally, I believe that in a dual-stack environment, if `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with one IP address range and the other IP address range is not configured, then the other IP address range cannot have all-zeros listening. Otherwise, the already configured IP address range may lose the non-all-zeros listening.

### What did you expect to happen?

In a dual-stack environment, if `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with one IP address range and the other IP address range is not configured, then the other IP address range cannot have all-zeros listening. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a dual-stack environment, `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with only one IP address range.Additionally, a Service with healthCheckNodePort is created.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
1.28.3
```

comments.text:
I think, the judgment condition of the following code should be:
from:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a07b1aaa5b39b351ec8586de800baa5715304a3f/pkg/proxy/util/nodeport_addresses.go#L53

to:
```golang
if len(npa.cidrStrings) == 0 && len(cidrStrings) == 0
```

The semantic is that an empty `--nodeport-addresses` means "open all", rather than "open nothing", so in that respect the current behavior is correct. The problem is that ipv6 "::" also includes ipv4 on Linux (but not on Windows I am told). If a fix for this is added, it should be to open "::" only for ipv6 if an ipv4 address is specified, but IMO that leads to confusion.

A _very simple_ work around is to include "::1/128" e.g. `--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24,::1/128`.
Discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114702

Thank you @uablrek 
My requirement is that in a dual-stack environment, if the --nodeport-addresses parameter is configured only with the IPv4 address range, then it should only listen on the IPv4 addresses and not have the possibility of listening on the all-zero IPv6 address. I wonder if this is reasonable?

"ugh"

(fixed in nftables! :slightly_smiling_face:)

> not have the possibility of listening on the all-zero IPv6 address

The work-around above, add "::1/128", does that. It still opens a listening port, but not exposing anything (e.g. in a port-scan).

[REDACTED] adds `--nodeport-addresses-primary`, to tell kube-proxy to only listen on the primary node IP, and also adds a warning specifically for the case in this bug (where you have a dual-stack cluster, but are passing a single-stack `--nodeport-addresses` value).

title: RecreatingTerminatedPod/RecreatingFailedPod/SuccessfulDelete events leak
description:
### What happened?

The event `RecreatingTerminatedPod` is emitted ~10 times simultaneously after evicting pods of a Statefulset.



### What did you expect to happen?

The event should only be emitted at most once.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a 1.29 kind cluster:
```
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.29
```
 (tested with `sha256:eaa1450915475849a73a9227b8f201df25e55e268e5d619312131292e324d570`)

- Deploy a statefulset:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: web
```

- Get the initial `RecreatingTerminatedPod` event count for that sts:
```
kubectl get events  --field-selector involvedObject.kind=StatefulSet,involvedObject.name=web,reason=RecreatingTerminatedPod -o json | jq '.items[].count'
```
(shoud return nothing)

- Taint the node:
```
kubectl taint nodes kind-control-plane foo=bar:NoExecute
```

- Get the event count now:
```
kubectl get events  --field-selector involvedObject.kind=StatefulSet,involvedObject.name=web,reason=RecreatingTerminatedPod -o json | jq '.items[].count'
```
(got: `10`, `11`,`9`...)

### Anything else we need to know?

From the kube-controller logs:

title: Do not set NetworkUnavailable condition on node controller for GCE
description:
### What happened?

This pertains more for clusters running in GCP but not necessarily in a GKE environment. Clusters that using a CNI supporting overlay such as Calico, do not need explicit routes to be created on the infrastructure level, meaning that the route controller should not be necessary. 

The following snippet https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L456-L468 sets the `NetworkUnavailable` condition for new GCE nodes when a new node is picked up by the node controller. This condition is supposed to be removed later by the route controller in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52457842d155743f0e3fc57ade87251cca37d375/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/route/route_controller.go#L397. However, as stated above there are cases where the route controller is not needed and should not be running.

When Calico is deployed in such a way that the calico-node pods are ignoring any and all `NoSchedule` taints including the cloudprovider's `node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized` taint (which we consider reasonable for a system pod such as calico), the above check creates the following race condition:  a Calico pod may start and set the node network conditions (`NetworkUnavailable` to false) before the node controller reconciles the node. After that the node controller picks up the node and sets the `NetworkUnavailable` condition to an otherwise healthy node.

Leaving aside the race condition itself, I have to ask whether the check is meaningful in the first place. AFAIK, the kubelet in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52457842d155743f0e3fc57ade87251cca37d375/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L338 ~~already sets the same condition, so I am not sure if there is any particular reason for the node controller to make the same operation.~~ Kubelet only sets the condition for `gce` provider, but clusters should already be using kubelet with cloudprovider=`external`


### What did you expect to happen?

For the node controller to not set the `NetworkUnavailable` condition unnecessarily. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

An easy way to do it with a custom CCM image is to introduce some delay in the node sync loop, enough for pods such as calico-node to start on that node.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# paste output here
```

GCP

</summary>

vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace/trace.go
vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace.go
vendor/golang.org/x/net/trace/trace.go
vendor/google.golang.org/grpc/trace.go
vendor/k8s.io/utils/trace/trace.go
```
</details>
These are pretty critical, these trace logs are latency based, so they only trigger when you have really slow requests which signal that something is going wrong.

In absolute terms - yes.

But really we have generic log rate-limiting rules, and this results in logs from APIServer not being forwarded to aggregator and getting "dropped" by forwarders. We are pursuing this issue with Kyverno separately about their excessive use of API / ETCD.

In the meantime there is no mechanism to suppress this behaviour. I would even be happy with a grep pipe to remove, but k8s images don't have shell.

Thinking out loud - if this is an important message we want to output, can it be suppressed into "<message> and 886 messages like it in the last minute". Each individual trace doesn't carry large amount of value when they are all caused by the same client calling same functions.

Thank you.

I'd like to revive this discussion since I ran into that recently and can't really understand why we skip log levels here.

> These are pretty critical, these trace logs are latency based, so they only trigger when you have really slow requests which signal that something is going wrong.

@logicalhan slowness can for sure indicate that something is going wrong, but this is a debug information at best. I don't really understand why it is critical to the point that it skips all log levels. In most cases this will be noisy with v=0 and hide all the critical information that are present in the logs with that level set.

If we go according to our [logging conventions](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use), it should be level 5 or higher, but I could see them useful at the level 4 since they are key debugging information in case of slowness.

FWIW, there was an effort long ago to move all nested traces to level 4 and higher (https://github.com/kubernetes/utils/pull/177) and I think we should generalize that to all the steps that are above threshold.

Still an issue with lastest 1.28 releases. ([Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C2P1JHS2E/p1701132279167519))

Is there any kind of expected 'next action' for fixing this?

>  and I think we should generalize that to all the steps that are above threshold.

I have seen many cases where these messages in `--v=2` mode led to diagnosis of problems. I consider these trace messages (above the threshold) as warnings of something wrong. In other words: I would not be happy to move them above `--v=2`, but would be totally on-board to disable the output below.
Log level 2 sounds fine by me :+1:

title: Tracing: precise spanName of apiserver webhook requests
description:
### What happened?

When enable apiserver tracing, the webhook request spans only show spanName as `GET`/`POST`,  mostly because `opentelemetry-go v0.20.0` use http request operations as default span name, https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/blob/v0.20.0/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp/handler.go#L54-L56
 which is hard to understand. ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10649416/186877756-cd7e6486-0c86-4a2b-b5a6-835ea953f7c1.png)

Following the open-telemetry standard of spanName, it's recommended to use `Method + Host` as spanName.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10649416/186878474-7cc8ad7b-78af-44b9-b35f-e62df3c5de38.png)

### What did you expect to happen?

SpanName of webhook request should be `Method + Host`, like 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10649416/186880111-20bd1a7a-0aeb-4a5e-b1da-4d1466ed8c8a.png)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. enable APIServerTracing feature gates of apiserver
2. create a pod

title: Service NodePorts can be accessed via LB IPs (iptables, at least)
description:
Create a single-port Service of type LB.  It gets nodeport 31234.

Wait for an LB IP to be assigned.

Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.

This is because the NodPorts chain doesn't necessarily check IPs (hence why it is the last chain).  It finds port 31234 and forwards it to the Service.

I think we need to add rules to "KUBE-PROXY-FIREWALL" to allow valid IP+port combos and then drop other uses of those IPs.  Or something.

@danwinship since you are elbow-deep in that area.

comments.text:
This problem does not exist for proxy-mode=ipvs.
```
vm-201 ~ # curl http://192.168.1.2:30018 > /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100   232  100   232    0     0  36907      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:-- 38666
vm-201 ~ # curl http://10.0.0.80:30018  > /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
  0     0    0     0    0     0      0      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:--     0
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.0.0.80 port 30018 after 2 ms: Connection refused
```
192.168.1.2 is a node address and 10.0.0.80 is a LB-address.
this one? https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110289

So, we _can_ work around this in kube-proxy, but I believe this bug is a side effect of GCE stuff which is not part of core Kubernetes. The rule that iptables kube-proxy creates to jump to the nodeports chain is:

    -A KUBE-SERVICES -m comment --comment "kubernetes service nodeports; NOTE: this must be the last rule in this chain"
        -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL -j KUBE-NODEPORTS

`--dst-type LOCAL` means it will only match for packets that are addressed to an IP which the routing table considers to be local (meaning either the IP is assigned to a local interface, or there is an `ip route` rule intercepting traffic for that IP and delivering it to a local interface). Neither iptables kube-proxy nor the GCP CloudProvider adds LB IPs as local IPs, or adds routes directing LB IP traffic to the local host, so this rule _should not match_ LB IP traffic unless something besides core Kubernetes is mucking with the routing of LB IP traffic.

I know in OpenShift-on-GCP, there _is_ a service that does special handling for LoadBalancer IPs, and I'm pretty sure it's a fork of something that runs on GCE. The behavior in OpenShift has changed over the years, and it now uses iptables rules rather than routes, but it ends up having [the same bug](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2094408) (which I had assumed GCE _didn't_ have), and my conclusion there was that we shouldn't be running that script for LB IPs that correspond to Kubernetes Services; it should only be used for LB IPs that _aren't_ being managed by kube-proxy. (Of course if there are LB IPs that are used for both kube-proxy-managed Services and for other things, then that rule wouldn't work...)

Assuming I'm right and this service does exist in GCE, we should probably document its existence and behavior better in the kube-proxy code/docs...
note: all implementations that add IP addresses to the node may be affected by this, per example, platforms that use Keepalived on nodes for ExternalIPs  or LoadBalancer IPs

Yeah, any LB implementation that is VIP-ish should have this problem - something needs to accept VIP traffic locally.

My fear is that we end up with 1 "ALLOW" `filter` rule for every service-ip-port and then final "DROP" rules, increasing the number of iptables rules.  With things like `externalIPs` it's not even obvious when to put that rule, since a single externalIP could be used on multiple Services (with disjoint sets of ports).  Also, annoyingly, this speaks to the value of KUBE-MARK-DROP, since we already enumerate all service-ip-ports in `nat`.

> My fear is that we end up with 1 "ALLOW" filter rule for every service-ip-port and then final "DROP" rules, increasing the number of iptables rules

Tim mentioned briefly in the meeting that we have all these problems with bad Service defaults, and I feel like part of the answer here might be to encourage people to use `--nodeport-addresses` or something similar; then we can just change the `KUBE-NODEPORTS` jump rule to only match traffic on those IPs, rather than having to un-match everything else.

(Also, if people use a `--nodeport-addresses` that doesn't include 127.0.0.1 then we can also get rid of the localhost-nodeport junk.)

But even without that, we still don't need 1 rule per IP; we can just make the iptables proxy use ipsets like the ipvs proxy does... there's no real reason other than "history" for why it doesn't.

> encourage people to use `--nodeport-addresses` or something similar

eg
`klog.Warning("--nodeport-addresses not specified; NodePorts will be available on all local IPs!")`
yeah, the `Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.`  is totally valid if the LB IP belong to the Node ... but is this new? this should be always working like this
Yes, it always worked like this, but it was never _intended_ to work like this.

If we added `--nodeport-addresses node-ip` meaning "only accept NodePort connections on the node's primary IP (of the relevant IP family)", would that work with the various cloud load balancers that actually use NodePorts? If not, would it work if we had it mean "only accept NodePort connections on IPs in `node.Status.Addresses`"? (Yes, in both cases it would imply "no NodePorts on localhost"; people who want localhost NodePorts would have to continue not using `--nodeport-addresses` or else specify the right IP/CIDR by hand.)

[REDACTED] implements the suggestion above, of adding a new option to request that NodePorts only work on the node's primary IP, and it adds a warning if you don't use that option and don't manually set `--nodeport-addresses`.

Additionally, the nftables backend implements that functionality by default [REDACTED] and we should update the `v1alpha2.KubeProxyConfiguration` plan (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4337) to enable this by default as well.

title: Resource Quotas does not work correctly for services.nodeports
description:
### What happened?

We have Resources Quotes for **services.nodeports** with an allowed limit of 5 and for **services.loadbalancers** with an allowed limit of 1.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: network-resources
spec:
  hard:
    services.nodeports: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-resources
spec:
  hard:
    services.loadbalancers: "1"
```

We deploy a **NodePort** type service in the amount of 1 with the publication of 4 ports, one **ClusterIP** type service and the use of the services.nodeports 4/5 resource quota.

```
k get Resourcequotas -n test
NAME                AGE   REQUEST                       LIMIT
compute-resources   18m   services.loadbalancers: 0/3   
network-resources   95s   services.nodeports: 4/5       

k get svc -n test
NAME                        TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)                                                     AGE
my-service-cip              ClusterIP   10.36.39.25    <none>        80/TCP                                                      31m
my-service-np   NodePort    10.36.36.151   <none>        80:30626/TCP,8081:25225/TCP,8083:28082/TCP,9000:26419/TCP   2m33s
```

We deploy a service of the **LoadBalancers** type in the amount of 1 with the publication of 1 port and get the use of the resource quota services.loadbalancers: 1/3   
services.nodeports: 5/5.

```
k get resourcequotas -n test
NAME                AGE     REQUEST                       LIMIT
compute-resources   20m     services.loadbalancers: 1/3   
network-resources   3m24s   services.nodeports: 5/5       

❯ k get svc -n test
NAME                        TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)                                                     AGE
my-service-lb                  LoadBalancer   10.36.32.236   <pending>     80:32268/TCP                                                16s
my-service-cip              ClusterIP      10.36.39.25    <none>        80/TCP                                                      33m
my-service-np   NodePort       10.36.36.151   <none>        80:30626/TCP,8081:25225/TCP,8083:28082/TCP,9000:26419/TCP   4m17s
```

The described behavior has been tested on versions Kubernetes 1.20, 1.27-1.30, and the result is the same for all.

### What did you expect to happen?

In  the documentation https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/#object-count-quota the use of the resource quota for **services.nodeports** is described as **"The total number of Services of type NodePort that can exist in the namespace."**

In fact, each published port is considered for the services.nodeports resource quota, regardless of the specified type of Load Balancer or NodePort service.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create Resource Quota

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: network-resources
spec:
  hard:
    services.nodeports: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-resources
spec:
  hard:
    services.loadbalancers: "1"
```

Create service

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service-cip
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: MyApp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
  type: ClusterIP
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service-np
spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  ports:
  - name: api
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080
  - name: probe
    port: 8081
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8081
  - name: prof
    port: 8083
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8083
  - name: metrics
    port: 9000
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 9000
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: my-service-np
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: NodePort
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service-lb
spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  ports:
  - name: api
    port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8080
  - name: probe
    port: 8081
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8081
  - name: prof
    port: 8083
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8083
  - name: metrics
    port: 9000
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 9000
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: my-service-lb
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: LoadBalancer
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

The described behavior has been tested on versions Kubernetes 1.20, 1.27-1.30, and the result is the same for all.

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
none
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
PRETTY_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)"
NAME="Debian GNU/Linux"
VERSION_ID="12"
VERSION="12 (bookworm)"
VERSION_CODENAME=bookworm
ID=debian
HOME_URL="https://www.debian.org/"
SUPPORT_URL="https://www.debian.org/support"
BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.debian.org/

$ uname -a
Linux k8s-xc-01.stage.xxx.ru 6.1.0-18-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.1.76-1 (2024-02-01) x86_64 GNU/Linu
```

</details>

</details>

The documentation is wrong , is not about the Type of Service is about the number of NodePorts allocated, services of Type LoadBalancer can allocate NodePorts too

### What did you expect to happen?

`kube-scheduler` should not crash, on v1.29.4 it doesn't happen.

On v1.29.4 the `kube-scheduler` is just printing these error logs, but doesn't crash:

```
E0517 13:19:26.611504       1 schedule_one.go:1003] "Error scheduling pod; retrying" err="nodeinfo not found for node name \"invalid-node\"" pod="default/break-kube-scheduler"
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod like this:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: break-kube-scheduler
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchFields:
          - key: metadata.name
            operator: In
            values:
            - invalid-node # a node that doesn't exist
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: alpine
    command: ["cat"]
    stdin: true
```
The important part is that the affinity doesn't match a real/valid node.

Once this pod is being processed by `kube-scheduler` it will crash and continue to do so until the pod is deleted.

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue was triggered during the rotation of control-plane nodes. In our setup we update the control plane by scaling from 1 to 2 instances. Once both a ready, the old is being terminated via EC2 API. At this stage the kube-controller-manager _sometimes_ manages to create a replacement daemonset pod once the old node is being deleted. This results in a pod targeting a no longer existing node via `affinity` as illustrated in the example above. For some reason, when the `kube-scheduler` is crashing the `kube-controller-manager` doesn't delete the extra/invalid daemonset pod. Not sure if this is another issue or it has always happened in our setup, but only v1.30 makes `kube-scheduler` crash which causes an actual issue.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.29.2
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.30.1
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
We run a custom Kubernetes setup on AWS EC2 (not EKS).
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="22.04"
VERSION="22.04.4 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)"
VERSION_CODENAME=jammy

title: Kubectl auth can-i doesn't know about the `approve` verb
description:
**What happened**:

If you use `kubectl auth can-i` to test whether a user can approve certificate signing requests, you get a response indicating that `approve` is not a valid verb

```bash
kubectl auth can-i approve certificatesigningrequests.certificates.k8s.io
Warning: resource 'certificatesigningrequests' is not namespace scoped in group 'certificates.k8s.io'

Warning: verb 'approve' is not a known verb
```

An example of the `approve` verb being used can be seen [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#approval-rejection-kubectl)

**What you expected to happen**:

`approve` should be recognized as a valid verb on `certificatesigningrequest` objects.


**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Run

```bash
kubectl auth can-i approve certificatesigningrequests.certificates.k8s.io
```

**Anything else we need to know?**:

I think that `approve` needs to be added to the kubectl auth can-i code [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/blob/514f46729f82412dd9cc41f206058bc4ae9b62b0/pkg/cmd/auth/cani.go#L106)

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes client and server versions (use `kubectl version`):
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):

comments.text: I don't think `approve` is a valid verb for kubectl auth command. Valid verbs are in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/blob/514f46729f82412dd9cc41f206058bc4ae9b62b0/pkg/cmd/auth/cani.go#L106

so in that line of code there are a number of verbs which are only usuable on specific objects for example `impersonate` which works on users. AFAIK the point of that line is to inform kubectl what the valid verbs are on *any* object in Kubernetes, so that it knows what's possible when users use the `kubectl auth can-i` command.

the `approve` verb is valid on certificate objects as shown in the docs example I listed. Without `approve` being present in that line of code, `kubectl auth can-i` will incorrectly state that there is no `approve` verb in Kubernetes.
I tested it, seems working when we add `approve` in that list. But the question is should we add it or not?

There have been cases where Kubectl has had additions to handle non-standard resources/verbs in the past (e.g. [this one](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/issues/1035) I raised a couple of years back).

AFAIK the explicit list of verbs here is designed to address this point, it's just not got approve in it. You could ask SIG-Auth about it, I'm sure they'd have more info.
Decision can be made by sig-auth
This will work even without adding verb there, adding verb just removes the warning. Submitted a PR to add that.

title: PersistentVolumeLabel admission blocks PVs on Azure + vSphere
description:
### What happened?

In 1.30, the PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin blocks creation of in-tree AzureDisk and vSphere PVs:

```
persistentvolumes "pvc-2d9b3999-f60d-4797-923f-210f1f75025d" is forbidden:
error querying AzureDisk volume pvc-2d9b3999-f60d-4797-923f-210f1f75025d:
unable to build Azure cloud provider for AzureDisk
```

The reason is that the cloud provider was removed (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122857), but the admission plugin still calls GetCloudProvider there, which fails: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/646fbe6d0a3fa1a100d90a429f039324de9c8138/plugin/pkg/admission/storage/persistentvolume/label/admission.go#L285


### What did you expect to happen?

The PV should be admitted + created.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin. For example, when running local-up-cluster.sh:
```
ALLOW_PRIVILEGED=true ENABLE_ADMISSION_PLUGINS="NamespaceLifecycle,LimitRanger,ServiceAccount,DefaultStorageClass,DefaultTolerationSeconds,Priority,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook,ResourceQuota,NodeRestriction,PersistentVolumeLabel" bash -x hack/local-up-cluster.sh
```

Create AzureDisk PV on _any_ 1.30 cluster, you don't need Azure cloud:

```
kubectl create -f <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: myvol
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi
  azureDisk:
    diskName: test2.vhd
    diskURI: https://someacount.blob.core.windows.net/vhds/test2.vhd
EOF
```

### Anything else we need to know?



### Kubernetes version

<details>

Today's master
```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.31.0-alpha.0.24+9791f0d1f39f3f
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Azure
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

### Install tools

<details>
local-up-cluster.sh
</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>

</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>

</details>

comments.text:
I am fixing the worst bug in [REDACTED] and I plan to backport it to 1.30. 

However, we should consider removing the whole PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin. Most of the cloud providers were removed, only GCE remains and IMO even that one will be removed sooner or later.  The admission plugin has no way to get volume zone + region and is therefore useless.

The admission said (in 1.26, where we had all in-tree cloud providers):
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b46a3f887ca979b1a5d14fd39cb1af43e7e5d12d/plugin/pkg/admission/storage/persistentvolume/label/admission.go#L74-L76

Such webhook never materialized for AWS, Azure nor vSphere and I am not aware of any plans for GCE.

> Such webhook never materialized for AWS, Azure nor vSphere and I am not aware of any plans for GCE.

It did materialize in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cloud-pv-admission-labeler

So removing it from k/k is the best way forward.

title: Daemonset RollingUpdate does not correctly count old non-ready pods towards MaxUnavailable budget
description:
### What happened?

Starting with a cluster of three nodes, with a healthy deamonset pod running on each, with `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable=1`.
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-7fmn7   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running   0          17s          
```

When performing three updates to the daemonset, each with some reason that prevents the new pods from becoming ready, I  ended up with zero ready pods.
```
kubectl get pods                                                                                                                                               
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-5sbf5   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-bswfc   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-jgdv7   0/1     Running   0          9s
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that when I apply an update, and the new pods fail to become ready, when I apply a second update the "new" failing pods are replaced before considering any of the oldest healthy pods.
This is similar behavior to how Deployments work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a three node (or any count really) cluster, create this daemonset, which is just an nginx pod with a startup probe hitting port 80.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: demo-daemonset
  namespace: 
  labels:
    app: demo-daemonset
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo-daemonset
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo-daemonset
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          failureThreshold: 5
          periodSeconds: 3
```
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-7fmn7   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          17s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running   0          17s          
```

Update the startup probe port to something other than port 80, which should cause the pod to never become ready, and apply again.
```yaml
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8081
```
You can see the new unhealthy pod, and the generation of each pod
```
kubectl get pods
NAME                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS      AGE
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running            0             5m41s
demo-daemonset-mflls   1/1     Running            0             5m41s
demo-daemonset-zmqnj   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6 (46s ago)   4m59s

kubectl get pods -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,generation:.metadata.labels.pod-template-generation,ready:status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'
NAME                   generation   ready
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1            True
demo-daemonset-mflls   1            True
demo-daemonset-zmqnj   2            False
```

Repeat this process for as many nodes/pods as you have (2 more in this example), changing anything that would cause the pods to be recreated (in this case I just cycled the startup probe port a few times).
```yaml
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8082
```
```
kubectl get pods                                                                                                                                               
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-4rpgq   0/1     Running   0          3s
demo-daemonset-7wfxm   0/1     Running   0          3s
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1/1     Running   0          6m27s

kubectl get pods -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,generation:.metadata.labels.pod-template-generation,ready:status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'
NAME                   generation   ready
demo-daemonset-4rpgq   3            False
demo-daemonset-7wfxm   3            False
demo-daemonset-f49kg   1            True
```

After the 2nd update, you can see that it has replaced both the 2nd generation pod (the one that was failing), and one of the first generation pods. Im now down to 1 out of 3, when I had specified `maxUnavailable=1`.

One more apply / update, and all generation 1 pods are gone, and all pods are unhealthy.
```
kubectl get pods                                                                                                                                               
NAME                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
demo-daemonset-5sbf5   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-bswfc   0/1     Running   0          9s
demo-daemonset-jgdv7   0/1     Running   0          9s

kubectl get pods -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,generation:.metadata.labels.pod-template-generation,ready:status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'
NAME                   generation   ready
demo-daemonset-5sbf5   4            False
demo-daemonset-bswfc   4            False
demo-daemonset-jgdv7   4            False
```

title: Enabling InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate causes restart of containers within the cluster
description:
### What happened?

We recently enabled the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate which caused the container spec of our containers to change which in turn triggered container restart logic on the kubelet. All the containers in our cluster we restarted at the same time.

### What did you expect to happen?

Containers shouldn't restart when the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate is enabled

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate, observe k8s events for pods after restarting apiserver:
```
1h39m  Normal   Killing    Container XXX definition changed, will be restarted
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue is caused since enabling the feature gate causes the apiserver to update the container spec with a default policy here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d61cbac69aae97db1839bd2e0e86d68f26b353a7/pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults.go#L181

That causes the logic here to restart the container since the container spec changed: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d61cbac69aae97db1839bd2e0e86d68f26b353a7/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L991

You can also easily verify that the container spec changed using kubectl:
```
# before apiserver restart with InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate 
$ kubectl get pod XXX -n NNN -o json | grep resize

# after apiserver restart with InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate 
$ kubectl get pod XXX -n NNN -o json | grep resize
                "resizePolicy": [
```

v1.27.5
