comments.text: cc @swatisehgal @ffromani

> cache0: 0-8 cpus, SMT enabled. And then using takePartialUncore to acquire 7 cpus, it will fail.

Can you provide more details of the failure? Is the failure SMTAlignment error?

Do you have both `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` and `full-pcpus-only` policy options enabled? 

With `full-pcpu-only` policy option we restrict the CPU Manager core allocation algorithm to full physical cores only. In case you have it enabled and are requesting number of CPUs (7 in your case) that is not multiple of cpusPerCore (2) then the failure is expected.

> Can you provide more details of the failure? Is the failure SMTAlignment error?
> 
It's not a SMTAlignment error, and kubelet will not report an error. Because although this method does not allocate an odd number of CPUs, there is a fallback strategy that will allocate the remaining available CPUs. While no error occurs, the CPUs actually allocated are not aligned by uncore cache, meaning the `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` option is not effectively applied.

```go

numCoresNeeded := a.numCPUsNeeded / a.topo.CPUsPerCore() 

claimed := (a.numCPUsNeeded == freeCPUs.Size()) 

```

You can see the ablove code block. whether `a.numCPUsNeeded` is 6 or 7, the result of `numCoresNeeded` both equal to 3. When `a.numCPUsNeeded` is 7, claim can never be true.

> Do you have both `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` and `full-pcpus-only` policy options enabled?
> 
> With `full-pcpu-only` policy option we restrict the CPU Manager core allocation algorithm to full physical cores only. In case you have it enabled and are requesting number of CPUs (7 in your case) that is not multiple of cpusPerCore (2) then the failure is expected.

I only enable the `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache`.
/cc @ajcaldelas @wongchar

Yes uncore cache alignment was implemented with the intent that full-pcpus-only would be used to reduce the noisy neighbor issue on SMT-enabled processors. However not a hard requirement for SMT/hyperthreading-disabled processors to enable full-pcpus-only.

I'll look into a fix and bring it up to sig-node.

title: externalIPs DNAT rules are not installed when clusterIP is None

comments.text:
@ttc0419 kube-proxy does noy handle headless services, it ignores headless services, so it is not possible to add ips for those. You can see that iptables kube-proxy behaves the same,

what it seems is a bug in validation for Services, does it make sense for a headless service to have external IPs?

> [@ttc0419](https://github.com/ttc0419) kube-proxy does noy handle headless services, it ignores headless services, so it is not possible to add ips for those. You can see that iptables kube-proxy behaves the same,
> 
> what it seems is a bug in validation for Services, does it make sense for a headless service to have external IPs? /kind bug
> 
> /cc [@danwinship](https://github.com/danwinship) [@thockin](https://github.com/thockin)

Maybe I want a monolithic service to be only accessible from outside and I do not want to waste a cluster ip for it.

Sure, that's a plausible thing to want, but it's not how Service is designed to work, unfortunately.

Given that `externalIPs` is a kind of deprecated feature due to CVEs anyway, I don't think we want to expand its functionality. It would make more sense to have a `Gateway` pointing to a headless Service. (I'm not sure if that's currently supported, but that seems like the right way to do it.)
for ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/pull/3608

Service API was intended to be "simple"" to use in simple cases. It was not designed to be infinitely flexible.  It sounds like you've hit the end of "simple cases".

Gateway API is intended to be more flexible and composable. That might be a better fit for what you want, but I feel obligated to point out that cluster IPS are virtual and are not usually worth economizing for.

Aside from the feature request for an LB without a clusterIP, this issue exposes a bug.  I am going to repurpose it.

Apparently, validation does not flag an error when:
- `type=ClusterIP`, `clusterIP=None`, and `loadBalancerIP` is set
- `type=ClusterIP`, `clusterIP=None`, and `externalIPs` is set

Note: we DO flag an error when trying to set `loadBalancerSourceRanges`.

Unfortunately, fixing validation bugs is always risky since there's very likely somebody who is using that configuration and it's not failing, even if it doesn't do what they intended.

What we CAN do is add API warnings for these cases.
@thockin  - I see that you've added `help wanted `. Do you plan to submit a PR, or  I can take over this issue?

help-wanted means that we acknowledge the problem and have a pretty good understanding of a fix that a relative newcomer could implement, but the core team is not prioritizing it at the moment.  In other words - go for it!

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Enable memory limit decrease
description:
When shrinking the pod-level memory limits (sum of container limits iff all containers have limits), the Kubelet checks the current pod memory usage, and doesn't apply the new limits if the new limits < current usage. However, the Kubelet doesn't place the same restriction on containers, and we don't require container runtimes to make the same check.

In practice, this means that for a single container pod, decreasing the memory limit below usage will result in the resize being indefinitely in progress, but for a multiple container pod, if some containers have sufficient free memory, you can shrink the memory limits below usage for a container in the pod, resulting in that container being OOM-killed.

What is the desired behavior here?

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1cEFLXKwNOSNLAkzyhoJUgkBW0OiX-9bXB_aJV7OAypw/edit?tab=t.0 provides more background information and several options for how this should be handled.

comments.text: In v1.33 we are going to forbid decreasing memory limits.
(please fix priority if this adjustment is wrong)
I'd like to at least make progress towards a design for this in the v1.34 timeline. TBD whether this is a GA blocker.

Wondering if there is a chance to get around the forbidden memory resize in case of restart not required containers.

I have a use case where I have multiple containers in the same pod, a few containers may end with status zero much before another long running container. Today, kubernetes doesn't allow me to mark the resources released as allocatable. I do not expect these containers to come back to life or even if they do due to extreme corner case of garbage collection, they wouldn't be consequential as they will go back to exit code 0 right away due to checkpoints.

With v1.32 and available feature flags, I am able to use resizing very well and release resources not under use easily. However, this issue discussion changes it all.

Forbidding resize in such cases doesn't look useful. I feel users should be allowed to choose the option here.

@santosh-d3vpl3x thank you for sharing your use case. Resizing memory requests should be sufficient to make the resources available to other pods, unless you're dealing with guaranteed pods?

In either case, this is only intended to be a temporary restriction until we figure out what the correct behavior is. The question basically boils down to: if limits are resized below usage and we can't reclaim enough memory, should the resize remain in progress indefinitely, or should we terminate (oomkill) the container?

> The question basically boils down to: if limits are resized below usage and we can't reclaim enough memory, should the resize remain in progress indefinitely, or should we terminate (oomkill) the container?

I believe the choice should be left to the users. Reasoning: given I see both of these to be correct approaches within my own set of use cases, I feel both of these are valid choices and I should be able to configure the behavior I want.

As a flow, it could also be that resize could be given a grace period after which it is OOMKilled. However, I would be cautious of introducing complexity of mixing these two behaviours together before we have a good signal indicating this complexity is totally worth it.

That’s is true , end user is responsible to patch accordingly with the application needs . I assume an operator or another entity with rights to resize will have a way with in-app metrics and check the memory usage before resizing . I understand however also from K8s point of view would be beneficial to have the ability to protect against an OOM situation .

As a consequence of today’s limitation if end user scales up memory please note it cannot scale down memory any longer. I think this contradicts with the previous claimed benefit of InPlacePodVerticalScaling being useful to accelerate startup time from a memory perspective ( ie increasing memory initially and then reducing ) , since we cannot reduce the memory now, for the moment. So yes it will accelerate startup but the memory resources will be under utilized 

In case of kubelet restart during recovery which memory will it maintained ? The original “lower memory” or the new resized “larger memory” ?  If the latest resized memory is maintained then we might end up in a case where kubelet could not start all PoDs ( since for each pod resized memory will be the last max memory )

Above we will need to consider in the journey from Beta to GA , looking forward for more feedback when it is beta. Necessity is the mother of invention :-)

> Resizing memory requests should be sufficient to make the resources available to other pods, unless you're dealing with guaranteed pods?

I have been able to reclaim resources back with no problems at all once the containers were downscaled, works on 1.32.
cc @roycaihw

My concern with providing a guarantee that downsizing memory won't force an oomkill is that if memory spikes right after the limit is decreased, that could still lead to an oomkill, so it seems like the added complexity is not worth it.

If we're not talking about race conditions around memory spikes, then I think this should be addressed by whoever is doing the resizing: look at memory usage (ideally with some history over a time window) before doing the scale-down, and document that scaling down _could_ trigger an oomkill.

I think the oomkill behavior could also be desired: we're talking about decreasing limits, not requests. What if my application has a memory leak, and is causing problems in the system? I want to decrease the limit, even if it triggers an oomkill, to constrain it to the new bounds.

+1 for your concern. 

Also when it comes to consistency, there are features where cgroup versions affect how the same input/condition will make system behave, for example, the oom killer for process groups. 

If cgroups provide no escape hatch, putting a band-aid at the feature level seems like a bad idea.

We should focus on the cgroups v2 behavior since cgroups v1 is in maintenance mode.

In cgroups v2, the behavior of shrinking `memory.max` below the non-reclaimable usage is that it invokes the oomkiller. The workaround is to set `memory.high` as a soft-limit trigger reclaim and throttle new allocations, and then check the usage without risk of a race condition before shrinking `memory.max`. However, this isn't the intended use for memory.high (it's intended to be used with a user-space oomkiller), and there are some warnings about using it along with `memory.max`. More research is necessary.

I'm not convinced this complexity is worth it, especially given the concerns in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129152#issuecomment-2798244734. I'm personally leaning towards just shrinking `memory.max` and letting it invoke the oomkiller as needed, but I'd like to hear more input from the community.

I'd like to re-enable memory limit decrease in v1.34. From offline discussions, I think the right behavior is to best-effort avoid triggering an oomkill:

- In nodes up to v1.33, the kubelet checks the pod's memory usage before lowering the limit, but doesn't perform a container-level check
- In v1.34, we should reenable memory limit decrease in the API (validation), and add in a container-level check (@tallclair)
- We can look for further improvements by leveraging kernel mechanisms in subsequent releases (@roycaihw)

description:
### What happened?

1. create the OrderedReady statefulset

```

      containers:

        image: ghcr.io/nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: web
```


2. wait for the 2nd pod to become ready, but not available (can also happen when the pod has lost availability)
3. scale the statefulset to 1 replica
 
```
kubectl scale statefulset nginx-roll --replicas=1
```

4. the 2nd pod should start terminating immediately but instead it hangs until the KCM is fully resynced


### What did you expect to happen?

the 2nd pod should start terminating immediately

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

see `What happened?`

we can see in the logs that the syncs are happening but the firstUnhealthyPod variable is not resolved, so the progress is stalled

```
stateful_set_control.go:509] "StatefulSet is waiting for Pod to be Available prior to scale down" statefulSet="test/nginx-roll" pod=""
```

We even get  the availability check scheduled and called, but because a prior scheduling already ocurred, the new check is thrown away (should not happen, but a similar issue was reported in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119352 and a fix is blocked on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112328)

```
stateful_set.go:243] "StatefulSet will be enqueued after minReadySeconds for availability check" statefulSet="test/nginx-roll" minReadySeconds=30

the sync will be called too soon and resolves again in 
```

```

The next sync will ocurr when KCM is fully resynced which can be a long time (depending on KCM resync period)



statefulset controller should scale down the first condemned pod as soon as it can, but keep the predecessor pods running available

title: PodresourceAPI reports about resources of pods in terminal phase
description:
### What happened?

PodResourcesAPI provide a `List()` endpoint which reports about all the resources that consumed by pods and containers on the node.

The problem is that pods which are in terminal phase (i.e. are in `Failed` or `Succeeded` status) are reported as well. about The internal managers reassign resources assigned to pods in terminal phase, so PodResources should ignore them, because they can still be in used.

### What did you expect to happen?

PodResources should ignore and not reports about resources which are in used by pods which are in terminal phase.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Provided a new test-case that demonstrates the exact problem and can be used as a reproducer:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119402 

### Anything else we need to know?

The docs that describes PodResourceAPI are not refer explicitly to whether `List()` should ignore terminal pod's resources or not, meaning it might not be a bug at all.

OTOH, internal managers reassign resources assigned to pods in terminal phase so it make sense to not account them.

comments.text:
I was thinking about this issue for a bit, and the root cause is probably that there is not a (good enough) formal spec for the API itself so the implementation is pretty much the reference.
We should probably improve here but not sure how (e.g. where to describe more formally the API, perhaps just in the docs?)

That said, my thoughts about the ideal semantics are:

1. Considering the [docs as the most accurate, possibly the only, spec](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/#monitoring-device-plugin-resources) "The List endpoint provides information on resources of **running** pods, with details such as the id of exclusively allocated CPUs, device id as it was reported by device plugins and id of the NUMA node where these devices are allocated. Also, for NUMA-based machines, it contains the information about memory and hugepages reserved for a container." This alone should be sufficient to exclude pods in terminal phase from the running set.
2. I need to doublecheck the actual behavior of the resource managers. If resources assigned to containers are NOT released until the containers are actually cleared by the system, then the API is returning the correct data because these resources can't be re-allocated to newly admitted containers, and the accounting must reflect that
3. But this brings us to the question: is the allocation behavior of the resource manager documented? should it?

I wonder if pod resources API may report the same set of resources used by two pods - one succeeded and one newly scheduled in a single response?

@ffromani should we try to summarize shortcomings at the page you listed as a starting point? We can start with the list of edge cases like:
- "You cannot rely on data completeness while kubelet is starting"
- "Succeeded or Failed pods may be listed"
- "When container has failed, can resources still be allocated?"
- "Is pod information guaranteed visible when NRI plugins are being called for this pod?"
- "what about init containers resources? When it will be returned and when not?"

I like the idea that podresources API is driven by the fact whether resources are actually in use, not by the Pod status" Thus the resource manager behavior ideally needs to be documented.

@SergeyKanzhelev I totally agree that the behavior should be documented in a more precse way. I'm just not sure that page is the best place for reference docs. I'll check with SIG-docs and get advice.

> I wonder if pod resources API may report the same set of resources used by two pods - one succeeded and one newly scheduled in a single response?

From top of my head, I'm not sure we have a code path which prevents this. It should be extremely unlikely (at very least you will need a very limited amount of resources, bypass the scheduler entirely and hit a race within the kubelet) but possible. Should also be transient - the next query should return the expected consistent result. But still, I'm not sure there's prevention for this flow. Also depends on the specifics of resource managers. 

The gist is that the podresources API is a thin layer which reformats and exposes the internal data of resource managers. This makes the code very simple, but leaks pretty badly the internal implementation of the resource managers allocation process.

This in turns makes the API not really formally specified and with perhaps poor stability guarantees.

I think the best approach would be extending https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/podresources/v1/api.proto#L36 to enable the client side to filter out or not pod in terminal phase. This way we fix the issue AND we preserve backward compatible.

This of course assuming we can extend the message in a backward compatible way. It should be the case, but we need to doublecheck.
+1 I like the ability to allow the client to filter the result based on pod phase or in general exposing the pod phase allowing the client to filter out the pods themselves.

The next question would be if such a change deserves a KEP or not. I quite strongly feel that this would still fall under the "bugfix" category - we had a rich history about "invasive" and sometimes behavior-changing fixes, and this change hardly look as a RFE.
But before to move forward with that we need a [better spec of the API behavior and more formalized guarantees](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423#issuecomment-1653407887). That would be the next step.

I'm digging in the history to come a conclusion about the `GetPods`  vs `GetActivePods`.
I think I eventually found strong enough conclusion that the API was never meant to return all pods like it does today, but rather indeed only Running ("or Pending" - sic) pods. This PR and its comments are quite informative: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/79409 . Especially noteworthy is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/79409#issuecomment-505975671 which documents the intent of the API matching what we inferred from the docs.

Back in time `GetActivePods` was not available (or was it but not used? history is not conclusive here), and even today it has its share of issues (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104824), but is now clear that
1. `List` was meant to return running pods as we were discussing
2. Using different pod sources `GetPods` in the API vs `GetActivePods` in the resource managers is a major and unnecessary sources of desyncs which creates all the mess we seen
3. Syncing the resource managers before collecting resource allocations is in hindsight not great. From a conceptual standpoint it forces a write within a pure read operation, and scales poorly when we added the managers

The problem, however, is this behavior has been like this since v1alpha1, for roughly 6 years. So we can't just fix the buggy behavior (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Hyrum%27s_law) even though the growing and IMO overwhelming evidence it was always buggy. We need an incremental fix to allow clients of the API move on, and then, maybe begin the process for a fixed v2 and deprecation of buggy version < v1.

Note that there is another minor bug: pods which do not have any resource assigned should not be `List`ed at all, while today they are.

Note: considering the userbase of this API I'm not completely sure a v2 is warranted, though.

Especially noteworthy is [#79409 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/79409#issuecomment-505975671) which documents the intent of the API matching what we inferred from the docs.
> 
> Back in time `GetActivePods` was not available (or was it but not used? history is not conclusive here), and even today it has its share of issues ([#104824](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104824)), but is now clear that
> 
>     1. `List` was meant to return running pods as we were discussing
> 
>     2. Using different pod sources `GetPods` in the API vs `GetActivePods` in the resource managers is a major and unnecessary sources of desyncs which creates all the mess we seen
> 
>     3. Syncing the resource managers before collecting resource allocations is in hindsight not great. From a conceptual standpoint it forces a write within a pure read operation, and scales poorly when we added the managers
> 
> 
> The problem, however, is this behavior has been like this since v1alpha1, for roughly 6 years. So we can't just fix the buggy behavior (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Hyrum%27s_law) even though the growing and IMO overwhelming evidence it was always buggy. We need an incremental fix to allow clients of the API move on, and then, maybe begin the process for a fixed v2 and deprecation of buggy version < v1.
> 
> Note that there is another minor bug: pods which do not have any resource assigned should not be `List`ed at all, while today they are.
> 
> Note: considering the userbase of this API I'm not completely sure a v2 is warranted, though.
> 
> AI: file a PR against website to be explicit about the API contract once we settled how to move forward in [REDACTED]

building on this, the correct behavior of `List` should be
1. List only active (as in "not in terminal phase") pods
2. Of active pods, list only pods which actually have resource assigned to them. e.g. don't list best effort pods, or guaranteed pods if no exclusive resource got assigned (e.g. memory manager policy is None)

point 1 is implemented in [REDACTED]
point 2 is trivial to do (perhaps as followup of 130228)

these changes will however mutate the observable behavior of the API call. Arguably for the better, removing noise, but still we need to do all the backward compatibility checks we begun to discuss in 132028

title: Statefulset with podManagementPolicy=Parallel ignores minReadySeconds on statefulset rollout update
description:
### What happened?

Deployed a statefulset with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` and with `minReadySeconds: 15`, have waited for all the pods being ready. Then, issued a rollout restart on the sts.

### What did you expect to happen?

Expected that the rollout update happens the same way as with `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady`, that is the last pod is terminated, then restarted, waited to be ready, and then waiting for the extra `minReadySeconds` to pass before moving the next pod. Instead, once the pod became ready, the rollout process instantly moved to the next pod, ignoring the `minReadySeconds` setting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply the following sts:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  minReadySeconds: 10
  podManagementPolicy: Parallel
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      application: web
  serviceName: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        application: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: web
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
```

Wait until all pods become ready. Then, issue a rollout restart:

```
$ kubectl rollout restart sts web
```

Then, observe that as soon a pod enters ready state, the upgrade process moves to the next pod, ignoring `minReadySeconds` value.

If the sts is created with default `podManagementPolicy`, the update procedure works as expected.


### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: In place pod resizing should be designed into the kubelet config state loop, not alongside it
description:
### What happened?

#102884 in its alpha state introduces a new challenge to the kubelet state machine - partial and deferred acceptance of spec changes to a pod in the kubelet, while at the same time we are realizing that the kubelet is not properly feeding actual state to  components #116970.

Last minute 1.27 fix #116702 works around but doesn't resolve a key side effect of this problem - reverting the pod state incorrectly / temporarily.  The pod worker receives new state (in an ordered fashion from admission, and before that podManager) and then invokes SyncPod with the "latest".  In-place resizing then mutates podManager directly, and continues its execution with a different syncPod.  However, once we fix #116970, this will be impossible - other components have to consult the pod worker for the latest state, not podManager.

Visually this is described at https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wbPFANXVbk-e-5BvVHaZScqoqJsfcU_FQVmG-N7pv3c/edit#slide=id.g1de8a1ca1a4_0_1673 (shared with kubernetes-sig-node google group)

To graduate to beta in-place resizing needs a new capability added to the kubelet state machine - the ability to decide when the spec change requested is "acted on" by the kubelet.  There are a couple of ways we could design this, but they need to fit harmoniously into the larger changes we're making to kubelet state vs being working around the kubelet state machine.

To do that we need to make sure we understand the rules that any "level driven update" to pod spec must follow and then implement a mechanism in the kubelet.  This issue covers articulating those rules and getting answers as an input to the change we should make to kubelet admission.

Question:

* What future spec changes to pods have been discussed that would have requirements?
* Can spec changes to a pod be rejected permanently (kubelet never accepts them)?
* When a spec change to a pod is rejected temporarily, what other aspects of the pod spec must be updated?
   * Jordan identified the container hash as a potential problem
   * Is the spec generation "locked" at the last accepted spec change?
* Does a temporary pod spec change block other temporary pod spec changes?  What should the generation be reported as in the kubelet?
* If multiple failed spec changes happen in a row, are there any observable side effects?
* Should we just support full conditional inplace pod changes?  What value comes from preventing in-place updates if we have to implement a full "spec admission" mechanism for a single set of fields?  We already have to support full in-place for static pods anyway.
* ??? (not complete list)

In general my preference is for all config spec changes to happen before a change is accepted by the pod worker, and the pod worker's state to reflect "admitted spec changes".  That means that we would remove the code from syncpod that alters pod, and move it up to right before admission.  It *also* means that we may need to abstract the code so that the kubelet resync loop (HandlePodCleanups) can recheck admission decisions.  A final option may be the soft admission handler inside syncPod, but I don't like that because we have to atomically record which version of the spec the kubelet is acting on while within a config loop which is racy.  

Outcome of this will be a KEP update to https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/1287-in-place-update-pod-resources/README.md#kubelet-and-api-server-interaction to cover these design details in greater detail before beta.



@bobbypage @vinaykul I'll use this for tracking the inputs we need to come up with a design change

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet spec changes and rejection is a fundamental part of the kubelet state machine, not part of syncPod (which is driven by the state machine).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A

### Anything else we need to know?

comments.text: A part of me is asking why we don't just allow all spec updates (we have to support it correctly for static pods anyway) and treat it as delete->create.  Would be confusing for users not to know what changes would cause full restart, but we could always preserve volumes or something.  Will take that separately.

> In general my preference is for all config spec changes to happen before a change is accepted by the pod worker, and the pod worker's state to reflect "admitted spec changes". That means that we would remove the code from syncpod that alters pod, and move it up to right before admission. It also means that we may need to abstract the code so that the kubelet resync loop (HandlePodCleanups) can recheck admission decisions. A final option may be the soft admission handler inside syncPod, but I don't like that because we have to atomically record which version of the spec the kubelet is acting on while within a config loop which is racy.

IIUC, your suggestion is closer to my [original KEP proposal of making the 'admit resize' decision in HandlePodUpdates](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/686#discussion_r297465042) and re-evaluating `Deferred` resize decisions in HandlePodRemoves. The concern with that approach was about [lack of reliable retries](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/686#issuecomment-490587073). Will adding this to HandlePodCleanups adequately address that concern? I'd love to solve this in the channel and get rid of that lock.

> Will adding this to HandlePodCleanups adequately address that concern?

HandlePodCleanups is the "backstop" to all retries, so yes, in a sense.  I think a question is whether those retries are latency sensitive or can wait the average 1s before a cleanup is invoked.  One advantage of having HandlePodCleanups handle it is we can batch up all the retries (for this or other cases) and execute them at once, which is easier to reason about.  A downside is that a new pod coming in might grab those extra resources before the deferred pod can take it, but there are other ways to solve that.

Summarizing some requirements:

* Static pods take priority (implicitly) over apiserver pods, but we don't model that in the kubelet today explicitly, it just happens "accidentally" due to choices in code:
   * static pod admission happens first on kubelet restart to on a restart static pods are likely to be admitted
   * a static pod can't be rejected in practice because there is no place to store it's phase outside the kubelet, and we generally don't want to reject static pods for admission (#116484)
   * static pods generally have low resource requests
* static pods have a fullname exclusion rule - we can't start a new static pod with the same fullname as a previous pod until it completes (even if UID is different), in order to allow updated static pods to behave the same way that regular pods do
  * that means that static pods that are admitted may not actually be running "yet", and thus not be consuming resources, but they intend to consume the resources of the previous pod
  * depending on how we handle the previous issue, we could model this as "delayed admission" (where fullname exclusion is just another kind of admission)
  * no guarantee the new pod has the same resource requirements as the old one, so at admission time we're double counting the resources needed for that update if the uid changes
* terminating pods consume resources (runtime, in CRI) that admission plugins can't track (because they're looking at pod manager, not pod worker)
   * if we have terminating pods holding exclusive resources that haven't been released, we might want to allow new pods to enter but not start

We also have to deal with user expectations - would users prefer pods take a bit longer to start before being rejected for admission (what we do today because we don't consider terminating pods, but termination could take seconds or hours), or is it better to aggressively reject pods so they can end up on other nodes.
since it is for the alpha feature, changing priority

I'm hoping we can tackle this in v1.34:
- Move the resize evaluation and allocation logic out of SyncPod
- Prioritize resizes

title: Garbage collector deletes DaemonSet after updating ownerReference and deleting previous owner
description:
### What happened?

In rare cases, I'm seeing the GC deleting a DaemonSet with a valid ownerReference. This issue looks like a time-of-check/time-of-use error in the garbage collector, although I'm unsure from the docs what behavior to expect.

I'm using a tool similar to `kubectl apply --prune`, called `synk`, except instead of using a label selector to prune old resources, it uses the Kubernetes garbage collector. However, I've found that some systems (single-node test clusters on VMs) break after a reboot, due to unexpected deletion of a DaemonSet. Strangely, I've not seen any other resources getting deleted (even DaemonSets in other manifests installed the same way), so I'm not sure what's special about this DaemonSet.

The order of events, when using this to install a manifest for kube-proxy, is as follows:

- setup (working as intended)
  - synk creates a new owner custom resource (the `ResourceSet`), kube-proxy.v1
  - synk creates the resources in the manifest, including the `kube-proxy` DaemonSet
- update (not always working)
  - synk creates a new owner custom resource (the `ResourceSet`), kube-proxy.v2
  - synk patches the `kube-proxy` DaemonSet to update its ownerReference to point to kube-proxy.v1
  - synk deletes the old owner, kube-proxy.v1
  - sometimes, the garbage collector deletes the DaemonSet, even though it still has a valid ownerReference

### What did you expect to happen?

The garbage collector should only delete resources with dangling ownerReferences. Alternatively, if it's impossible to handle the case of updated ownerReferences in general, the [GC docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/garbage-collection/) should tell you how to update the ownerReference and wait for the GC to become aware of this, before deleting the obsolete owner (eg can the GC enforce some ceiling on the time between fetching the ownerReferences and checking them for existence?).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I don't have a repro I can share I'm afraid. It requires setting up a VM and rebooting it ~100 times. A colleague has tried triggering it by running the command that updates the ownerReference at the same time as restarting cluster services like etcd, kube-controller-manager, etc - but this doesn't seem to trigger the problem.

### Anything else we need to know?

Looking at the GC source code, I don't see any protection against the race between awareness of updated ownerReferences and awareness of the deletion of the old owner:

- on [line 512](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/garbagecollector.go#L512) it gets the "latest" ownerReferences
- on [line 544](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/garbagecollector.go#L544) it checks if these owners exist
- on [line 615](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/garbagecollector.go#L615) it deletes the object, without checking if the ownerReference has changed. I don't see any timeouts (and the code uses context.TODO()) so I guess there is an arbitrary period of time between time of check and time of use here.

I also found this quote from the `kubectl delete` docs, which suggests that the fix is not as simple as including the resourceVersion in the DELETE request. The [API concepts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/) doc doesn't explictly state whether/how resourceVersion can affect deletes, so I'm not sure if this is just for `kubectl delete` or all deletion requests.

> Note that the delete command does NOT do resource version checks, so if someone submits an update to a resource right when you submit a delete, their update will be lost along with the rest of the resource.

Audit / GC logs seem to agree with this:

Here are the audit logs during the event (annotated by me)

title: Parallel pod management with maxUnavailable set should not ignore minReadySeconds
description:
### What happened?

StatefulSet spec's template was updated:

<details>

```apiVersion: v1
items:
- apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: StatefulSet
  # many other unrelated stuff
  spec:
    replicas: 5
    minReadySeconds: 300
    podManagementPolicy: Parallel
    updateStrategy:
      rollingUpdate:
        maxUnavailable: 1
```
</details>

Kubernetes has updated all pods one-by-one in a quick succession, the next pod was updated as soon as previous one has passed the startup probe.
`status.availableReplicas` has dropped from 5 to 0 over the course of the push (which took ≈3 minutes).

### What did you expect to happen?

I did expected that kubernetes would update pods one-by-one, taking `minReadySeconds` into account, the next pod was expected to be updated `minReadySeconds` seconds after previous one has passed the startup probe.
`status.availableReplicas` should not have been dropped below 4 at any point (as `maxUnavailable` is explicitly set to 1).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a `StatefulSet` with the spec above, and update its `spec.template` field to trigger a rollout.
`MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` and `StatefulSetMinReadySeconds` feature gates must be enabled.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: Kubernetes controller manager may fail to manage deployment rollout with minReadySeconds and pod restarts
description:
### What happened?

```
kubectl rollout restart deployment alpine ; kubectl rollout status deployment alpine
``` 

may exceed the deployment rollout progress deadlines if the deployment sets `minReadySeconds` and a new pod restarts during the rollout before the minimum ready seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

Deployment rollout is successful.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply the following deployment on a 3 node cluster.  We are using 3 nodes here to simulate a multi zone cluster that spreads pods across zones.


```
kind: Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
metadata:
  labels:
    app: alpine
  name: alpine
spec:
  minReadySeconds: 30
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: alpine
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 3
      maxUnavailable: 1
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: alpine
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values: ["alpine"]
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - image: alpine:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: alpine
        command: ["sh", "-c", "if [[ ! -e /tmp/okay ]]; then touch /tmp/okay; sleep 15; exit; else sleep 100000; fi"]
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /tmp
          name: tmp
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
```

then run `kubectl rollout restart deployment alpine ; kubectl rollout status deployment alpine`.


### Anything else we need to know?

Removing `minReadySeconds` from the example deployment will yield a successful rollout.  In addition, finding the Kubernetes controller manager leader via `kubectl get leases -n kube-system` and killing the leader will also allow the rollout to be successful.  The rollout will also succeed if the old replicaset is scaled down to zero replicas.

### Kubernetes version

Failure occurs on Kubernetes versions 1.20, 1.21, 1.22, 1.23 and 1.24.

### Cloud provider

N/A

### OS version

N/A


### Install tools

IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service

N/A

N/A

Removing `podAntiAffinity` by itself also resolves the problem.

### Replica sets
As mentioned, the most problematic parts of the issue mainly apply to replica sets.

The timeline of a problematic pod (there needs to be other unready pods for this to occurr)
```
0s    pod NotReady -> Ready (check for available scheduled in 30s)
15s   pod Ready -> NotReady
15.5s pod NotReady -> Ready (wishing for a check for available in 30s, but only previous check in 15s is kept and no new check is scheduled)
30s   replica set checks the replica for availability, which it is not  (schedules check in next 30s)
60s .status.availableReplicas gets incremented which is too late
```

 We are using delaying queue to schedule availability checks. The problem is that once we schedule availability check we cannot postpone it in the future (when pod readiness changes). Delaying queue only allows speeding of the items that should be processed: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d62cc3dc6d5c07fea79eafd866ac7e1217000ea8/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set.go#L464

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f536b3cc4fb8e396086bc6a0108018a783bf3cad/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go#L272 

But we need the opposite. We either want to postpone the readiness check or delete the past readiness check and schedule a new one.  

This also happens with more pods where some pods steal the availability scheduling window of others (pods do not have to flip readiness multiple times in this case). 

### Stateful sets and daemon sets
This issue manifests also in stateful set and daemon set but to a lesser extent since we will schedule available check eventually but at an incorrect time.  These controllers are forcefully running checks for availability each minReadySeconds period and thus it can take up to  minReadySeconds additional time before the pod availability is recognized. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a27a323419a52b0b287ee1bdb4f3339b03ade798/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set.go#L488

This could hurt the progress of the stateful set especially when working with large minReadySeconds values.

### Not a real workaround

It is possible to sort of workaround this issue by setting `--min-resync-period` to a lower value in kube-controller-manager but this will impact performance of all the controllers.

title: Pod probes lead to blind SSRF from the node
description:
Note: I disclosed this private and was asked to open in public

#### What happened:

A pod probe can be configured to send readiness probes to arbitrary destinations, including localhost on the node. This is similar to CVE-2020-8555.

Kubernetes Version:
v0.20.0 (Kind) and v1.19.6 (GKE) were tested. I suspect its an issue on all versions

Steps To Reproduce:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
  - image: docker.io/kennethreitz/httpbin
    name: httpbin
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        host: 169.254.169.254
        httpHeaders:
        - name: Metadata-Flavor
          value: Google
        path: /computeMetadata/v1/
        port: 80
        scheme: HTTP
```

This shows an example of accessing GCE metadata.

Other possible targets are localhost endpoints, such as 127.0.0.1:2381/metrics (etcd metrics), or external targets (httpbin.org, for example).

Note that because this is coming from the node, we can also access internal targets (pods) running on the same node, **bypassing NetworkPolicy restrictions**.

In generally, the attack only allows sending GET requests, and does not allow viewing the data in the response.

The status code of a response is, however, returned in pod events: "HTTP probe failed with statuscode: .... This could be used to extract some degree of private information about the node.

Additionally, access to kubelet logs with verbosity >= 4 will log the full body, which would make this much work severe.

Other possible risks are that these external calls are now coming from the k8s node which may have differing firewall/routing rules than a pod would.

#### What you expected to happen:

I don't know. Its certainly a tricky problem since its a part of the API and hard to change.

comments.text:
The documentations states that readiness probes can be used to check external services
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/#define-readiness-probes
> Define readiness probes
Sometimes, applications are temporarily unable to serve traffic. For example, an application might need to load large data or configuration files during startup, or depend on external services after startup.

and I think that people is using readiness probes to poll external services, changing that behaviour will break those scenarios ....

I agree someone <could> do that, but not that they should. Typically people are doing those checks within their application,not at the probe level. This is important since you may have multiple dependencies or want to better exercise the logic - you care if your pod can reach it, not kubelet. As an anecdote, Istio (accidentally) breaks any external probe and there has never been a single bug report on it so I am assuming it's extremely rare.

It is tricky though since it's a part of a core API.

The core issue is the user/admin assuming the requests a pod can make overlaps with the probes.  I could maybe see filtering the outbound liveness by network policy but typically the CNI plugin has control over other assumptions there and it may be inappropriate to assume network policy alone can tell the full story.

I could imagine an allowlist of acceptable IP ranges or a denylist provided to the Kubelet that causes probes to fail with an error (for instance local addresses).  If we had such a list, we might recommend a common set of blocks that are reasonable (but I don’t know that we could do so by default).

The status code could also be elided when targeting something the pod should not see (or we could simply elide it since health probes are binary).  Eliding status code / info about reachability would be painful for end users (I know I use that message when I screw up my probe definitions).

The v=4 is less concerning because node log access should be assumed to overlap with permission to be high privilege on the node for sanity (node logs can already disclose PII on pod definitions or termination messages), so I’d say that’s acceptable within the commonly understood threat model.

Quoting Tim from a doc comment from an old discussion of this issue:

> Honestly, I think Host was intended to be a host header, but got misinterpreted and now we're sort of stuck with it. I don't know if we have ever EOL'ed a feature for security reasons, but there's a first for everything.
> E.g. maybe this could be part of PSP or something - don't allow probe hosts. Also could maybe be for redirects, but that's more likely to be used by someone.

Based on that, following the [same approach we used for external IP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/2200-externalips-admission) seems like the obvious choice, but I worry about the manageability getting out of hand if we add a new admission controller for every feature we'd like to deprecate...

I agree the externalIP admission is the best precedent to follow.  I also agree that it breaks down as a pattern, at scale.  There are a handful of features that probably fit this bill ("such a bad idea and so little used that disabling it is reasonable for almost everyone") and many more which might appear to fit the bill but don't (hostPath, hostPort, hostNetwork, hostPID, everything in PSP).

So I'd be OK to clone the externalIPs approach for this, though maybe we want a meta-admission that is "BlockDumbStuff" or something, which covers them all?
hi @khenidak , do you need anything from the netpol subproject on this one? if so  just reach out to me or @rikatz
ping to @khenidak

> So I'd be OK to clone the externalIPs approach for this, though maybe we want a meta-admission that is "BlockDumbStuff" or something, which covers them all?

I think the approach proposed in [PSP Replacement KEP #2582](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/2582) might be a good one to follow for a general solution to this. Specifically, the idea of versioned profiles that can be applied in enforcing, warning and/or audit modes. I'm not sure if it would make sense to reuse the pod security labels for the general case, but I could be convinced that they fit the bill.

cc @liggitt

FWIW Readiness probe configured with an arbitrary IP is a perfectly valid scenario. A deployment may be dependent on external endpoint and having liveness probe looking at it is perfectly valid. It **not** valid for *all* scenarios but there are some. So we can not just block it for all.

To lock down a solution, I am looking for thoughts around:
1. Admission controller does not solve the problem for existing pods. Are we thinking of helping the user list these?
2. Admission controller will have to exclude Pod Status Updates. In other words it will have to `allow updates that does not change an already non compliant external IP. i.e. not in allowList`. This situation does not apply on `services` (e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/2200-externalips-admission) because they don't receive status updates. Nor do they generally get updated as frequent as a pod status.
3. Are we looking at one general `AllowList` for the entire cluster (via api-server config) or namespaced or hierarchical (default and then namespace override)?

@thockin @aojea

There are layers to the question.  Yes it is valid in concept (that's why we added it) but is it the best possible implementation?  Doubtful.  If we were presented with this as a net-new idea, would we merge it?  I doubt that.  We'd probably suggest something like a sidecar which does the external query and then reports back as a "normal" probe.

To your (1) I think the best we can do is shut the door and then show people how to figure out if the horses have already escaped.

To your (2) Yes, we can't break existing users.  The good news is that pods are largely immutable, so we can ignore pod updates.  The bad news is that failing pod creation is pretty hostile.  We actually need to admission-control pods, replicasets, deployments, daemonsets, etc. and we cannot ignore updates to those.

To your (3) I think we need to keep this simple.  Ideally zero config.  If we do any config at all it needs to be super simple.  I'd say something like an allow-list for the whole cluster (e.g. "allow 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16") at most, but even that quickly slides into complexity (allow-list vs deny-list? "except" clauses?  DNS names?)  The nice thing about a simple on/off switch is we can punt ALL non-binary policy to policy-engine-of-your-choice.
Not to sound like a broken record, but all 3 of the points @thockin made are tackled by the PSP replacement KEP mentioned above.

@tallclair -- I would love to have this as part of opa, saves a lot of the code and agony around getting a configuration that works for all people. But to my understanding, it is not a default component, **right**? (i.e. not part of core)

@khenidak The PSP replacement KEP is an in-tree validating admission controller. It's good stuff :-)
Unlike PSP today it would be enabled by default as well. But like today it is not a replacement for OPA / arbitrarily complex user policies.

~~I would really like to see probes moved to be executed within the pods network namespace (maaaybe only when the host is set). I have no idea what that would entail though.. I imagine it would probably require CRI to expose an API for it.~~

EDIT: eh, I change my mind. This case should really be handled by the application performing it's own checks, or if that's not feasible just use an exec probe with something like `curl`.

It might be worth exploring, but I suspect this would need to be handled by the CRI, and I'm not sure it's worth the complexity. If we can achieve it in a runtime-agnostic way from the Kubelet directly then it might be worth it.

This is issue is always cited when closing PRs which try to aid debugging by including the failed response of an HTTP-probe into the output.

Why is this a security issue?
* If a malicious actor has access to see events / output of HTTP-probes, can he not already see a lot of information he is not supposed to see?
* If that is not the case, could the access to the response-body be limited to a new role/permission?

@fab1an this is the case we're concerned about:

> Users are granted the ability to run and debug pods in a tightly constrained namespace (pod-security=restricted, or sandboxed runtime), with NetworkPolicy ensuring that the pods cannot communicate with pods in other namespaces.

This bug means that HTTP probes with a hostname set can bypass the network policy, so the users could issue requests to other namespaces. It's already a bad situation, but slightly constrained by the fact that you can only send a GET request, and can't see the response.

Now, that said, this is not the common case, and I'm sympathetic to the annoyance of trying to debug the failing probe. I think a good compromise could be to include the the response body, but _only_ if the `host` field is unset.

> If that is not the case, could the access to the response-body be limited to a new role/permission?

We already capture the response in the kubelet logs, which is an elevated cluster-wide permission.

title: Missing validation in HPA
description:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

> Uncomment only one, leave it on its own line: 
>

> /kind feature


**What happened**:
It looks like validation of HPA is insufficient:
- metric name in pods and object metrics should be checked using IsValidPathSegmentName as they're used as part of request to custom metrics API (this is analogous to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/60433).
- ValidateCrossVersionObjectReference allows for empty apiVersion, leading to non-functional HPA.

title: kubectl cp fails on large files
description:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:



**What happened**:
Copying either a large file, or a large directory from a container via `kubectl cp` results in the error of `error: unexpected EOF` and a failure to transfer.  In my case, the file is 1.7G.

I executed the following command

```bash
kubectl cp infra-cassandra-global-0:cassandra.tar.gz infra-cassandra-global-0-cassandra.tar.gz
```

The command executes, however the terminal will print the error below after 10-14 seconds of execution, and no file is copied. 

```bash
error: unexpected EOF
```


**What you expected to happen**:

The large file to be downloaded from the container.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Add a large file >= 1.7G to any location in the pod.  I was able to re-create this will the file on a PV, or locally on the image file system. 

Execute `kubectl cp` to download the large file.  It will fail.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): v1.8.6, client v1.8.5
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: AWS
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): k8s-1.8-debian-jessie-amd64-hvm-ebs-2017-12-02 (ami-06a57e7e)
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
- Install tools: Kops
- Others:

comments.text: @tnine this is most likely due to a network setup in your specific environment; like a load balancer timeout. How long is the download taking before it times out? Is it always the same amount of time which would indicate a timeout?
Cannot reproduce in my environment.

I had the same issue when running kubectl from my local machine and attempting to move a large file (~700mb). I only overcame this issue by running the copy from another machine within the same network as the kubernetes cluster (an adjacent VM). 

The failures that I saw typically took place within 5-20 seconds of starting the transfer (and indeed, only transferred a tiny fraction of the file in question). This was over an OpenVPN connection to the cluster.

I found the issue here in our environment.  We had blocked ICMP packets in the SG attached to the ENI of our API ELB (CLB these days).  This meant that requests to fragment large packets were not getting back to the ELB.  Because of that, the packet was never re-sent by the ELB, which meant it was lost.  This breaks the TCP session and the connection resets.

In short, make sure that ICMP is allowed between your Load Balancer and your hosts, and your MTU settings are correctly calibrated.

title: DefaultTolerationSeconds admission plugin flags pollute all commands
description:
The DefaultTolerationSeconds admission plugin configures itself via globally registered flags, rather than via plugin config, as expected.

This has several negative effects:
* The global flags are visible in completely unrelated commands, like kubectl:
    ```
    $ kubectl options
    The following options can be passed to any command:
    ...
    --default-not-ready-toleration-seconds=300: Indicates the tolerationSeconds of the toleration for notReady:NoExecute that is added by default to every pod that does not already have such a toleration.
    --default-unreachable-toleration-seconds=300: Indicates the tolerationSeconds of the toleration for unreachable:NoExecute that is added by default to every pod that does not already have such a toleration.
    ```
* The admission plugin is not positioned to receive config as apiserver config is updated to be able to be consumed from files, and then dynamically

The global flags should be deprecated, and a config type created to hold the config for this admission plugin (like other configurable admission plugins)

cc @kubernetes/sig-scheduling-bugs

comments.text: I would like to have a fix on it, and post a PR ASAP.
As @wackxu mentioned, admission initialresources seems faced the same scenario.

title: kube-proxy v1.34.* fails to start if ipv4 or ipv6 are unavailable
description:
### What happened?

we started seeing timeout failures in our minikube kvm driver integration tests with kubernetes v1.34.*, whereas v1.33.4 does not have this specific problem

further looking into the kube-proxy code and changes made between k8s v1.33.4 and v1.34.*, i think i found the issue:
- introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131534 - returning error if not both ipv4 and ipv6 work
- the issue is nicely explained in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132170, but i think not completely fixed

namely, in our kvm vm, we only use ipv4, which still makes the [NewDualStack()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/091f87c10bc3532041b77a783a5f832de5506dc8/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go#L94) func call to fail and thus prevents kube-proxy from starting

-		ipts, err = utiliptables.NewDualStack()

+		ipts, errDS = utiliptables.NewDualStack()
 
 		ipv4Supported = ipts[v1.IPv4Protocol] != nil
 		ipv6Supported = ipts[v1.IPv6Protocol] != nil
 
 		if !ipv4Supported && !ipv6Supported {
-			err = fmt.Errorf("iptables is not available on this host : %w", err)
+			err = fmt.Errorf("iptables is not available on this host : %w", errDS)
 		} else if !ipv4Supported {

title: SELinux warning controller does not report conflicts with ""
description:
### What happened?

A pod with label `:::s0:c0,c2` should conflicts with a pod with label `:::` (or `""`).

Kubelet defaults the first three components of the label to `system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c0,c2` / `system_u:object_r:container_file_t:` and these are two different labels. If the pods have `spec.securityContext.seLinuxChangePolicy: MountOption`, kubelet correctly reports the conflict + refuses to run the second pod with something like:
```
Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[vol], unattached volumes=[], failed to process volumes=[vol]: conflicting SELinux labels of volume pvc-3f62d9ae-7ad0-47d4-8b5a-72656ace42e6: "system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c0,c2" and ""
```

However, the SELinux warning controller does not report any conflict and it should. 

### What did you expect to happen?

SELinux warning controller should emit something like:

```
SELinuxLabel "" conflicts with pod testpod-c2 that uses the same volume as this pod with SELinuxLabel ":::s0:c0,c2". If both pods land on the same node, only one of them may access the volume.
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run two pods, one with `spec.securityContext.seLinuxOptions.level = "s0:c0,c2"` and the second one with `nil`.

### Anything else we need to know?

The controller runs in KCM, who does not know the operating system defaults for SELinux labels and thus skips comparison of empty SELinux label components. It should compare at least the last one, with SELinux level and categories. Those are not defaulted by the OS.

title: DaemonSet wrongfully reported as misscheduled on added node
description:
### What happened?

Since we upgraded from v1.32 to v1.33, we are having with DaemonSets getting (and keeping) flagged as misscheduled on newly added nodes. 

The DS seems to be able to get scheduled very early before the node gets tainted as not ready, and later (when it does have the taints) it gets flagged as "misscheduled" (due to the taints). After the taints dissapear when the node is ready, this status does not get updated and the DS is still reported as misscheduled. Triggering a status update by adding a bogus label removes the misscheduled status. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expected either or both of these things:

1. The pod not to get scheduled before the not ready taint is set
2. The DS status update routine to get triggered by node taint removal

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Set up a cluster
2. Add a couple of DS-es (we have 4 of these) without tolerations
3. Gracefully shutdown a node
4. Kubectl delete that node
5. Boot that node (so it will be added to the cluster)
6. Wait until that node is ready
7. `kubectl get -A ds -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.status.numberMisscheduled > 0) | .metadata.name'` if empty, goto 3

We are able to reproduce this behavior with 4 DS every 3-6 of above cylces.

### Anything else we need to know?

We are unable to reproduce above problem on 1.32, even after 100 cycles

title: Int overflow in hpa causing incorrect replica count
description:
### What happened?

The setup:
I am using keda with the prometheus scaler. The query I am using, returns the lag in the message queue i am using, and the threshold is set to `0.1`.

What happened:
The lag was increasing for a long time, and the replica count reached the max setting as expected. Everything was running fine for some time. When the lag value reached `214,748,364` hpa decided to reduce the replicas from the max limit to `1`.

What I think is the problem:
When the lag passes `214,748,364`, the calculation [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7b80cdb66a390f225d23cd612950144e3a39d1ae/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L278) divides by the threshold `0.1` and it passes the max int32 value. causing hpa to scale to the minimum value, 1.
It also seems like a lot of other places in this file cast a 64 bit float to a 32 bit int. Should there maybe be a check everywhere this is done?

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the replica count to stay at the max value. Or alternatively, get an error that we have reached the max value for an external metric value

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use an external metric, and set it above `214,748,364` with a threshold of `0.1`.

This is happening for me too. I have 8 nodes in an EKS cluster, and for some reason only one node is having this GC issue.   This has happened twice, and the below steps are what I've done to fix the issue.  Does anyone know of a better / supported method for doing this? https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/cluster-management/#maintenance-on-a-node

1. Increase autoscaling group for EKS by +1 (replacement node for the bad one)
2. Cordon off the bad node (kubectl cordon)
3. Drain the bad node (kubectl drain), to kick the pods off this node and onto one of the other nodes
4. Add downscaling protection all nodes except the bad node
5. Decrease the autoscaling group for EKS by -1 (this deletes the bad node, since it's the only one not protected)
6. Remove downscaling protection from all nodes

Faced the same problem.

`kubectl drain --delete-local-data --ignore-daemonsets $NODE_IP && kubectl uncordon $NODE_IP` was enough to clean the disk storage.

We must use a secondary (SSD) disk for /var/lib/docker to address EKS performance issues (see https://github.com/awslabs/amazon-eks-ami/issues/454 ).    But the garbage collection doesn't fire and we sometimes overflow that secondary disk.

We've started suffering this issue in the last week. Kubernetes 1.17.9, built with Kops 1.17.1, self-hosted in AWS, using the k8s-1.17-debian-stretch-amd64-hvm-ebs-2020-01-17 AMI, docker 19.03.11.

This has happened on two separate Nodes within the last week, both of which presented with this:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason               Age                  From                                                Message
  ----     ------               ----                 ----                                                -------
  Warning  FreeDiskSpaceFailed  10m (x204 over 17h)  kubelet, ip-10-224-54-0.us-west-2.compute.internal  (combined from similar events): failed to garbage collect required amount of images. Wanted to free 5877565849 bytes, but freed 101485977 bytes
  Warning  ImageGCFailed        18s (x205 over 17h)  kubelet, ip-10-224-54-0.us-west-2.compute.internal  (combined from similar events): failed to garbage collect required amount of images. Wanted to free 5886654873 bytes, but freed 0 bytes
```

`du` and `df` on the Node don't agree on how much space is used:

```
admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ df -h /
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on


admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ sudo du -sh /
du: cannot access '/proc/9856/task/9856/fd/3': No such file or directory
du: cannot access '/proc/9856/task/9856/fdinfo/3': No such file or directory
du: cannot access '/proc/9856/fd/4': No such file or directory
du: cannot access '/proc/9856/fdinfo/4': No such file or directory
11G     /

admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ sudo du -sh --one-file-system /
6.6G    /
```

Mounting the root device to another mountpoint to get rid of the other mounted filesystems gets `du` to agree consistently on the used space, but `df` still disagrees:

```
admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ mkdir tmproot
admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ sudo mount /dev/nvme0n1p2 /home/admin/tmproot
admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ df -h tmproot/
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on

admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ sudo du -sh tmproot/
6.6G    tmproot/
admin@ip-10-224-54-0:~$ sudo du -sh --one-file-system tmproot/
6.6G    tmproot/
```

I think this can be due to processes holding open deleted files. But restarting kubelet doesn't free up this space, and it would be the process I'd suspect of causing this. Restarting docker also didn't free up the space.

The first time this happened, I ended up terminating the Node after several hours of fruitless investigation, but now that it's happening again, I can't make that the permanent solution to the issue.

title: [sig-network] Conntrack proxy implementation should not be vulnerable to the invalid conntrack state bug [Privileged] failing due to bug in test
description:
### Description

`[sig-network] Conntrack proxy implementation should not be vulnerable to the invalid conntrack state bug [Privileged]` has been historically flaking in downstream OpenShift CI jobs. However, the flakes were very random and couldn't be easily reproduced for debugging.

### Details

As per the test [details](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9a55d78c773fb4fa4a586919d4eff6b4a59c4f9/test/e2e/network/conntrack.go#L544-L668), the test should pass if `nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` is enforced. The test expects that when the server sends an out-of-window TCP packet, it should either be dropped or should be correctly NAT-ed and forwarded to the client. The test fails when the server receives an RST packet from the client which is expected happen when the out-of-window packet is not dropped and also not correctly NAT-ed.

OpenShift uses OVN-Kubernetes CNI and `nf_conntrack_tcp_be_liberal` is always [enforced](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/5aca7966d2a7255ba92fd5e63268dd767b223aa5/net/openvswitch/conntrack.c#L832). Thus, the issue of incorrect NAT should not arise. However, the test still randomly flaked because the server had received an RST packet from the client.

Recently, we took an effort to understand the reason why the test was flaking. For reproducing the issue, the test was run for longer duration of time and packets were captured. The test eventually did fail, however looking at the packet captures it became evident the test failed due to an incorrect logic in the server code, instead of incorrect packet NAT.

9889    2025-09-09 16:58:57.219444    10.129.0.42    172.30.47.170    TCP    66    38949 → 9000 [ACK] Seq=2 Ack=2 Win=62080 Len=0 TSval=3989801036 TSecr=1962482570

9719 16:58:37 - Invalid packet injected as part of the test(should be the only one) to the client on port 36955
9802 16:58:47 - The client initiates a new connection on port 38949
9803 16:58:47 - The server closes the connection with 36955 after 10s as part of the test and the client ACKs it in 9804
9808 16:58:47 - Invalid packet injected to the client on port 36955 - BUG, this should not happen, it should be sent to 38949
9817 16:58:47 - Same thing happens again
9818 16:58:47 - The client is not happy with that because the connection was already closed, it sends RST to the server (using the clusterIP) because the connection was already closed

Looking at the [server code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9a55d78c773fb4fa4a586919d4eff6b4a59c4f9/test/images/regression-issue-74839/main.go) the bugs becomes apparent:
1. SYN from 36955 adds 10.129.0.42 to the `pending` map
2. ACK from 36955 causes the invalid packet to be injected to that connection and 10.129.0.42 is removed from the `pending` map
3. SYN from 38949 adds 10.129.0.42 to the `pending` map again
4. ACK to from 36955(pkt 9804)  causes the invalid packet to be injected again which is not correct

### Expected behavior

The server should not re-inject the out-of-window packet for an already closed connection.

### Expected fix

The fix should be to key the `pending` map by IP+ClientPort instead of the only the IP. This will ensure that packets are not injected for any closed connections.

Thanks to @kyrtapz for reproducing the issue and debugging it.

title: kubectl prints a warning about spec.SessionAffinity being ignored when creating a headless service
description:
### What happened?

When creating a headless service (see manifest in the reproducer section) without session affinity defined, kubectl (version v1.34.1) always prints a warning:

```
Warning: spec.SessionAffinity is ignored for headless services
````

As  far as I can tell, session affinity when unset defaults to `None` so there's no way for the validation to determine whether or not a value was defined by the client.

### What did you expect to happen?

No warning.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run this command

```
kubectl create -f -<<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: headless
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
  - name: web
    port: 9090
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: web
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus

EOF

title: ClusterIP load balancers intermittently deleted in HNS by Windows KubeProxy when internalTrafficPolicy is set to Local
description:
### What happened?

When internalTrafficPolicy was set to Local, Windows KubeProxy intermittently deleted the corresponding ClusterIP load balancers in HNS. This caused service connectivity disruptions since the load balancer rules were unexpectedly removed.

### What did you expect to happen?

ClusterIP load balancers in HNS should remain consistently present and stable, even when internalTrafficPolicy is set to Local. The configuration should not trigger deletion of the load balancer or service disruptions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a ClusterIP service in a multi node cluster with internalTrafficPolicy tag set to Local.
- Scale up the pods to some good number so that few of the pods came up in remote node (Node B).
- Keep monitoring the traffic initiated from a different client pod to the clusterip after the scale.
- Scale up or down, but make sure the new pod coming up or new pod getting deleted happens in node b (neighbor node).

title: Regression 1.34 -- Kubelet requires restart after gRPC connection to DRA driver goes idle
description:
This issue describes a bug in DRA's plugin communication with the kubelet that causes pods to get stuck in the Terminating state. This only occurs after waiting a *long* time (in my original test case 75 minutes).

After some testing, I've concluded that this occurs when gRPC connections to DRA plugins go idle after their configured timeout period. The issue becomes reproducible after 1 minute by shortening the idle timeout to 1 minute using `grpc.WithIdleTimeout(time.Minute)`, showing that the problem is related to gRPC's idle connection handling.

Once we reach this point where the gRPC connection has gone idle, attempting to terminate a pod with DRA allocated resourcces hang during cleanup, with the kubelet logging `Calling NodeUnprepareResource rpc` but never logging the corresponding `Done calling` message. The gRPC calls to the DRA plugin never complete despite having a 45-second context timeout.

Note, that The DRA plugin never receives the `NodeUnprepareResources` requests that kubelet claims to be sending. This indicates that the hang occurs after the kubelet sends the request but before it reaches the plugin, pointing to an issue in gRPC's internal connection management.

The only current workaround for users is to restart kubelet, which forces fresh connection establishment and resolves the stuck pods until the next idle timeout period expires.

Several remediation approaches were tested with mixed results. Adding fallback timeouts and manual connection closure attempts failed to unblock the hanging calls. However, enabling the `ResourceHealthStatus` feature gate *does* resolve the issue because it maintains persistent gRPC streams that prevent connections from going idle. Two other solutions I tried worked: disabling idle timeouts with `grpc.WithIdleTimeout(0)`, and implementing connection health checking that recreates connections when they're not in the `Ready` state.

The proposed (short-term) fix combines both approaches. It disables idle timeouts, and adds connection state validation before each RPC call, automatically recreating connections that have gone idle. This should provide protection against both the immediate idle timeout bug and other potential connection staleness issues in long-running kubelet processes.

In the long run, we need to dig into `gRPC` itself and see why this hang is occurring at all.

## Steps to reproduce

* Install the NVIDIA DRA driver for GPUs

```shell
helm install nvidia-dra-driver-gpu deployments/helm/nvidia-dra-driver-gpu \
    --create-namespace \
    --namespace nvidia-dra-driver-gpu \
    --set nvidiaDriverRoot=/run/nvidia/driver \
    --set gpuResourcesEnabledOverride=true
```

* Run a workload

```shell
kubectl apply -f demo/specs/imex/mn-channel-injection.yaml
```

* See the relevant pods running

```shell
$ kubectl get pod -A
...

default                 mn-imex-channel-injection-57b546bc47-s6jwt                    1/1     Running     0             7s

nvidia-dra-driver-gpu   imex-channel-injection-62rcp-c8jxb                            1/1     Running     0             6s
```

* Wait for a long time (not sure how long but I waited around 2 hours) and delete the workload

```shell
kubectl delete -f demo/specs/imex/mn-channel-injection.yaml
```

* Workload stuck in the terminating state forever

```shell
$ kubectl get pod -A
...

```

* Observe DRA driver still healthy

```shell

nvidia-dra-driver-gpu   nvidia-dra-driver-gpu-kubelet-plugin-l9sb6                    2/2     Running       0             3h8m

* DRA driver logs don’t show any incoming `NodeUnprepareResources()` calls

```shell

```
