-- IMEX Daemon pod
Sep 06 04:41:14 gb-nvl-043-compute04 kubelet[2245881]: I0906 04:41:14.573225 2245881 dra_plugin_manager.go:295] "Preferring connected plugin" logger="DRA registration handler" driverName="compute-domain.nvidia.com" endpoint="/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/compute-domain.nvidia.com/dra.sock"
Sep 06 04:41:14 gb-nvl-043-compute04 kubelet[2245881]: I0906 04:41:14.573239 2245881 dra_plugin.go:173] "Calling NodeUnprepareResource rpc" request="&NodeUnprepareResourcesRequest{Claims:[]*Claim{&Claim{Namespace:nvidia-dra-driver-gpu,UID:5cb193b8-4ad4-4821-b841-fa3ada037b9b,Name:imex-channel-injection-szkpc-tsmml-compute-domain-daemon-sgvz8,},},}"
```

* With *no* matching log lines similar to the following (from a different, successful iteration of this call)

```shell
Sep 05 06:33:57 gb-nvl-043-compute02 kubelet[1739058]: I0905 06:33:57.933433 1739058 dra_plugin.go:194] "Done calling NodeUnprepareResources rpc" driverName="compute-domain.nvidia.com" endpoint="/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/compute-domain.nvidia.com/dra.sock" response="&NodeUnprepareResourcesResponse{Claims:map[string]*NodeUnprepareResourceResponse{f627927a-b39a-4fd1-9f0d-0f2851a015ce: &NodeUnprepareResourceResponse{Error:,},},}" err=null
```

* Relevant code snippet from [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d9b31d602d833b8a45b31f720eed4534c769772b/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin.go#L167)

```go
func (p *DRAPlugin) NodeUnprepareResources(
    ctx context.Context,
    req *drapbv1.NodeUnprepareResourcesRequest,
    opts ...grpc.CallOption,
) (*drapbv1.NodeUnprepareResourcesResponse, error) {
    logger := klog.FromContext(ctx)
    logger.V(4).Info("Calling NodeUnprepareResource rpc", "request", req)
    logger = klog.LoggerWithValues(logger, "driverName", p.driverName, "endpoint", p.endpoint)
    ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, logger)

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, p.clientCallTimeout)
    defer cancel()

    var err error
    var response *drapbv1.NodeUnprepareResourcesResponse
    switch p.chosenService {
    case drapbv1beta1.DRAPluginService:
        client := drapbv1beta1.NewDRAPluginClient(p.conn)
        response, err = drapbv1beta1.V1Beta1ClientWrapper{DRAPluginClient: client}.NodeUnprepareResources(ctx, req)
    case drapbv1.DRAPluginService:
        client := drapbv1.NewDRAPluginClient(p.conn)
        response, err = client.NodeUnprepareResources(ctx, req)
    default:
        // Shouldn't happen, validateSupportedServices should only
        // return services we support here.
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("internal error: unsupported chosen service: %q", p.chosenService)
    }
    logger.V(4).Info("Done calling NodeUnprepareResources rpc", "response", response, "err", err)
    return response, err
}
```

It should not be possible for the first log line to be called without the second.

It suggests the call to `client.NodeUnprepareResources(ctx, req)` never returns (despite the context with the timeout). Note that the call into `client.NodeUnprepareResources()` is into the *generated* PB code (which feels unlikely to be incorrect). We also *never* see `"internal error: unsupported chosen service"` anywhere in the logs.

Not sure how this is possible or what is going on here.

The only way to recover from this is to trigger a kubelet restart.

Once the kubelet is restarted, it rediscovers the DRA driver and issues a `NodeUnprepareResources()`, which the DRA driver receives and carries out the deletion.

## Reproducibility

After a bunch of the remediation attempts listed below, I zeroed in on the fact that this issue happens when the gRPC connection goes into the Idle state. In the original code I would have to wait up 30 minutes to see the issue (because the default idle timeout is 30min). However, if I tweak `WithIdleTimeout` to 1 minute I am able to trigger the issue much more quickly. This suggests, the issue truly is related to the connection going idle, and I now have way to run with a smaller debug loop.

```go
       target := "unix:" + p.endpoint
       logger.V(4).Info("Creating new gRPC connection", "target", target)
       conn, err := grpc.NewClient(
               target,
               grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()),
               grpc.WithChainUnaryInterceptor(newMetricsInterceptor(p.driverName)),
               grpc.WithStatsHandler(mp),
+              grpc.WithIdleTimeout(time.Minute),
       )
       if err != nil {
               return fmt.Errorf("create gRPC connection to DRA driver %s plugin at endpoint %s: %w", p.driverName, p.endpoint, err)
       }
```

## Remediation attempts

* Add a fallback timeout that waits twice as long as the original timeout. In a normal operating state, it should **never** get called because it gets canceled if this function ever ends (which should happen if either the call completed or the original timeout was reached). Unfortunately, I see it get triggered, suggesting that we truly are hung in the `client.NodePrepareResources()` call. We also still never see the call ever complete, suggesting that my manual calls to `conn.Close()` and `cancel()` when the fallback timeout expires don’t trigger the hang to unblock.

```go
func (p *DRAPlugin) NodeUnprepareResources(
        ctx context.Context,
        req *drapbv1.NodeUnprepareResourcesRequest,
        opts ...grpc.CallOption,
) (*drapbv1.NodeUnprepareResourcesResponse, error) {
        logger := klog.FromContext(ctx)
        logger.V(4).Info("Calling NodeUnprepareResource rpc", "request", req)
        logger = klog.LoggerWithValues(logger, "driverName", p.driverName, "endpoint", p.endpoint)
        ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, logger)

        // Force the gRPC connection to be reestablished if necessary
        conn, err := p.getOrCreateGRPCConn()
        if err != nil {
                return nil, err
        }

        // Start the gRPC call with a timeout
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, p.clientCallTimeout)
        defer cancel()

        // Force close the plugin connection if the underlying gRPC call hangs.
        // Wait twice the length of a p.clientCallTimeout.
        fallbackCtx, fallbackCancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*p.clientCallTimeout)
        defer fallbackCancel()

        go func() {
                <-fallbackCtx.Done()
                if fallbackCtx.Err() == context.DeadlineExceeded {
                        logger.V(4).Info("Force closing plugin connection due to hanging rpc", "plugin", p.driverName, "request", req)
                        conn.Close()
                        cancel()
                }
        }()

        var err error
        var response *drapbv1.NodeUnprepareResourcesResponse
        switch p.chosenService {
        case drapbv1beta1.DRAPluginService:
                client := drapbv1beta1.NewDRAPluginClient(p.conn)
                logger.V(4).Info("Calling NodeUnprepareResources from V1Beta1Client")
                response, err = drapbv1beta1.V1Beta1ClientWrapper{DRAPluginClient: client}.NodeUnprepareResources(ctx, req)
        case drapbv1.DRAPluginService:
                client := drapbv1.NewDRAPluginClient(p.conn)
                logger.V(4).Info("Calling NodeUnprepareResources from V1Client")
                response, err = client.NodeUnprepareResources(ctx, req)
        default:
                // Shouldn't happen, validateSupportedServices should only
                // return services we support here.
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("internal error: unsupported chosen service: %q", p.chosenService)
        }
        logger.V(4).Info("Done calling NodeUnprepareResources rpc", "response", response, "err", err)
        return response, err
}
```

* Add a keepalive to the gRPC connection created for the client. I was hoping this would trigger the connection to stay alive so that it never gets a chance to hang. This did not help though, and we see the same issue.

```go
        logger.V(4).Info("Creating new gRPC connection", "target", target)
        conn, err := grpc.NewClient(
                target,
                grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()),
                grpc.WithChainUnaryInterceptor(newMetricsInterceptor(driverName)),
                grpc.WithStatsHandler(mp),
                grpc.WithKeepaliveParams(keepalive.ClientParameters{
                        Time:                30 * time.Second, // Send keepalive pings every 30 seconds
                        Timeout:             5 * time.Second,  // Wait 5 seconds for ping ack
                        PermitWithoutStream: true,             // Send pings even when no active RPCs
                }),
        )
```

* Enable the `ResourceHealthStatus` feature gate. This feature gate is designed to keep the connection alive. It continuously validates the gRPC connection is working and automatically retries stream connection every 5 seconds if it fails. **This fixed the problem(\!)**, but at the cost of having to enable an alpha feature gate. We need something that can be added to the existing code without a feature gate.

```go
        ResourceHealthStatus: {
                {Version: version.MustParse("1.31"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
        },
```

* Force a new connection at the top of every call to `NodePrepareResources` / `NodeUnprepareResources` whenever we detect that the existing connection is unhealthy. This also does not fix the issue, unfortunately. My call to `reconnect()` is never triggered, meaning the state changes I check never happen. I know this because the log within the reconnect call does not appear in the kubelet logs.

And it fails and hangs despite the call timeout:
```
go test -v -run=TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle .
=== RUN   TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle
    dra_plugin_manager.go:366: I0908 07:43:04.359157] DRA registration handler: Creating new gRPC connection target="unix:/tmp/TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle1883222059/001/dra.sock"
    dra_plugin_manager.go:412: I0908 07:43:04.359521] DRA registration handler: Registered DRA plugin driverName="dummy-driver" endpoint="/tmp/TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle1883222059/001/dra.sock" chosenService="v1.DRAPlugin" numPlugins=1
    dra_plugin_manager.go:303: I0908 07:43:04.359549] DRA registration handler: No plugin connected, using latest one driverName="dummy-driver" endpoint="/tmp/TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle1883222059/001/dra.sock"
    dra_plugin_test.go:213: I0908 07:43:04.359580] Waiting for idle connection...
    dra_plugin_manager.go:132: I0908 07:43:04.359958] DRA registration handler: Connection changed driverName="dummy-driver" endpoint="/tmp/TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle1883222059/001/dra.sock" connected=true
    dra_plugin.go:144: I0908 07:43:09.371283] Calling NodePrepareResources rpc driverName="dummy-driver" endpoint="/tmp/TestGRPCConnUsableAfterIdle1883222059/001/dra.sock" request="claims:{namespace:\"dummy-namespace\" uid:\"dummy-uid\" name:\"dummy-claim\"}"
    contexthelper.go:69: 
        INFO: canceling context: call timed out
```

Next step is to reproduce it with less of our boilerplate code, i.e. just using plain gRPC.

According https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/connectivity-semantics-and-api.md, an idle connection should automatically become active again when it is used. That doesn't seem to work here.

Found it:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d9b31d602d833b8a45b31f720eed4534c769772b/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L118

That code is triggered when the connection goes idle. `Connect` then deadlocks - but only in the case of an idle connection. It does not deadlock when the connection is really lost, which is what we had covered by our unit tests already.

The fix is simple:

```patch
diff --git a/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go b/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go
@@ -115,7 +118,12 @@ func (m *monitoredPlugin) HandleConn(_ context.Context, stats grpcstats.ConnStat
        case *grpcstats.ConnEnd:
                // We have to ask for a reconnect, otherwise gRPC wouldn't try and
                // thus we wouldn't be notified about a restart of the plugin.
-               m.conn.Connect()
+               // This must be done in a goroutine because gRPC deadlocks
+               // when called directly from inside HandleConn when a connection
+               // goes idle (and only then). It looks like cc.idlenessMgr.ExitIdleMode
+               // in Connect tries to lock a mutex that is already locked by
+               // the caller of HandleConn.
+               go m.conn.Connect()
        default:
                return
        }
```

This is therefore really a regression, because this code is new in 1.34.

title: [cli-runtime] [client-go] ConfigFlags when set cert/key fields get validation error when merging with kubeconfig data
description:
### What happened?

When using ConfigFlags with CertFile and KeyFile set to override a kubeconfig configuration that contains inline certificate data (ClientCertificateData and ClientKeyData), the configuration merge process fails with validation errors: 

```sh
invalid configuration: [client-cert-data and client-cert are both specified for <user>. client-cert-data will override., client-key-data and client-key are both specified for <user>; client-key-data will override]
```

Also ConfigFlags does not allow to set ClientCertificateData and ClientKeyData.

### What did you expect to happen?

When  user sets CertFile of ConfigFlags expects override value of `overrides.AuthInfo.ClientCertData` to be set nil.
When  user sets KeyFile of ConfigFlags expects override value of `overrides.AuthInfo.ClientKeyData` to be set nil.

And during merge process override value are both taken into account. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) prepare kubeconfig with ClientCertData and ClientKeyData
2) instantiate ConfigFlags with CertFile and KeyFile
3) call to configFlags.ToRESTConfig() -> receive validation error.

```go

				Cluster:  "test-cluster",

			},

title: CRD validation warning on valid formats
description:
### What happened?

In #132532 and #133136 a warning was added for unrecognized formats. However, the `int32`, `int64`, `float`, and `double` formats are flagged ~~and this conflicts with public docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#format which say that these values are supported formats~~. Warning: unrecognized format "int64"
customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/resourcegraphdefinitions.kro.run created

            type: string

            type: object

            description: WarningFormatSpec defines the desired state of

                description: int32 format

                description: int64 format

> Valid

> "intSixtyFour": 9223372036854776000,

I think the "valid" int64 in your example *is* out of range, which means the server will parse it as a double (json is ambiguous, the server [parses as ints until it exceeds int64, then falls back to parsing as a double](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/json/blob/2d320260d730f3842fef7b08d9a807bdbc617824/internal/golang/encoding/json/decode.go#L928-L934)).

That's why the CRD validation of the out-of-range int64 complained about a float ("number").

> If I'm reading this right, we do have actual gaps in validation:
> 
> * Out of range number/float is not validated
> * Out of range integer/int32 is not validated

Yeah, that's what it looks like, and what is catching the int64 / double cases doesn't appear to be format validation at all, but unmarshaling / type validation:
* An integer field > int64 fails int-parsing, so falls back to using float64, which fails type=integer validation.
* A double field > float64 fails parsing completely, and results in a 400 error and never gets to API validation.

Ok, so I think there's two things needed here:

1. Avoid emitting warnings for `type=integer,format={int32,int64}` and `type=number,format={float,double}` per https://swagger.io/docs/specification/v3_0/data-models/data-types/#:~:text=An%20optional%20format%20keyword (and backport this to 1.34)
2. Fix number/float and integer/int32 validation (master / 1.35+ only, most likely)

title: Race condition in kubelet's PodCertsManager might lead to memory leaks
description:
### What happened?

Introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4624cb9bb92186358e001be392e50e5d23b5cdd9, and only observable after enabling the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate.

When https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2825 gets called, it queues PCRs for a given pod to be handled by a `podcertificate.Manager` instance.

However, if the queue keys for these PCRs get async-processed before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2826 is called, the `podcertificate.Manager` will never again attempt to clear its internal state for these PCRs as kept in its `Manager.credStore` map.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet's state gets cleaned for a given pod when the pod is removed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a unit test that runs https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2822, expose the `podcertificate.Manager{}.credStore` variable, and observe what happens to the `credStore` variable when a cached PCR's state is supposed to get removed. Run a couple hundred times to make sure the race condition appears.

### Anything else we need to know?

Discussed at https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C05MW3382US/p1754992465556979

title: Connection leak in cri-client
description:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9eb462ef4a86cc68c545a88392e8b78ddfefec84/staging/src/k8s.io/cri-client/pkg/remote_runtime.go#L83 creates a connection to the specified endpoint, howewer, it is not possible for the caller to later close it. CRI-O uses this method for its internal [health check](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/cb591e06e245d0e2409ed263b1b70f3ab3cf5f8a/server/health.go#L21). As client connections dont get closed, nor do server ones, and then they'll eat up resources.

No memory/connection leaks in client libraries too.

title: Kubelet shutdown manager not properly initialized due to race condition in systemd-logind configuration reloading
description:
### What happened?

Observed error log 
`
kubelet.go:1667] "Failed to start node shutdown manager" err="node shutdown manager was unable to update logind InhibitDelayMaxSec to 30s (ShutdownGracePeriod), current value of InhibitDelayMaxSec (5s) is less than requested ShutdownGracePeriod"
`

And the shutdown inhibitor is not registered to the system so shutdown manager would not be in effect.

The bug seems to be a race condition between systemd-logind config reloading and getting the updated `InhibitDelayMaxSec`. The root cause is the reload command is signaled to systemd-logind with no waiting until the reload is complete.

I am thinking a low cost fix,  rather than properly implementing something to get the reload completion signal, is to just backoff wait up to 5 retries to get the new `InhibitDelayUSec` value

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet shutdown manager should work properly

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Wrote a program trying to reproduce it

```go
package main

import (
        "fmt"
        "math/rand"
        "os"

        "github.com/godbus/dbus/v5"
)

const (
        logindConfDir = "/etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/"
        tempConfFile  = logindConfDir + "99-test-inhibit-delay.conf"
        logindService = "org.freedesktop.login1"
        logindObject  = dbus.ObjectPath("/org/freedesktop/login1")
)

func main() {
        // This program must be run as root to modify systemd config and call D-Bus methods.
        if os.Geteuid() != 0 {
                fmt.Println("This program must be run as root (sudo).")
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        neg, total := 0, 100000
        for i := 0; i < total; i++ {
                if test() {
                        neg++
                }
                if i%500 == 0 {
                        fmt.Printf("Tested %d times, reproduced the bug %d times\n", i, neg)
                }
        }
        fmt.Printf("Tested %d times, reproduced the bug %d times", total, neg)
}

func test() bool {
        newInhibitDelaySec := rand.Intn(100) + 15
        conn, err := dbus.SystemBus()
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to connect to system D-Bus: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
        defer conn.Close()

        if err := os.MkdirAll(logindConfDir, 0755); err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to create logind.conf.d directory: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        confContent := fmt.Sprintf("[Login]\nInhibitDelayMaxSec=%ds\n", newInhibitDelaySec)
        err = os.WriteFile(tempConfFile, []byte(confContent), 0644)
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to write temporary config file: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
        defer os.Remove(tempConfFile)

        obj0 := conn.Object("org.freedesktop.systemd1", dbus.ObjectPath("/org/freedesktop/systemd1"))
        obj1 := conn.Object(logindService, logindObject)

        call := obj0.Call("org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager.KillUnit", 0, "systemd-logind.service", "all", 1)
        if call.Err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Reload call failed: %v\n", call.Err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
        variant, err := obj1.GetProperty("org.freedesktop.login1.Manager.InhibitDelayMaxUSec")
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to get property: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        updatedInhibitDelayUSec, ok := variant.Value().(uint64)
        if !ok {
                fmt.Println("Failed to assert property type to uint64.")
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        expectedUSec := uint64(newInhibitDelaySec * 1_000_000)

        return expectedUSec != updatedInhibitDelayUSec
}
```

, which had pretty low reproduction rate (`Tested 80500 times, reproduced the bug 1 times/Tested 257500 times, reproduced the bug 4 times`) but on real cases, it should significantly higher because the kubelet is started during OS boot period and a lot of churns on systemd so the logind reload takes more time to take effect.

title: CRD conversion webhooks should not be called for unused apiVersions
description:
### What happened?

We have CRDs with multiple apiVersions. Even if the old (non-storage) apiVersions are not used at all we regularly receive conversion requests for them.

We roughly get 1 conversion request for each non-storage apiVersion per kube-apiserver instance for every CR create/update (actually a little bit less than that, but not sure why).

So if we have a CRD with 5 old apiVersions and a cluster with 3 kube-apiservers

=> we get roughly 15 conversion requests for every create/update on a CR (it's slightly less than that - not sure why though)

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect to only get conversion requests when conversion is required, e.g. if a client requests a CR in a different apiVersion than the one in which the object is stored in etcd.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a Kubernetes cluster via kind
```
kind create cluster
```

Deploy the Cluster CRD
```
$ kubectl apply -f ./crd_cluster.yaml
```

<details>

<summary>crd_cluster.yaml</summary>

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  annotations:
    controller-gen.kubebuilder.io/version: v0.17.0
  name: clusters.cluster.x-k8s.io
spec:
  conversion:
    strategy: Webhook
    webhook:
      conversionReviewVersions: ["v1", "v1beta1"]
      clientConfig:
        service:
          namespace: system
          name: webhook-service
          path: /convert
  group: cluster.x-k8s.io
  names:
    kind: Cluster
    listKind: ClusterList
    plural: clusters
    singular: cluster
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - deprecated: true
    name: v1alpha3
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        properties:
          spec:
            properties:
              paused:
                type: boolean
            type: object
        type: object
    served: false
    storage: false
  - deprecated: true
    name: v1alpha4
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        properties:
          spec:
            properties:
              paused:
                type: boolean
            type: object
        type: object
    served: true
    storage: false
  - name: v1beta1
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        properties:
          spec:
            properties:
              paused:
                type: boolean
            type: object
        type: object
    served: true
    storage: true
```

</details>

Deploy the Cluster CR
```
$ kubectl apply -f ./cr_cluster.yaml
```

<details>

<summary>cr_cluster.yaml</summary>

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
metadata:
  name: cluster-1
  namespace: default
```

</details>

Observe kube-apiserver logs

```
$ kubectl -n kube-system logs -f kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane
...
E0204 13:21:54.207206       1 watcher.go:567] failed to prepare current and previous objects: conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1, Kind=Cluster failed: Post "https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s": service "webhook-service" not found
...

E0204 13:30:47.583960       1 cacher.go:478] cacher (clusters.cluster.x-k8s.io): unexpected ListAndWatch error: failed to list cluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4, Kind=Cluster: conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1, Kind=Cluster failed: Post "https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s": service "webhook-service" not found; reinitializing...
W0204 13:30:48.586795       1 reflector.go:569] storage/cacher.go:/cluster.x-k8s.io/clusters: failed to list cluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4, Kind=Cluster: conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1, Kind=Cluster failed: Post "https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s": service "webhook-service" not found
...
E0204 13:30:45.575802       1 cacher.go:478] cacher (clusters.cluster.x-k8s.io): unexpected ListAndWatch error: failed to list cluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha3, Kind=Cluster: conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1, Kind=Cluster failed: Post "https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s": service "webhook-service" not found; reinitializing...
W0204 13:30:46.579452       1 reflector.go:569] storage/cacher.go:/cluster.x-k8s.io/clusters: failed to list cluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha3, Kind=Cluster: conversion webhook for cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1, Kind=Cluster failed: Post "https://webhook-service.system.svc:443/convert?timeout=30s": service "webhook-service" not found
```

Some comments:
* First we deploy a CRD with the following apiVersions:
  * v1alpha3: served: false, storage: false
  * v1alpha4: served: true, storage: false
  * v1beta1: served: true, storage: true
* Then we deploy a v1beta1 Cluster CR
* We can then see in the apiserver logs that the apiserver tries to create a ListWatch for v1alpha3 & v1alpha4
  * This simple example to reproduce the issue doesn't implement an actual conversion webhook, so we simply get errors.
  * If we would implement a conversion webhook the ListWatch would be created successfully and we could observe conversion requests for v1alpha3 / v1alpha4 (as mentioned above roughly for every single create/update of a Cluster CR)
* As not a single CR has been read or written with v1alpha3 or v1alpha4 I would have expected to receive no conversion requests at all. Instead we see a very high number of conversion requests. This problem multiplies with the number of kube-apiserver's.

### Anything else we need to know?

We opened a Slack thread for this issue and did some initial triage: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1736528576393239

While debugging through the apiserver we found the following:
* A GET request to one of our APIs leads to a call of [https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/439d2f7b4028638b3d8d9261bb046c3ba8d9[…]apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/customresource_handler.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/439d2f7b4028638b3d8d9261bb046c3ba8d9bfcb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/customresource_handler.go#L611)
* `getOrCreateServingInfoFor` then iterates through all versions of our CRD and calls customresource.NewStorage for them
* Then a few layers deeper reflectors are created for all versions

So if we understand this correctly the apiserver creates reflectors (with list & watch) for all versions of all CRDs (also independent of if the versions are served or not):
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cff93477-913e-4811-aeca-de7dadbe0a43)

We think these reflectors are then later calling the conversion webhooks:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/36dc7888-95c3-4e2e-89e8-471f2668090a)

@sttts opened a PR with the goal to stop creating ListWatches for unserved versions: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129709

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.32.0
Kustomize Version: v5.5.0
Server Version: v1.32.0
```

title: Eviction manager should evict terminated pods before running pods
description:
### What happened?

Consider two pods are running on the node:
1.  pod with a large image size but in terminated state.
2.  running pod which is utilizing disk space just above the eviction limit.

kubelet's eviction manager will evict the running pod first instead of evicting the terminated pod and cleaning up the image.

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet should evict terminated pods and clean up images first beforing deciding to evict the running pod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a pod with large image size and let it run to completion (you can write some data to writable layers if there's no large image).
2. create a pod with different image but it should utilize disk space until eviction limit.
3. watch kubelet evict the running pod first.

### Anything else we need to know?

I think we should modify our node reclaim funcs to prioritize terminated pods first - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c9092f69fc0c099062dd23cd6ee226bcd52ec790/pkg/kubelet/eviction/helpers.go#L1222

`DeleteAllUnusedContainers()` looks to already delete terminated pods.

I tried running the following pods on my laptop with kind where `eviction-hard` is `nodefs.available<(availableBytes)-1GB`:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  labels:
    run: termpod
  name: termpod
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - sh
    - -c
    - dd if=/dev/random of=largefile bs=1048576 count=500 2>/dev/null
    image: busybox
    name: termcontainer
    resources: {}
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Never
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: null
  labels:
    run: activepod
  name: activepod
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - sh
    - -c
    - for i in `seq 800`; do dd if=/dev/random of=file${i} bs=1048576 count=1 2>/dev/null; sleep .1; done;
    image: busybox
    name: activecontainer
    resources: {}
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Never
```

These pods are expected to work as following:
1. `termpod` gets terminated after consuming 500MB.
2. When `activepod` consumes 500MB, `termpod` is evicted, which means the container and sandbox are deleted in the runtime.
3. `activepod` gets completed without being evicted.

As far as I tried a few times, there were both cases where `activepod` gets succeeded and evicted.

I suspect the disk usage might be updated asynchronously after the terminated pod is deleted so that the summary might has an older value:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f3cbd79db7f0c86a2d3602fdff6b174543d2cf1c/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L477

@hshiina , `DeleteAllUnusedContainers` does not delete terminated pods by default. It deletes terminated pods only if you use the deprecated flag [`minimum-container-ttl-duration`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubelet/app/options/options.go#L313C44-L313C74).

Can you check if you're using that?

> [@hshiina](https://github.com/hshiina) , `DeleteAllUnusedContainers` does not delete terminated pods by default. It deletes terminated pods only if you use the deprecated flag [`minimum-container-ttl-duration`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/cmd/kubelet/app/options/options.go#L313C44-L313C74).
> 
> Can you check if you're using that?

I didn't use `minimum-container-ttl-duration`.

My understanding is:
1. Without `minimum-container-ttl-duration`, all containers that are not running are regarded as evictable no matter when they are created because `minAge` is `0`:
   https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2d0a4f75560154454682b193b42813159b20f284/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_gc.go#L197-L207
2. Then, containers in terminated pods are deleted because `evictNonDeletedPods` is `true`:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2d0a4f75560154454682b193b42813159b20f284/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_gc.go#L237-L238

I verified the behavior mentioned by @hshiina, and effectively the `DeleteAllUnusedContainers` and `DeleteUnusedImages` are already cleaning up the containers belonging to terminated pods.

I tried multiple times, and found that the behavior was consistent when the corresponding image to be deleted was older than the default `minAge` required for an image to be eligible for cleanup. I used the following pods:

#### Terminated pod
This pod should be marked as `Completed` before executing the Running pod, and its image is big enough (4.67GB) to remove disk pressure when the image is cleaned up.
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: android
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: android
    image: cimg/android:2024.11.1-ndk
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 0"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp-volume
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp-volume
    emptyDir: {}
```

#### Runnning pod
This pod writes 10GB of storage, and is expected to continue running even when it causes disk pressure on the node, as the cleaning of the terminated pod frees up enough resources to remove the disk pressure.
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: over-limit
spec:
  containers:
  - name: over-limit
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/largefile bs=1M count=10000 && sleep infinity"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp-volume
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp-volume
    emptyDir: {}
```

title: Confusing use of TooManyRequests error for eviction
description:
### What happened?

When the Kubernetes API server returns a 429 (throttled), the response may include misleading cause information.

We observed that a pod eviction API call received a response that included _**both**_ of the following fragments:

``` json
"responseStatus": {
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "reason": "TooManyRequests",
  "code": 429
},
```

and

``` json
"responseObject": {
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.",
  "reason": "TooManyRequests",
  "details": {
    "causes": [
      {
        "reason": "DisruptionBudget",
        "message": "The disruption budget [elided] needs 11 healthy pods and has 12 currently"
      }
    ]
  },
  "code": 429
},
```
Note that the `message` given above is confusing, as there are more currently healthy pods than the required number.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a request is rejected due to throttling (429 HTTP response), either
* no other error information should be included; or
* the included error information should indicate throttling

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Provoke a 429 HTTP response and inspect the response. 

### Anything else we need to know?

Issue #88535 seems to be similar - it also describes a 429 response where inclusion of a cause resulted in confusion.

### Kubernetes version

Version: 1.20.9


### Cloud provider

Azure Kubernetes Service

```console

$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture
# paste output here
```

comments.text: for PDB

@liggitt , are you sure?

As far as I've been able to work out, the 429 HTTP response is correct and the PDB error is a red herring. 

The PDB error we observed doesn't even make sense, given the number of healthy pods (12) was _more_ than the needed (11):

> The disruption budget [elided] needs 11 healthy pods and has 12 currently

(My experience is that I spent a bunch of time digging into possible causes of the PDB error before realizing that I'd been ignoring the HTTP response code - and once I started paying attention to that, everything started to make sense. Of course, you understand this area far better, I just don't want you to fall into the same trap that I did!)
any message coming back with PDB language in it belongs to sig-apps

It looks like eviction has some creative uses of `TooManyRequests` errors. Why is this conflict error converted to TooManyRequests?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/786316f0b6bb9078cd564ebf5401bb2e9ac7f2a2/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L294-L305

Also this observed generation mismatch (stale cache?):

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/786316f0b6bb9078cd564ebf5401bb2e9ac7f2a2/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L419-L422

Violating the disruption budget is more debatable, but I still don't think a 429 error is right:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/786316f0b6bb9078cd564ebf5401bb2e9ac7f2a2/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L429-L433

> It looks like eviction has some creative uses of `TooManyRequests` errors. Why is this conflict error converted to TooManyRequests?

that was added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94381/files#r507982781 with some discussion there

I think the short answer is we wanted to drive an automatic retry (which the server returning TooManyRequests with a RetryAfter does), and returning a conflict when the user did not set a precondition on the request did not seem correct

`pdb.Status.DisruptionsAllowed = 0` is set as a fail safe when the DesiredHealthy / CurrentHealthy pods can't be calculated so those numbers are not trustworthy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bb838fde5bb9df4becb9fd267c84759be9f5400f/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go#L944-L962

If the `type=DisruptionAllowedCondition, status=False` condition is present, we should probably use the message from that condition rather than the pdb.Status.DesiredHealthy and pdb.Status.CurrentHealthy fields
I will work on this issue :)

> > It looks like eviction has some creative uses of `TooManyRequests` errors. Why is this conflict error converted to TooManyRequests?
> 
> that was added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94381/files#r507982781 with some discussion there
> 
> I think the short answer is we wanted to drive an automatic retry (which the server returning TooManyRequests with a RetryAfter does), and returning a conflict when the user did not set a precondition on the request did not seem correct

My apologies, @liggitt , I ran into this issue only today trying to understand why my k8s client all of a sudden gets "rate limited".
I disagree not 100% but 1000% with the usage of the 429 HTTP status code here. IMHO this is not a "creative" usage of it, but actually an ABUSE of it. It looks like the intelligent API server tries to drive the stupid clients into a certain behaviour, and I am sorry to tell you - it is neither its responsibility nor its job. Let the clients decide what they want to do when requests fail.
The reason a pod cannot be evicted due to PDB is a classic [409 Conflict](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/409): `request conflict with the current state of the target resource`. It doesn't matter the client "did not set a precondition", this is an excuse, you don't have a 5xx status code to describe conflicts. The only thing you have is 409. This is NEVER EVER a 429.
In my case, all I try to do is to perform a pod eviction `in All dry-run mode`, to see if it's possible. If it is, evict the pod.
I set up a test case with a Deployment of 2 replicas and PDB with min healthy of 2. Maybe stupid, but that's something k8s API gladly allows. The VERY FIRST `/eviction` REQUEST gets a 429 which actually can never be recovered, this will be an endless loop with 429s... Thank you for this, API server.
It gets worse if the client uses an HTTP retry library - like [this](https://github.com/hashicorp/go-retryablehttp). These libraries are trained to retry to a **genuine** 429 due to rate-limiting. This required ideally the `Retry-after` HTTP response header (which the current API server doesn't even bother to set).
So all I am left with is to have to analyze the response for a 429 (which should never ever have been done as it's not part of the HTTP 429 "standard") i.s.o. the response header. This is not ugly, this is FUGLY.
Please just return a standard 409 like us mortals would return. Thank you.

title: kubernetes 1.34: The result of kubectl get cgroupDriver from the node configz is not right.
description:
### What happened?

Issue: The result of kubectl get cgroupDriver from the node configz is not right. 

Test bed:  
containerd v2.1.4
kubelet v1.34.1

Test:
Set "SystemdCgroup = true" in containerd;   
Remove cgroupDriver from kubelet config;  

Result: 
From kubelet logs:
```
# journalctl -u kubelet -f | grep -i cgroup
... kubelet[575214]: I1002 16:39:50.418991  575214 server.go:1423] "Using cgroup driver setting received from the CRI runtime" cgroupDriver="systemd"
```
Using kubectl to get cgroupDriver from the node, the result is not right, it showed "cgroupfs" like below:
```
# kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/testnode/proxy/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.cgroupDriver'
"cgroupfs"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

let "kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<testnode>/proxy/configz | jq '.kubeletconfig.cgroupDriver'   "
to show right cgroupDriver name. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Test bed:  
containerd v2.1.4
kubelet v1.34.1

title: APF significantly under-reporting seats for watches without RV
description: From a recent study, we observed API server’s CPU usage (on a 96 vCPU instance) vs "current_executing_seats" was extremely skewed: Computing the CPU usage/seat during that time, it swings quite a bit (0.4-2.0): For that period in the middle where CPU usage/seat is relatively high, majority of the seat usage comes from "workload-low" priority level: Dissecting it further, we can correlate the usage to watch calls from a particular client: These were all watches with RV unset (could've also been RV set to 0): Such calls are expensive upfront due to initial "Add" events being generated for the entire collection, as required by our [API semantics](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch). **So why do they have such low seat usage?** The API server's seat calculation logic intends to count watch calls that don't need to send init events at the lowest cost. It does this by checking SendInitialEvents parameter isn't set to true ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8471a6f5b00e93409422f1a39e4655651c105a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/request/list_work_estimator.go#L91-L95)). But that misses the RV unset/0 cases (i.e. legacy watches), under reporting their penalty too. We need to exclude those from incorrectly being assigned minimum seats. **What's the problem with low seat usage?** APF doesn't provide enough protection to CPU usage (as seen above) if a barrage of such legacy watch requests strike the API server. cc @MikeSpreitzer @wojtek-t @serathius - I can send out a fix for this if no objections.

title: kubectl events --for does not show events where involvedObject.apiVersion is missing
description:
### What happened?

When running `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`, some events (such as OOMKilling events from kernel-monitor node-problem-detector) do not appear, even though they are visible in `kubectl get events`. Upon investigation, these missing events have an `involvedObject` without an `apiVersion` field.

Example:

This event is **not** shown by `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`:

```yaml
kind: Event
count: 1074
eventTime: null
firstTimestamp: "2025-10-07T22:00:52Z"
involvedObject:
  kind: Node
  name: XXXXXXXXXX
  uid: XXXXXXXXXX
# apiVersion is missing
message: ...
reason: OOMKilling
source:
  component: kernel-monitor
```

But this event **is** shown:
```yaml
kind: Event
count: 11
eventTime: null
firstTimestamp: "2025-10-09T01:19:49Z"
involvedObject:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Node
  name: XXXXXXXXXX
  uid: df71ea00-f008-41b2-bb6e-a21466b7bf38
# apiVersion is present
message: ...
reason: DisruptionBlocked
source:
  component: karpenter
```

The relevant code in `kubectl events` sets a field selector:
```go
listOptions.FieldSelector = fields.AndSelectors(
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.kind", o.forGVK.Kind),
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.apiVersion", o.forGVK.GroupVersion().String()),
    fields.OneTermEqualSelector("involvedObject.name", o.forName)).String()
```
Events missing `involvedObject.apiVersion` are excluded from the results.

### What did you expect to happen?

Events for the specified Node should be shown even if their `involvedObject.apiVersion` field is missing, as long as `kind` and `name` match.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install node-problem-detector in the cluster
2. Generate a node event with OOMKilling (e.g., run a memory-hogging process on a node).
3. Ensure an event is created that is visible in `kubectl get events` but missing `involvedObject.apiVersion`.
4. Run `kubectl events --for Node/<node-name>`
5. Observe that the event does not appear, but it does with `kubectl get events`.

### Anything else we need to know?

This bug can be worked around by omitting `--for`, but that makes filtering by object impossible. The filtering logic should be more tolerant to missing fields.

$ kubectl version

title: DRA: Device Taints: tolerating NoExecute is broken
description:
### What happened?

When a ResourceClaim is affected by a NoExecute taint and has a toleration for that taint, then the scheduler schedules a Pod using that ResourceClaim correctly. But it does not copy the toleration into the allocation result and then the eviction controller evicts the Pod more or less instantaneously before it even starts to run.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod should run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See description.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Kubernetes >= 1.33 where the feature was introduced.

title: capz-windows-master job does not report tested kubernetes version
description:
This makes it much harder to determine if a kubernetes regression was involved in test failures.

Jobs that report the tested version allow dragging between the passing/failing runs to launch a github diff link.

This metadata is missing for the CAPZ job, you can only find the versions by digging through the logs.

title: API Server returns panic message to caller when Creating CronJob with Some Invalid Schedule Format
description:
### What happened?

API Server panics when creating a CronJob with an invalid schedule format like `"TZ=0"`. This causes a slice bounds out of range error in the robfig/cron parser.

### What did you expect to happen?

API Server should return a proper validation error instead of panic.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a CronJob YAML with invalid schedule:
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-backup
spec:
  schedule: "TZ=0"  # Invalid: missing space and cron expression
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: alpine
            command: ["/bin/sh"]
            args: ["-c", "echo 'Starting backup...' && date"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

2. Apply the YAML:
```bash
kubectl apply -f test-cron-job.yaml
```

**Actual behavior:**
The API server panics with:

error: error when creating "test-cron-job.yaml": Post "https://127.0.0.1:56870/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/default/cronjobs?fieldManager=kubectl-client-side-apply&fieldValidation=Strict": stream error: stream ID 7; INTERNAL_ERROR; received from peer

title: Preemption process does not leave a trait in the scheduler cache causing a race
description:
### What happened?

The preemption process that is initiated by the scheduler does not leave the immediate trait in the cache. Due to a race, a pod may come back to the scheduling queue before the in-memory state gets updated (receives a notification about a pod being deleted or marked for deletion DeletionTimestamp != nil) and start the same preemption process again.

Whenever the preemption process identifies a pod eligible for preemption, but learns the pod does no longer exist, it immediately puts the preemptor back to scheduling queue (since it may never receive a notification that wakes it up from the unschedulable queue) and the process repeats in a tight loop, each time producing a pod delete api call.

The factor that triggers this issue is the fact that when a pod being preempted is in the binding process, the scheduler lets it finish the process and IGNORES pod delete notifications, waiting for this async binding process to fail. This creates quite a wide window making the problem very likely to happen in a specific use case, like autoscaling when initial pods jump into nodes they were not intended to and need to be preempted right after). Large number of outgoing api-calls (to delete non-existing pod) generates a big load on the api-server and may generate a snowball effect.

The issue itself exists from a long time, but the PR which closed the loop by activating preemptor pod on failure was added to 1.34 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/133213

### What did you expect to happen?

The information about a non-existing pod should be reflected in the in-memory cache to cut that loop.

It could be either recorded right after pod delete was accepted or even better whenever any attempt to delete it failed (non-existing pod)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We haven't managed to reproduce it in isolation

title: AssumeCache may detect the PersistentVolume update later than the scheduler's event handlers
description:
### What happened?

Let's say we have a scenario where Pod is rejected waiting for a PersistentVolume to be available.
When the PersistentVolume status is updated to `Available`, the scheduler is notified via event handlers.

One of such handlers, in [eventhandling.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L566) is responsible for triggering the Pod's scheduling retry. In this case, the reason is valid, so the Pod is placed in the activeQ (or backoffQ) and then taken to the scheduling.

However, during the (pre)filtering of VolumeBinding plugin, the PersistentVolume objects are [listed](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L825) from the plugin's AssumeCache, which have its own set of the [event handlers](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L208-L214). If these handlers receive the PV update event later than the main scheduler's handlers, VolumeBinding takes the decision based on an old data, e.g. a PersistentVolume with an old state. As a result, the Pod is [rejected](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/18c188467d8ae00042b61f82aa159094336b657e/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L885) and goes back to the scheduling queue.

Ultimately, there won't be any event that would wake up such Pod again, so it will wait indefinitely (precisely, it will be retried by the flushing mechanism that we would like to eventually remove).

This behavior causes the `volumescheduling` integration test to flake: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#integration-master

### What did you expect to happen?

VolumeBinding should have a consistent view of PersistentVolumes with the main scheduler's event handlers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the integration tests with low parallelism:
```sh
KUBE_INTEGRATION_TEST_MAX_CONCURRENCY=2 make test-integration WHAT="test/integration/volumescheduling" KUBE_TEST_ARGS="-run TestVolumeBindingRescheduling"
```

title: Kubelet Volume Manager can erroneously mark volume as unmounted.
description:
### What happened?

We observed an edge case where an API server transient issue can cause a volume to be marked as unmounted in the volume manager's ASW, and making the subsequent `NodeVolumeUnstage` calls to fail due to dangling publish mounts.

The sequence of events is:
1. A map volume operation is kicked off.
2. The API server has a transient issue, causing the map volume operation to fail with `Error: MapVolume.MarkVolumeAsMounted failed while expanding volume for volume $PVC`. This error happens after the `MapPodDevice` (and therefore the `NodePublishVolume`) call has already succeeded. This causes the volume mount to be marked as uncertain and the map to be requeued.
3. When the operation retries,  the api server issue causes the MapPodDevice to fail with `blockMapper.publishVolumeForBlock failed to get NodePublishSecretRef`
4. This error causes `markVolumeErrorState` to be called. The logic here[0] falls into a branch that marks the volume as unmounted in ASW, since the mount is marked uncertain.
5. At this point the pod is deleted, so the map operation doesn't happen again. Since the volume is marked unmounted, the VM reconciler doesn't call unpublish for this pod and volume pair.

[0] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/56dd5ab10ff19aa9ebe438122a00472c4135de23/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L819

### What did you expect to happen?

All volumes are unpublished correctly after the pod is deleted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Once `MapPodDevice` completes, trigger pod deletion and inject API failures. This should cause the pod to be deleted without unpublish being called.

> I'm not sure about that. That node status isn't about cluster-level resources.

> I suspect it is more because the kubelet cannot distinguish between "device plugin temporarily down" and "permanently removed".

It's not that sophisticated, at least to my knowledge. When plugin deregistered or disconnected, Kubelet sets all its devices as `Unhealthy`, but includes them into the node status' `Capacity`. @yliaog 
> node.status.Allocatable/Capacity is owned by kubelet, hence i think so, though i have not verified it. @bart0sh did you have a chance to verify it?

So far I've changed Kubelet code to set both fields to 0 when plugin is unregistered and they stay unchanged for a long time. After that I went further - changed the code to stop publishing those fields if they're set to 0 and they've disappeared from the node status. That worked well.

However, I suspect that it was a design decision to publish them and also count Unhealthy devices as capacity to make them visible. For example if Allocatable is set to 0 and Capacity to 2, educated user/admin would understand that there are 2 unhealthy devices on the node and most probably it means that device plugin is disconnected.

@yliaog No, it was not a design decision. [Device Plugin KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3573-device-plugin) explicitly states that 
```
In general we expect Kubelet to remove any devices that are owned by
the failed device plugin from the node capacity.
We also expect node allocatable to be equal to node capacity.
```
which is good for us as we can consider current Kubelet behaviour as a bug and fix it.

[@ffromani](https://github.com/ffromani) [@swatisehgal](https://github.com/swatisehgal) [@SergeyKanzhelev](https://github.com/SergeyKanzhelev) Is it correct assumption?

I can only quickly comment before I'm going OOO for the full next week (till Sep 1).
This is likely correct, and there is no clear decisive record of why it is implemented like that. To be reasonnably sure, we need to reconstruct history from comments (both design docs at time) and reviews. Is not unheard that a [very early implementation bug survived till today,](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119423#issuecomment-2934790530) and I won't be surprised if we find more instances along the way.

Another main problem is this behavior has been with us since many years. It's very likely someone depends on it in a way we can't imagine (Hyrum's law in full swing). So, albeit I stress that the suggested behavior looks better from every angle we can think of, we need to be super careful about the fix.

I think we need to carefully address these 2 items before we can move on.
And, to be redundant: I agree and I like much more if kubelet clears the extended resources as proposed.

@ffromani Thank you for the detailed answer! To trigger the discussion I've submitted [REDACTED] so we can discuss it further. The change is simple, but I agree that we need to be careful with it due to the reasons you've explained.
@yliaog While we're discussing the fix (which can take long, I suspect), can you give us more details about the issues the current behaviour creates for the extended resources support for DRA?

> if kubelet keeps the extended resources from uninstalled device plugin in node.status.Allocatable: 0, then admin should restart the kubelet to clear it.

@klueska said that restarting the kubelet does *not* clear the status.

> can you give us more details about the issues the current behaviour creates for the extended resources support for DRA?

I [believe](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3204285168) updating a node from device plugin to DRA does not work unless the admin also manually fixes the status.

I agree that fixing kubelet is going to take time. Even if gets fixed, due to version skew clusters might use an older kubelet without the change. We should also look into fixing this in the scheduler. I think it should be safe to try with DRA when `allocatable` is zero: if the scheduler was trying to schedule without DRA, it would simply fail. With DRA there is at least a chance that it works.

> I think it should be safe to try with DRA when allocatable is zero

zero capacity and zero allocatable even safer. It means that plugin either unregistered or disconnected **at least** [5 minutes ago](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.34/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/types.go#L116-L120).

> I https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133488#issuecomment-3204285168 updating a node from device plugin to DRA does not work unless the admin also manually fixes the status.

I'm guessing here, but stopping Kubelet, removing its checkpoint file and starting it again should do the trick as well.

> zero capacity and zero allocatable even safer.

Safer in which sense? What problem does waiting for 5 minutes avoid?

If `allocatable` dropped to zero only because the device driver temporarily got stopped (e.g. for an update), then it's still safe to try scheduling with DRA because there won't be DRA devices for the node, because those are still owned by the device driver.

> Safer in which sense?

In a sense that there are more chances that the scheduled workload will be successfully executed on the node. We don't support running both DRA and DP on the same node, do we?

> In a sense that there are more chances that the scheduled workload will be successfully executed on the node.

I think it's the other way around. If `allocatable` is zero, scheduling is guaranteed to fail unless we try to use DRA. Trying with DRA immediately *increases* the chances that scheduling will succeed. Waiting for `capacity` to become zero is *reducing* the chances.

> We don't support running both DRA and DP on the same node, do we?

Not for the same hardware.

> i see is it may cause application operators confusion, they see their pods are scheduled to a node with allocatable == 0.

But only if the DRA driver has been installed, right? Why would this be confusing? The admin clearly wants to manage the hardware with DRA, so scheduling the pod is what they want.

title: After getting UserNamespaces configured and setting idsPerPod, the uid/gid maps inside containers are not seeing the settings propagate
description:
### What happened?

Now that I have the UserNamespaces working thanks to the documentation updates in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132966, I have reconfigured my kubelet on each node to have `idsPerPod: 1048576`. However containers are not seeing the change and are limited to `65536` ids in their maps.

The process followed was:

* Edit the kubelet-configmap in kube-system to add the following:
```
userNamespaces:
  idsPerPod: 1048576
```

* Run `sudo kubeadm upgrade node phase kubelet-config`
* Run `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Check that the setting has propagated to each node:
```
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/green02/proxy/configz" | yq -p json -o yaml | grep idsPerPod

    idsPerPod: 1048576

```

However when I hop into a usernamespaced pod on a kubelet with this config - I see the following:

```shell
cat /proc/self/uid_map
          0    5898240      65536 
```

So I can see the UID is remapped, but there's only 65536 assigned to the pod, even after deleting it an having it recreated. I'm missing something here and I do not see the answers I need in docs.

Open questions:
1. How does this propagate to the containers? Should I automatically see the new value in column 3 of the uid_map?
2. I notice the docs state that this id setting is _per pod_ - so what is the implication of ids per container in a multi container pod? Do I need to multiply up for that? Or is the limit in fact _per container_ and the naming here is misleading?
3. What is missing from the document here to get the e2e configuration working for a pod?

Details:
* `kubeadm`, `kubectl`, `kubelet` and `cri-o` at version `1.33.2`
* Baremetal hosts are Debian 12 running backport kernel `6.12.32-1~bpo12+1 (2025-06-21) x86_64`

Context:
I am trying to run a buildkit container in a UserNamespace, and it cannot write to the `uid_map` - After trying `procMount: Unmasked`, ensuring the container is unconfined, and even marking it privileged the process keeps failing to start with `newuidmap: write to uid_map failed: Operation not permitted` and all evidence is pointing to the id allotment to the usernamespace being too small.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that the `uid_map` and `gid_map` in the `/proc` mount of the containers would have an allocation of `1048576` ids.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Install Debian 12
* Install Kernel 6.12.* from backports to bring in supported features needed for this added in kernel 6.3
* Install crio, kubeadm, kubelet and kubectl version 1.33.2 as per the kubeadm cluster creation docs
* Install `uidmap` package via apt
* Configure kubelet user for submapping: `sudo adduser --system --no-create-home --disabled-login --group kubelet kubelet`
* Add following line to both `/etc/subgid` and `/etc/subuid` as per documentation: `kubelet:65536:7208960`
* Restart kubelet or restart node
* Edit the `kubelet-config` in `kube-system` and add:
    ```
    userNamespaces:
      idsPerPod: 1048576
    ```
* Run `sudo kubeadm upgrade node phase kubelet-config`
* Run `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Check that the setting has propagated to each node:
    ```
    kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/green02/proxy/configz" | yq -p json -o yaml | grep idsPerPod
    
        idsPerPod: 1048576
    
    ```
* Create a simple pod with `hostUsers: false`
    ```yaml
    ---
    kind: Pod
    apiVersion: v1
    metadata:
      name: admin-pod
    spec:
      hostUsers: false
      containers:
        - name: test
          image: debian:12
          # Write to a file inside our NFS
          command: ["sleep", "999999"]
    
    ```
* Check the resulting `uid_map` and `gid_map`:
    ```shell
    routhinator@routhinator-desktop [06:21:25] [~/projects/routh-forgejo/routh-ca/cluster-config/util] [main *]
    -> % kubectl exec -it admin-pod -- cat /proc/self/uid_map    (⎈|kubernetes-admin@red-squadron:default) 
             0    4849664      65536
    
    routhinator@routhinator-desktop [06:22:09] [~/projects/routh-forgejo/routh-ca/cluster-config/util] [main *]
    -> % kubectl exec -it admin-pod -- cat /proc/self/gid_map    (⎈|kubernetes-admin@red-squadron:default) 
             0    4849664      65536
    ```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

routhinator@red-leader01:~$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.33.2
Kustomize Version: v5.6.0
Server Version: v1.33.2

title: Kubelet's e2e tests need a new mechanism for private image pull tests
description:
### What happened?

Current private image pull e2e tests for kubelet rely on hardcoded credentials to a public repo that is getting decommissioned as a part of https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/issues/1469. These tests will permafail once that happens.

### What did you expect to happen?

comments.text: @BenTheElder what is the timeline for this? Is it absolutely critical for 1.33 or we can do it later?

TLDR: no

---

> @BenTheElder what is the timeline for this?

We are not setting any timeline ourselves, but the existing usage is an unfunded liability.

SIG K8s Infra is not going to repeat this on community infra with having a hardcoded service account baked into the tests that must remain valid for a publicly reachable SaaS endpoint (!), this is not sustainable to guarantee. It's amazing it has worked this long.

Nobody at Google is staffing this either, and the existing endpoints are not owned by SIG K8s Infra.

I don't currently have direct control over these, and nobody has responded to previously raising this repeatedly, while it only impacts a handful of tests for pulling private images, so I haven't been planning to do anything further either way.

> Is it absolutely critical for 1.33 or we can do it later?

It's not tied to 1.33, though GCR turndown is ~now, and we have to hope somebody went in and migrated this to AR to keep it functional for now (and hope the GCR enabled service account still continues to work).

My previous suggestion was an in-cluster registry, deployed by the tests, with some trivial image (pause?) and fixed credentials  pre-populated. 

The details may be tricky for portability though, it might have to be hostPort on a particular node or something like that to guarantee reachability by the runtime.

Not that cri-proxy would be less tricky to deploy portably.

It's possible to check if migrated, but we'll have to dig up the specific registries, and like everyone else code freeze is busy.

I outlined one way to check here: https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15199#issuecomment-2637803054

But either way:
- **This can likely wait another release or two or five**
- **This is bound to break eventually, probably without notice**, and when it does we're not going to copy-paste the unsupportable approach, so if anyone is invested in private image pull functionality, finding a better alternative ahead of time would be a good plan

This is currently slated to break in two weeks, I've requested an extension but we have to stop depending on this.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132882 seemed closely related.
FYI @kubernetes/sig-node-bugs
ok, one week is left...
I don't think we will be able to fix it today before code freeze. But maybe we will be able to get exception for test-only update next week

This test: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e_node/runtime_conformance_test.go#L53 should be easy to switch to use cri proxy instead of the "real" registry.

This test https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/common/node/runtime.go#L286 cannot be tested with the cri proxy. We can either try to create a "real" registry on the fly. Alternatively maybe we can fake the registry by deploying some host network enabled DaemonSet that will expose the registry endpoint on some localhost port. I wonder wht you think @BenTheElder on using this approach for cluster tests?
Another thing - we may limit tests to e2e_node-only. Since tests in common are not marked as conformance, we can remove them.

2. run the registry once, run a proxy daemonset on every host just to expose it as a hostport to the CRI reliably

there's also a third approach where instead of a proxy daemonset you use a clusterIP service but that's harder to make portable ...

We could possibly locally, in-cluster run something like the [CNCF distribution registry](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/). It seems to be quite easy to deploy and takes the [good old htpasswd ](https://distribution.github.io/distribution/about/deploying/#native-basic-auth) as an input for authn config.
I'm not sure which networks are available to the nodes, service network would be the easiest but I guess if that's not an option, having the service exposed via HostIP might be somewhat ok?

The registry would have to be fed some images somehow, too. I haven't done much around actually working with the OCI artifacts, but I guess the simplest thing would be to just do a couple HTTP calls as described in https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/registry/latest/#tag/pull (replacing docker specifics with standard OCI).
Perhaps something like https://github.com/containers/oci-fetch/tree/master, but simpler, more single-purpose built.

title: Pod Crashloop backoff requeue issues
description:
When stepping through the pod crashloop backoff implementation, I noticed a few issues:

1. Backoff errors are unsuccessfully suppressed:
  - This code is non-functional, since there will always be a non-error result present (`ConfigPodSandbox`) with a nil error: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf4fbe524ca1479607a4880949a032064556f76/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1964-L1971
2. The propogated backoff error means that the pod worker always immediately requeues the pod: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf4fbe524ca1479607a4880949a032064556f76/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1495-L1497
  - If the backoff error were suppressed, then the default 1m sync frequency would be used, which would cause very long initial backoffs.

The result of these issues are:
1. Log spam: `E0301 01:06:01.286649    1869 pod_workers.go:1294] "Error syncing pod, skipping" err="failed to \"StartContainer\" for \"alpine\" with CrashLoopBackOff: \"back-off 5m0s restarting failed container=alpine pod=restarting-pod_default(ca0d5836-1435-497e-9a41-547fbcc10484)\"" pod="default/restarting-pod" podUID=ca0d5836-1435-497e-9a41-547fbcc10484` get's logged in a frequent loop
2. Kubelet does unnecessary work to reexamine pods and containers in backoff
3. (minor) the error retry period is 10s, which adds up to 10s to the backoff time

I think the ideal fix is to propagate the backoff retry time up from SyncPod [1] to the pod worker [2], so that the pod can be requeued with the exact (jittered) right amount of retry time. One option is to use a custom error type to encapsulate the backoff time, which I started working on here: https://github.com/tallclair/kubernetes/commit/5d89eb2538cc8929540476f436d4a1b92c9babee

Of course, there is very little test coverage across these code paths too.

[1]: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf4fbe524ca1479607a4880949a032064556f76/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1325
[2]: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf4fbe524ca1479607a4880949a032064556f76/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1484

title: `RelaxedServiceNameValidation` feature gate does not cover ingress `spec.defaultBackend`
description:
### What happened?

The `RelaxedServiceNameValidation` feature gate implementation in `allowRelaxedServiceNameValidation()` might be incomplete. It checks service names in `spec.rules` but does not check `spec.defaultBackend.service.name`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go#L701

This creates inconsistent behavior: Ingresses with relaxed service names in rules can be updated, but those with relaxed names only in defaultBackend cannot.

### What did you expect to happen?

The feature gate should consistently handle relaxed service name validation for both `spec.rules` and `spec.defaultBackend`. When the feature gate is disabled, existing Ingresses with RFC 1123-compliant but RFC 1035-noncompliant service names (e.g., "1-default-service") should remain updatable regardless of whether those names appear in `rules` or `defaultBackend`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate
2. Create Ingress with defaultBackend with a service name starting with a digit
3. Disable RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate
4. Attempt to update this Ingress
5. The update fails because the old service name starts with a digit.

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy namespace lookup raced newly created namespaces, produces spurious "namespace not found" rejections
description:
### What happened?

When creating new workload (observed with Deployment and StatefulSet) immediately after creating its namespace, there is a possibility that watch case has not yet caught up to the new namespace existing.

Naively, this would result in frequent failures, but apiserver guards against this by falling back to live client when namespace was `NotFound`. Example: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ab3e83f73424a18f298a0050440af92d2d7c4720/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/predicates/namespace/matcher.go#L88

The issue happens infrequently but can be forced by overriding informer lister to always return NotFound for a specific namespace (see repro instructions below). This way, the call to informer's lister would always fail, while the call to client would remain unaffected - this would force the fallback path, ensuring it is present.

### What did you expect to happen?

No 404 errors when creating StatefulSets in existing namespaces - even immediately after ns creation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
@@ -20,7 +20,6 @@ package v1

 import (
        corev1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
-       errors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        labels "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels"
        listers "k8s.io/client-go/listers"
        cache "k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache"
@@ -47,17 +46,3 @@ type namespaceLister struct {
 func NewNamespaceLister(indexer cache.Indexer) NamespaceLister {
        return &namespaceLister{listers.New[*corev1.Namespace](indexer, corev1.Resource("namespace"))}
 }
-
-// Get retrieves the Namespace from the index for a given name.
-// Objects returned here must be treated as read-only.
-// This method overrides the embedded Get to add custom logic.
-func (nl *namespaceLister) Get(name string) (*corev1.Namespace, error) {
-       // 1. Check if the requested namespace is "lalala"
-       if name == "lalala" {
-               // 2. Return not found error if it is
-               return nil, errors.NewNotFound(corev1.Resource("namespace"), name)
-       }
-       // 3. Otherwise, use the parent implementation from the embedded ResourceIndexer
-       return nl.ResourceIndexer.Get(name)
-}
-
```

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Apply the diff above to apiserver code.
  2. Set up a cluster using that apiserver.
  3. Create the namespace "lalala"
  4. Create a StatefulSet in that namespace
  5. Observe the request failing with 404 - it should succeed despite the damaged lister code

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Based on our (limited) set of observations, we believe the regression happened between 1.32 and 1.33

### Cloud provider

Observations were made in GKE

### OS version

N/A

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicies that use a CRD with a property of type=object and additionalProperties=true in matchConstraints crash kube-controller-manager
description:
### What happened?

A CRD that includes an object property defined as `type: object` and `additionalProperties: true` is used in a `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` in the `matchConstraints` field.

As soon as the `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` is created, the `validatingadmissionpolicystatus` controller in `kube-controller-manager` does type-checking on the resource specified in the `matchConstraints` field and panics when it tries to type-check the problematic object property.

The `kube-controller-manager` keeps crashing after a restart, when it reconciles `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` objects.

See the attached [log.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23369749/log.txt) for the stacktrace.

### What did you expect to happen?

Type-checking of the `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` either succeeds or fails, `kube-controller-manager` does not panic or crash.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add the supplied [crd.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23369934/crd.yaml) and [validating-admission-policy.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23369933/validating-admission-policy.yaml) to a kubernetes cluster.

As soon as the `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` is submitted, `kube-controller-manager` keeps crashing.
